Bālavagga Bhayasutta (The Discourse on Fear) “Monks, there are these three fears that arise from within oneself. What three? The fear of being reborn in hell, the fear of being reborn as an animal, and the fear of being reborn in the realm of ghosts. These, monks, are the three fears that arise from within oneself.”
(AN 3.1, PTS AN i 101) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Whatever calamities arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise man.”
Whatever misfortunes arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise man. Just as, monks,
a fire released from a reed-thicket or a grass-thicket burns even gabled houses— those plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind,
with doors bolted and windows closed— even so, monks, whatever fears arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Whatever misfortunes arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Whatever calamities arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Thus, monks, the fool is full of peril, while the wise man is free from peril.
The fool is beset by calamity; the wise person is free from calamity.
The fool is beset by misfortune; the wise person is free from misfortune.
Monks, there is no fear arising from the wise person, no calamity arising from the wise person, and no misfortune arising from the wise person.
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
'Having avoided those three qualities by which a fool is to be known, we shall undertake and abide in those three qualities by which a wise person is to be known.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
First. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.2 1.
Bālavagga (The Chapter on Fools)
The Discourse on Characteristics (Lakkhaṇasutta):
“Monks, a fool is characterized by his actions; a wise person is characterized by his actions. Wisdom is what shines through one’s deeds.”
“Monks, one who possesses three qualities should be known as a fool.
Which three?
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.”
“Monks, one who possesses these three qualities should be known as a fool.
Monks, one who possesses three qualities should be known as a wise person.
Which three?”
By good conduct of body, by good conduct of speech, and by good conduct of mind.
By these three qualities, monks, a wise person is to be known.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

“Bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Having avoided those three qualities by which a fool is to be known, we will undertake and abide in those three qualities by which a wise person is to be known.
This is the second [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.3 1.

Bālavagga Cintīsutta – The Discourse on Thinking “Monks, there are these three kinds of thinking. What three? Thinking that is accompanied by sensual lust, thinking that is accompanied by ill will, and thinking that is accompanied by cruelty. These, monks, are the three kinds of thinking.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, and manifestations of a fool. What are the three? [The Buddha said:]”
In this case, monks, a fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds.
If, monks, this fool were not one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds, how would the wise know him, thinking:
‘This worthy person is a fool, an untrue man’?
But because, monks, a fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds, therefore the wise know him:
"This venerable one is a fool, an untrue man.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a fool, the marks of a fool, the manifestations of a fool.
“Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person, marks of a wise person, and attributes of a wise person.
What are the three?
Here, monks, a wise person is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-performed deeds.”
If, monks, this wise man were not one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds, how would the wise know him as:
"This venerable one is a wise person, a true man"?
But because, monks, the wise man is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds, therefore the wise know him as such.
‘This worthy person is wise, a true man.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a wise person, the marks of a wise person, the footprints of a wise person.
Therefore, monks, ... [as before].
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.4 1.
Bālavagga (The Chapter on Fools)
The Discourse on Transgressions:
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses three qualities is to be known as a fool.
Which three? [The Buddha continued:]”

One does not see a transgression as a transgression; having seen a transgression as a transgression, one does not make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma; and when another confesses a transgression, one does not accept it in accordance with the Dhamma.
By these three qualities, monks, a fool is to be known.
Monks, by three qualities a wise person is to be known.
Which three?

One sees a transgression as a transgression; having seen a transgression as a transgression, one makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma; and when another confesses a transgression, one accepts it in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is by possessing these three qualities, monks, that a person should be known as wise.
Therefore, in this case … [as before] … The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.5
1. The Chapter on the Foolish (Bālavagga) The Discourse on Improper Attention (Ayonisosutta):
“Monks, one who possesses three qualities should be known as a fool.”
Which three?

He asks questions improperly; he answers questions improperly; and when another has answered a question properly with well-rounded words and phrases that are smooth and coherent, he does not express his approval.
By these three qualities, monks, a fool is to be known.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses three qualities should be known as wise.
Which three?

He asks a question methodically; he answers a question methodically; and when another has answered a question methodically with well-rounded words and phrases that are coherent and relevant, he expresses his appreciation. Possessing these three qualities, one should be known as wise.”
“Monks, one who possesses these three qualities should be known as wise.
Therefore, in this regard… [as before]… Fifth.”
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.6 1.

Bālavagga Akusalasutta “Monks, there are these three unwholesome roots. What three? The unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion. These, monks, are the three unwholesome roots.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses three qualities is to be known as a fool.
Which three?
Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and unwholesome mental action.”
“Monks, one who possesses these three qualities should be known as a fool.
Monks, one who possesses three qualities should be known as a wise person.
Which three?”
By wholesome bodily action, by wholesome verbal action, and by wholesome mental action.
It is by being endowed with these three qualities, monks, that a wise person is to be known.
Therefore, in this regard… [as before].
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.7 1.
Bālavagga (The Chapter on Fools)
Sāvajjasutta:
“Monks, one who possesses three qualities is to be known as a fool.
Which three? [The Buddha continued:]”

By means of blameworthy bodily action, by means of blameworthy verbal action, by means of blameworthy mental action … [and so on] … by means of blameless bodily action, by means of blameless verbal action, by means of blameless mental action … [and so on] … Seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.8
1. Bālavagga Sabyābajjhasutta:
“Bhikkhus, one should recognize a fool by three qualities.
Which three?
Harmful bodily action, harmful verbal action, and harmful mental action … [and] harmless bodily action, harmless verbal action, and harmless mental action.
It is by possessing these three qualities, monks, that one should be known as wise.
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
'Having avoided those three qualities by which a fool is to be known, we shall undertake and abide in those three qualities by which a wise person is to be known.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.9 1.
Bālavagga (The Chapter on Fools)

The Discourse on the Wounded (Khaṭasutta) “Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit. What are the three? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”
By misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.

Possessing these three qualities, monks, the fool, the incompetent, the untrue person maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he produces much demerit.
Possessing three qualities, monks, the wise, the competent, the true person maintains himself unwounded and uninjured; he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he produces much merit.
Which three?
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a wise, competent, and true person remains unhurt.
“He preserves himself unharmed, he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.10.

1. Bālavagga, Malasutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.10, PTS AN i 105) “Monks, there are these five stains. What five? The stain of lust, the stain of hatred, the stain of delusion, the stain of anger, and the stain of hypocrisy. These, monks, are the five stains.”
“Monks, one who possesses three qualities and has not abandoned three stains is deposited in hell as if carried there.
Which three?
One is immoral, and the stain of immorality has not been abandoned by him;”
He is envious, and the stain of envy has not been abandoned by him;
he is miserly, and the stain of miserliness has not been abandoned by him.
Possessing these three qualities, monks, and without having abandoned these three stains, one is deposited in hell just as if carried there.
“Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities and having abandoned three stains, one is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the three?
One is virtuous, and the stain of immorality has been abandoned by him.”
“He is not envious, and the stain of envy has been abandoned by him;
he is not stingy, and the stain of stinginess has been abandoned by him.
Possessing these three qualities and having abandoned these three stains, monks, one is deposited in heaven just as if carried there.”
The tenth.
The first chapter, the Chapter on the Fool (Bālavagga).
Its summary verse (uddāna):
Fear, one who contemplates characteristics,
and an unwise transgression;
that which is unwholesome and blameworthy—
That which is afflicted by ill will is called "stain.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.11 2. Rathakāravagga (The Chapter on the Cartwright)
The Ñāta Sutta (AN 3.11, PTS AN i 106): “Bhikkhus,

possessing three qualities, a well-known bhikkhu practices for the harm of many people, for the suffering of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including gods and humans.”
Which three?
He incites others to improper bodily action, he incites others to improper verbal action, and he incites others to improper states of mind.

Possessing these three qualities, monks, a well-known monk practices for the harm of many people, for the suffering of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.

“Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a well-known bhikkhu practices for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including devas and humans.
What are the three?

He encourages others in bodily actions that are in accordance with the Dhamma; he encourages others in verbal actions that are in accordance with the Dhamma; he encourages others in mental states that are in accordance with the Dhamma.”

“Monks, a well-known monk who possesses these three qualities practices for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including devas and humans.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.12

2. Rathakāravagga: The Discourse on What is to be Remembered (Sāraṇīyasutta) At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He is learned, possessing the Dhamma that has been well learned by heart, which is the basis for wisdom, leading to stilling, and leading to nibbāna. He is a speaker on the Dhamma, one who utters words that are polished, clear, articulate, expressive of the meaning, and conducive to concentration. He is one who encourages, rouses, excites, and gladdens his fellow monks with talk on the Dhamma. He is one who possesses the four bases for psychic power, developed, cultivated, made much of, pursued, consolidated, and properly instigated. Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [The Buddha then spoke further: “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he trains in them. He is learned... [as above] ...conducive to concentration. He is a speaker on the Dhamma... [as above] ...conducive to concentration. He dwells with a mind that is free from stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing. He is one who possesses the four bases for psychic power... [as above]. Bhikkhus, these five things lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller. “Bhikkhus, there are these three things that a head-anointed khattiya king should remember for as long as he lives.
What are the three?
The place, bhikkhus, where the head-anointed khattiya king was born.”
This, monks, is the first thing that should be remembered for as long as life lasts by a head-anointed kṣatriya king.
Furthermore, monks, in whatever place a head-anointed kṣatriya king resides—
this, monks, is the second thing that should be remembered for as long as life lasts by a head-anointed kṣatriya king.
Furthermore, monks, in whatever place a consecrated kṣatriya king, having won a battle, dwells at the very head of that battlefield after the battle has been won—
this, monks, is the third thing that should be remembered for as long as life lasts by a consecrated kṣatriya king.
These, monks, are the three things that should be remembered for as long as life lasts by a consecrated kṣatriya king.
In the same way, monks, there are these three things that should be remembered by a monk for as long as life lasts.
What are the three?
That place, monks, where a monk, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.
This, monks, is the first thing that is to be remembered by a monk for as long as life lasts.
Furthermore, monks, in whatever place a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering," understands as it really is:
"This is the origin of suffering," and understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"—
He understands, as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, monks, is the second thing that should be remembered by a monk for as long as life lasts.

Furthermore, monks, there is that place where a monk, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, enters and dwells therein.
“Monks, this is the third thing that should be remembered by a monk for as long as life lasts.
These, monks, are the three things that should be remembered by a monk for as long as life lasts.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.13 2.

Rathakāravagga Āsaṁsasutta – The Discourse on Hopes “Monks, there are these three hopes. What three? The hope for sensual pleasures, the hope for life, and the hope for heaven. These, monks, are the three hopes.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three persons found existing in the world. Which three? [Text continues].”
One who is without hope, hopeful, and free from hope.
And what, bhikkhus, is the person without hope?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is reborn into a low family—either a family of outcasts (caṇḍāla) or a family of bamboo-workers (vena).
Or he is born into a family of hunters, or a family of chariot-makers, or a family of scavengers— poor, lacking food and drink,
with a difficult livelihood, where even basic sustenance and clothing are obtained with great hardship.
And he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, afflicted by many diseases, blind in one eye, or has crooked limbs, or is lame, or has a withered arm.
Or, not being a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings,
or lighting, he hears:
"It is said that a certain kshatriya has been consecrated by the kshatriyas with the kshatriya-consecration."
It does not occur to him:
‘When indeed will they anoint me too with the kshatriya consecration?
This, monks, is called the person who is free from hope.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the person who has hope?
Here, bhikkhus, a king of the Khattiya caste, anointed and consecrated, has an eldest son who is entitled to the consecration but has not yet been consecrated and has reached a state of security.
He hears: [that his father is ill...]"
‘It is said that a certain kshatriya has been consecrated by the kshatriyas with the kshatriya-consecration.
It occurs to him:
‘When indeed will they also consecrate me with the kshatriya-consecration?’
“Monks, this person is called one who has hope.
And what, monks, is the person who is free from hope?
Here, monks, there is a king, a kshatriya, anointed on the head.”
He hears:
“It is said that a certain kshatriya has been consecrated by the kshatriyas with the kshatriya-consecration.
It does not occur to him:
‘When indeed will they anoint me too with the kṣatriya consecration?
For what reason?
Because, monks, whatever desire he previously had for the consecration when he was not yet consecrated has now subsided.
This, monks, is called a person who is free from expectation.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
In the same way, monks, these three persons exist and are found among the bhikkhus.
Which three?
The one who is hopeless, the one who has hope, and the one whose hope has vanished.
And what, monks, is the person who is hopeless?
In this case, monks, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions;
though not an ascetic, he claims to be an ascetic, and though not living the holy life, he claims to live the holy life;
he is inwardly rotten, leaking, and corrupt.
He hears:

“It is said that a certain monk, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein.
It does not occur to him:

‘When indeed shall I, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwell therein?
This, monks, is called the person who is hopeless.
And what, monks, is the person who has hope?
In this case, monks, a monk is virtuous and of good character.
He hears:

"It is said that the monk named so-and-so, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein."
It occurs to him:

‘When indeed shall I too, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwell therein?
Monks, such a person is called one who has hope.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is free from longing?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is an arahant whose taints are destroyed.
He hears:..."

‘It is said that a certain monk, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, enters and dwells therein.
It does not occur to him:
‘When indeed shall I too, through the destruction of the taints... [realize]... enter and dwell therein?’
For what reason?
Because, monks, that hope for liberation which he previously had while unliberated has been stilled.
This, monks, is called the person who is free from hope.
“Monks, these three types of persons are found existing among the monks. Thus [ends] the third [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.14.

Rathakāravagga: Cakkavattisutta (AN 3.14, PTS AN i 109) “Monks, suppose there were a wheel-turning monarch who, having conquered the earth as far as its ocean boundaries, dwelt in happiness, righteously, without rod or sword. Then, monks, a certain man would come along and say: ‘I wish to go forth from the household life into homelessness under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. “If, monks, that wheel-turning monarch were to say to him: ‘Come, good man, do not go forth from the household life into homelessness; rather, remain here as a householder, enjoy the wealth, and perform meritorious deeds,’ would he, monks, be able to turn back that man who desires to go forth from the household life into homelessness? “No, venerable sir. “Monks, even though the wheel-turning monarch might say this, it is impossible for him to turn back that man who desires to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Why is that? Because, monks, the mind of one who desires to go forth from the household life into homelessness is inclined toward renunciation, not toward worldly attachment. “In the same way, monks, if a person has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, it is impossible for anyone—whether a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—to turn them back from the path of the wholesome, the path of the Dhamma, the path of truth, the path leading to peace, the path leading to Nibbāna. Why is that? Because, monks, the mind of one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness is inclined toward renunciation, not toward worldly attachment.”
“Bhikkhus, even that wheel-turning monarch, the righteous king who rules by Dhamma, does not turn the wheel without a king.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:
“But who, Bhante, is the king of the righteous wheel-turning monarch who rules by Dhamma?”
“Dhamma, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said,
“in this case, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, relying only on Dhamma,
honoring Dhamma, revering Dhamma, respecting Dhamma, having Dhamma as his banner, Dhamma as his standard, and Dhamma as his authority— ”
He provides righteous protection, defense, and security for his household.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch who is righteous, a king of Dhamma, relies solely on the Dhamma, honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, and venerating the Dhamma;
he has the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard, and the Dhamma as his authority.
He provides righteous protection, defense, and security for his kshatriya vassals, his followers, his army, the brahmins and householders,
the people of the towns and countryside, the ascetics and brahmins, and even for the beasts and birds.
That bhikkhu, a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king of Dhamma, relies solely upon the Dhamma...

Honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma, having the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard, and the Dhamma as his authority, he established righteous protection, defense, and security for his household;
he established righteous protection, defense, and security for the kṣatriyas...
[and so on] ...for his followers, for the army, for the brahmins and householders, and for the people of the towns and countryside.
Among ascetics and brahmins, and among beasts and birds, he turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone.
That wheel is unassailable by any human adversary or living being.
In the same way, bhikkhu, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the righteous one, the King of Dhamma, [turns] only the Dhamma...

Relying on the Dhamma, honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma—having the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard, and the Dhamma as his authority—he provides righteous protection, defense, and security regarding bodily action:
"Such bodily action should be practiced; such bodily action should not be practiced."
Furthermore, bhikkhu, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is righteous, a king of Dhamma, relying on the Dhamma alone,
honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma— having the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard,
and the Dhamma as his authority— provides righteous protection, defense, and security regarding verbal action:
‘Such verbal action should be cultivated; such verbal action should not be cultivated’ … [and so on] … regarding mental action:
‘Such mental action should be cultivated; such mental action should not be cultivated.
Now, that Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the righteous one, the King of Dhamma, [teaches] only the Dhamma...

Relying on the Dhamma, honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, making the Dhamma his banner, making the Dhamma his standard, having the Dhamma as his authority, he provides righteous protection, defense, and security in bodily action;
he provides righteous protection, defense, and security in verbal action; [he provides righteous protection, defense, and security]... in mental action.
Having established himself in mental action, he sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma by means of the Dhamma alone.
That wheel cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
This is the fourth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.15 2. Rathakāravagga Sacetanasutta “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is conscious of both the present and the future; the person who is conscious of the present but not of the future; and the person who is conscious of neither the present nor the future. And how, monks, is one a person conscious of both the present and the future? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Thus, monks, a noble disciple possesses this aggregate of virtue, this aggregate of concentration, and this aggregate of wisdom. This, monks, is called a person conscious of both the present and the future. And how, monks, is one a person conscious of the present but not of the future? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... But he does not possess the wisdom of discernment regarding the rise and fall of phenomena, the noble penetration of the way things are, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Thus, monks, this is called a person conscious of the present but not of the future. And how, monks, is one a person conscious of neither the present nor the future? Here, monks, an ordinary person is devoid of confirmed confidence in the Buddha... devoid of confirmed confidence in the Dhamma... devoid of confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha... devoid of the virtues dear to the noble ones. Thus, monks, this is called a person conscious of neither the present nor the future.”
(AN 3.15, PTS AN i 110) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Sacetana.
Then, monks, King Sacetana addressed his chariot-maker:
‘Friend chariot-maker, six months from now I shall have a battle.’”
“Can you, my dear chariot-maker, fashion for me a new pair of wheels?
“I can, Your Majesty,” the chariot-maker replied to the conscious king.
Then, monks, the chariot-maker completed one wheel in six months less six days.
Then, monks, the conscious king addressed the chariot-maker:
"Friend chariot-maker, will my battle take place six days from now, and will the new pair of wheels be finished?
"Your Majesty, with these six months less six days, one wheel has been finished."
“But, my dear chariot-maker, will you be able to complete a second wheel for me within these six days? “I am able, Your Majesty,” the chariot-maker replied.
Having completed the second wheel in six days and taking a new pair of wheels, he approached King Sacetanaka; having approached him, he said this to King Sacetanaka:
‘Your Majesty, this new pair of wheels has been completed for you.
‘My dear chariot-maker, what is the difference between this wheel of yours that was completed six months less six days ago, and this wheel of yours that was completed just six days ago?
I see no difference at all between them.’
‘There is a distinction between them, Your Majesty;
let Your Majesty see the distinction.
Then, monks, the wheelwright set in motion that wheel which had been completed in six days.
Once set in motion, it traveled as far as the momentum of its formation would carry it, then whirled around and fell to the ground.
But that wheel which had been completed in six months— having set it in motion six days short of a full year—
it traveled as far as the momentum of its formation would carry it and then stood still, as if struck by an axle-pin.
“What, friend chariot-maker, is the cause, what is the reason, why this wheel that was finished in six days, having been set in motion,
went only as far as the momentum of its formation carried it, then whirled around and fell to the ground?
But what, friend chariot-maker, is the cause, what is the reason, why this wheel that was finished in six months less six days...”
“Once it had been set in motion, having gone as far as the range of its momentum, it stood still as if struck by an axle-pin?
“Your Majesty, this wheel that was finished in six days—its rim was crooked, flawed, and tarnished; its spokes were also crooked, flawed, and tarnished;
and its hub was also crooked, flawed, and tarnished. Because of the rim being crooked, flawed, and tarnished, and because of the spokes being crooked, flawed, and tarnished...”

Because its hub was crooked, flawed, and stained, even though it had been set in motion, it traveled only as far as the momentum of its conditioning allowed, then whirled around and fell to the ground.

But that wheel, O King, which was completed in six months less six days—its rim was not crooked, not flawed, and not stained; its spokes were not crooked, not flawed, and not stained; and its hub was not crooked, not flawed, and not stained.
‘Because its rim was not crooked, not defective, and not warped; because its spokes were not crooked, not defective, and not warped;
and because its hub was not crooked, not defective, and not warped, it continued to roll until, having gone as far as the range of its momentum, it stood still as if struck by an axle-pin.’”
“Bhikkhus, it may be that you think:
‘Perhaps at that time he was some other chariot-maker.
But, bhikkhus, this should not be viewed in such a way.
At that time, monks, I was that cartwright.
Back then, monks, I was skilled in the crookedness of wood, the defects of wood, and the knots in wood.
But now, monks, as an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, I am skilled in the crookedness of the body, the defects of the body, and the blemishes of the body.
He is skilled regarding bodily crookedness, bodily faults, and bodily impurities; he is skilled regarding verbal crookedness, verbal faults, and verbal impurities;
he is skilled regarding mental crookedness, mental faults, and mental impurities.
Monks, for whichever monk or nun bodily crookedness has not been abandoned, bodily fault...
"Bhikkhus, bodily crookedness that has not been abandoned, bodily fault, bodily impurity;
mental crookedness that has not been abandoned, mental fault, mental impurity—in this way, bhikkhus, they have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya, just as that wheel was finished in six days.
Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has abandoned bodily crookedness and bodily fault..."
"Bodily crookedness has been abandoned, as well as verbal fault and verbal impurity; mental crookedness has been abandoned, as well as mental fault and mental impurity.
Thus established, monks, are you in this Dhamma and Vinaya, just as that wheel was completed in six months less six days."
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

'We will abandon crookedness of body, corruption of body, and impurity of body; we will abandon crookedness of speech, corruption of speech, and impurity of speech; we will abandon crookedness of mind, corruption of mind, and impurity of mind.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.16 2.
Rathakāravagga (The Chapter on Cartwrights)
Apaṇṇakasutta: “Bhikkhus,
possessing three qualities, a bhikkhu has entered upon the unmistakable way and has laid a foundation for the destruction of the taints.”
Which three?
Here, monks, a monk is one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.
And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary details.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[might arise].
If unwholesome states were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and attains mastery over the mind-faculty.
In this way, monks, a monk is one whose sense-doors are guarded.
And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating?
In this case, monks, a monk reflects wisely before partaking of food:

"Neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty or adornment, but only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thus I shall put an end to old feelings of discomfort and..."
‘I shall not give rise to new feeling, and I shall maintain myself, be blameless, and dwell at ease.
In this way, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.
And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness?
In this case, monks, during the day a monk purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking and sitting;
during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking and sitting;
during the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot upon the other.

Having laid down [the body], mindful and clearly comprehending, and having directed his mind toward the perception of rising, he rises during the last watch of the night and purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
In this way, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities has entered upon the unmistakable way and has laid a foundation for the destruction of the taints.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.17

2. Rathakāravagga Attabyābādhasutta (AN 3.17, PTS AN i 114) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who harms himself; the person who harms others; and the person who harms neither himself nor others. And how, monks, is one a person who harms himself? Here, monks, someone has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects thus: ‘Alas, this is suffering! Alas, this is suffering! He dwells with his mind obsessed by that reflection on suffering. Because he dwells with his mind obsessed by that reflection on suffering, he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Because he does not understand these things as they really are, he does not develop the path; because he does not develop the path, he does not cultivate the path; because he does not cultivate the path, he does not realize the fruit of the path. Thus, monks, one is a person who harms himself. And how, monks, is one a person who harms others? Here, monks, someone goes to a village or town and says: ‘Come, sirs, give me what you have; do not give it to others. And those people, being pressured by him, give him what they have, even taking from their own children and wives. Thus, monks, one is a person who harms others. And how, monks, is one a person who harms neither himself nor others? Here, monks, someone has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. He dwells with his mind not obsessed by that reflection on peace. Because he dwells with his mind not obsessed by that reflection on peace, he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Because he understands these things as they really are, he develops the path; because he develops the path, he cultivates the path; because he cultivates the path, he realizes the fruit of the path. Thus, monks, one is a person who harms neither himself nor others. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are three things that lead to one’s own affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both.
What are the three?
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.”
“Monks, these three things lead to one’s own affliction, lead to the affliction of others, and lead to the affliction of both.
Monks, there are these other three things that lead neither to one’s own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both.
What are the three?”
“Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
These three things, monks, lead neither to one’s own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.18 2. Rathakāravagga Devalokasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is a deva among devas, the person who is a deva among humans, and the person who is a deva among devas and humans.

And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is a deva among devas? Here, someone is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is called a person who is a deva among devas. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is a deva among humans? Here, someone is virtuous... [as above] ...he trains in them. He is one who gains internal serenity of mind, but not the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. With the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes an attainer of nibbāna in the interval. This is called a person who is a deva among humans. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is a deva among devas and humans? Here, someone is virtuous... [as above] ...he trains in them. He is one who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. With the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes an attainer of nibbāna upon landing. Or with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes an attainer of nibbāna without exertion. Or with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes an attainer of nibbāna with exertion. Or with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one bound upstream, heading toward the Akaniṭṭha realm. This is called a person who is a deva among devas and humans. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you:
‘Friends, for the sake of rebirth in the world of the devas, do you lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama?’”
“Monks, would you not be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted if you were asked such a question?
“Yes, venerable sir.

“So it seems, monks, that you are distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by divine life-span; you are distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty.”

“Indeed, monks, you should be ashamed, humiliated, and disgusted by bodily misconduct; you should be ashamed, humiliated, and disgusted by verbal misconduct; and you should be ashamed, humiliated, and disgusted by mental misconduct.
(The Eighth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.19

2. Rathakāravagga First Discourse on the Merchant (Paṭhamapāpaṇikasutta) “Monks, suppose a merchant, while traveling along a highway, were to see a great heap of treasure—gold coins, silver coins, pearls, gems, cat’s-eye gems, and coral—lying on the ground. Having seen it, he would think: ‘This is a great heap of treasure—gold coins, silver coins, pearls, gems, cat’s-eye gems, and coral—lying on the ground. It would be well for me to take this great heap of treasure. Then, monks, that merchant would take that great heap of treasure and, having taken it, would depart from that highway onto another highway. While traveling along that second highway, he would see a great body of water. Having seen it, he would think: ‘This is a great body of water; it would be well for me to cross over this great body of water by means of a raft. Then, monks, that merchant would bind together a raft made of reeds, bamboo, wood, grass, and clay. Having bound it together, he would mount the raft and, with his hands and feet, would cross over the great body of water. Having crossed over, he would stand on dry land. In the same way, monks, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact, he is said to have crossed over the flood, to have gone beyond the mire, to be a brahmin, a true ascetic, and a true follower of the holy life. He has laid down the burden, accomplished his task, removed the fetters of existence, and, through the complete destruction of craving, has attained liberation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and departed. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, what was the meaning of the Blessed One’s brief statement when he said: ‘When a noble disciple understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact...’? “Friend, suppose a man were traveling along a highway and saw a great heap of treasure—gold coins, silver coins, pearls, gems, cat’s-eye gems, and coral—lying on the ground. Having seen it, he would think: ‘This is a great heap of treasure... [as above]. In the same way, friend, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact, he is said to have crossed over the flood, to have gone beyond the mire, to be a brahmin, a true ascetic, and a true follower of the holy life.

He has laid down the burden, accomplished his task, removed the fetters of existence, and, through the complete destruction of craving, has attained liberation. “This is the meaning, friend, of what the Blessed One spoke in brief. [The Venerable Sāriputta then repeated the entire discourse to the Venerable Ānanda, who replied: “It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this was stated by the Blessed One in brief, and how well it was explained by you in detail. This is the meaning, friend, of what the Blessed One spoke in brief. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven, which, when practiced and cultivated, lead to rebirth in a heavenly world. What five? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. These, monks, are the five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven, which, when practiced and cultivated, lead to rebirth in a heavenly world. [The Blessed One then further elaborated on each of these qualities, concluding: “When a noble disciple possesses these five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven, and when he understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact, he is said to have crossed over the flood, to have gone beyond the mire, to be a brahmin, a true ascetic, and a true follower of the holy life. He has laid down the burden, accomplished his task, removed the fetters of existence, and, through the complete destruction of craving, has attained liberation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven... [as above] ...he has attained liberation. [The Blessed One then further elaborated on each of these qualities, concluding: “When a noble disciple possesses these five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven, and when he understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact, he is said to have crossed over the flood, to have gone beyond the mire, to be a brahmin, a true ascetic, and a true follower of the holy life. [The Blessed One then further elaborated on each of these qualities, concluding: “When a noble disciple possesses these five bases of meritorious action that lead to heaven, and when he understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the six bases of contact, he is said to have crossed over the flood, to have gone beyond the mire, to be a brahmin, a true ascetic, and a true follower of the holy life. “Bhikkhus, a shopkeeper endowed with three factors is incapable of acquiring wealth not yet acquired, or of increasing wealth already acquired.
With which three?
Here, bhikkhus, in the morning a shopkeeper does not diligently attend to his work; at midday he does not diligently attend to his work; and in the evening he does not diligently attend to his work.
“Monks, a shopkeeper endowed with these three factors is incapable of acquiring wealth not yet acquired, or of increasing wealth already acquired.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is incapable of acquiring wholesome states not yet acquired, or of increasing wholesome states already acquired. With which three?
[The three qualities follow].”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu does not earnestly fix his mind upon the sign of concentration in the morning;
he does not earnestly fix his mind upon the sign of concentration at midday; and he does not earnestly fix his mind upon the sign of concentration in the evening.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these three qualities is incapable of attaining an unattained wholesome state, or of increasing a wholesome state already attained.
Monks, a shopkeeper endowed with three factors is capable of acquiring wealth not yet acquired, or of increasing wealth already acquired.
With which three?
“Here, monks, a shopkeeper carefully attends to his work in the morning, carefully attends to his work at midday, and carefully attends to his work in the evening.
Endowed with these three factors, monks, a shopkeeper is capable of acquiring wealth not yet acquired, or of increasing wealth already acquired.
“In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is capable of attaining wholesome states not yet attained, or of increasing wholesome states already attained.
What are the three?

Here, monks, in the morning a monk earnestly fixes his mind on the sign of concentration; at midday he earnestly fixes his mind on the sign of concentration; and in the evening he earnestly fixes his mind on the sign of concentration.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is capable of attaining the wholesome state not yet attained, or of increasing the wholesome state already attained.
Thus was the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.20

2. Rathakāravagga The Second Discourse on the Shopkeeper (Dutiyapāpaṇikasutta) “Monks, suppose a shopkeeper or his apprentice were to sell goods that are inferior, counterfeit, and false, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. What do you think, monks? Would that shopkeeper or his apprentice be a person of integrity? “No, venerable sir. “Monks, that shopkeeper or his apprentice would indeed be a person of no integrity. Why is that? Because, monks, he sells goods that are inferior, counterfeit, and false, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. This, monks, is how one is a person of no integrity. But suppose, monks, a shopkeeper or his apprentice were to sell goods that are superior, genuine, and true, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. What do you think, monks? Would that shopkeeper or his apprentice be a person of integrity? “Yes, venerable sir. “Monks, that shopkeeper or his apprentice would indeed be a person of integrity. Why is that? Because, monks, he sells goods that are superior, genuine, and true, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. This, monks, is how one is a person of integrity. In the same way, monks, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, some person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He is one who does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from destroying life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. He does not honor them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher. He does not train himself in accordance with their Dhamma. This, monks, is the first kind of person found existing in the world. Then, monks, another person destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. But he honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things; he honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and he trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma. This, monks, is the second kind of person found existing in the world. Then, monks, another person destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. He does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things; nor does he honor them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, nor does he train himself in accordance with their Dhamma. However, he does not destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. He honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things;

he honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and he trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma. This, monks, is the third kind of person found existing in the world. Then, monks, another person does not destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. He honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things; he honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and he trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma. This, monks, is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. Of these four persons, monks, the one who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, nor honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, nor trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is similar to the shopkeeper or his apprentice who sells goods that are inferior, counterfeit, and false, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. But the person who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, yet who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is similar to the shopkeeper or his apprentice who sells goods that are superior, genuine, and true, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. The person who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, yet who does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, nor honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, nor trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—but who himself does not destroy life... [as above] ...nor indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is similar to the shopkeeper or his apprentice who sells goods that are superior, genuine, and true, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. And the person who does not destroy life... [as above] ...nor indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is similar to the shopkeeper or his apprentice who sells goods that are superior, genuine, and true, while claiming they are superior, genuine, and true. Of these four persons, monks, the one who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, nor honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, nor trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is the most inferior of the four. The person who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, yet who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is more excellent than the former and is the second among the four. The person who destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, yet who does not honor, respect, revere, or venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, nor honors them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, nor trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—but who himself does not destroy life... [as above] ...nor indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is more excellent than the former two and is the third among the four. And the person who does not destroy life... [as above] ...nor indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence, and who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and trains himself in accordance with their Dhamma—this person, monks, is the most excellent of the four. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not destroy life... [as above] ...nor shall we indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence; and we shall honor, respect, revere, and venerate those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from these things, honoring them as one would honor a teacher, or one equal to a teacher, and we shall train ourselves in accordance with their Dhamma. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
“Monks, a shopkeeper endowed with three factors will before long attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
With which three?
Here, monks, a shopkeeper is one who has keen vision, one who is diligent, and one who is well-supported.
And how, monks, is a shopkeeper one who possesses vision?
Here, monks, a shopkeeper knows his merchandise:
"This merchandise was bought at such a price; being sold in this manner, it will yield such a cost and such a profit."
In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is one who possesses vision.
And how, monks, is a shopkeeper experienced?
Here, monks, a shopkeeper is skilled in buying and selling merchandise.
In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is diligent.
And how, monks, is a shopkeeper endowed with support?
Here, monks, those householders or sons of householders who are wealthy, of great riches, and of great possessions know of the shopkeeper thus:
‘This worthy shopkeeper is sighted, capable, and competent to support his wife and children and to provide for us from time to time.
They then approach him with wealth, saying:
‘Good shopkeeper, having earned wealth from this, support your wife and children and provide for us from time to time.’
"In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is endowed with support.
Endowed with these three factors, monks, a shopkeeper before long attains greatness and abundance in wealth.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities before long attains greatness and abundance in wholesome states."
By which three?
Here, monks, a monk is possessed of vision, is resourceful, and is endowed with support.
And how, monks, is a monk possessed of vision?
In this case, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
In this way, monks, a monk is one who possesses vision.

And how, monks, is a monk steadfast? Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is firm, of strong resolve, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who is independent.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with support?

Here, monks, a monk approaches from time to time those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā, and he questions them and inquires of them:
“Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?
Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been clarified, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that give rise to uncertainty.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is endowed with support.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities will before long attain greatness and abundance in wholesome states.
Tenth.
The first recitation section is finished.
The second chapter, on the Cartwright.
Its summary:
The well-known monk Sāraṇīya,
The Wheel-turning Monarch who is conscious,
the Deity because of his certainty,
and two [cases] by way of the shopkeeper.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.21 3. Puggalavagga Samiddhasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Samiddha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Samiddha: “Samiddha, do you remember the Dhamma as it was taught by me? “Venerable sir, how could I not remember the Dhamma as it was taught by the Blessed One? The Blessed One has taught the Dhamma out of compassion for us. “Then, Samiddha, do you remember even a single verse that you have learned from me? “Yes, venerable sir, I remember a single verse that I have learned from the Blessed One. “And what, Samiddha, is that verse? “‘One who does no evil with the body, Who does no evil with speech, And who does no evil with the mind— Such a person is called a good person. This is the verse, venerable sir, that I remember as having been taught by the Blessed One. “Good, good, Samiddha! It is good that you remember this verse as taught by me. For this is indeed the verse taught by me: ‘One who does no evil with the body, Who does no evil with speech, And who does no evil with the mind— Such a person is called a good person. It is in such a way, Samiddha, that you should remember the Dhamma as it was taught by me. When this was said, the Venerable Samiddha said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘One who does no evil with the body, Who does no evil with speech, And who does no evil with the mind— Such a person is called a good person. But, venerable sir, how is it that one comes to be a bad person? “Samiddha, one who destroys life is a bad person; one who takes what is not given is a bad person; one who engages in sexual misconduct is a bad person; one who speaks falsehood is a bad person;

one who speaks divisively is a bad person; one who speaks harshly is a bad person; one who indulges in idle chatter is a bad person; one who is full of longing is a bad person; one who harbors ill will is a bad person; one who holds wrong view is a bad person. In this way, Samiddha, one comes to be a bad person. But in what way, Samiddha, does one come to be a good person? “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or showing the path to one who is lost, or lighting a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. “Samiddha, one who destroys life is a bad person... [as above] ...one who holds wrong view is a bad person. In this way, Samiddha, one comes to be a bad person. But in what way, Samiddha, does one come to be a good person? “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! (AN 3.21, PTS AN i 118) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the Venerable Samiddha and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. As the Venerable Samiddha was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to him:
"Friend Samiddha, these three types of persons are found existing in the world."
Which three?
The body-witness, the one attained to vision, and the one liberated by faith.
These, friends, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
“Friend, among these three types of persons, which person do you consider to be more excellent and more sublime?
“Friend Sāriputta, there are these three types of persons found existing in the world. Which three? [The rest of the passage follows].”
The body-witness, the one attained to vision, and the one liberated by faith.
These, friends, are the three persons found existing in the world.
Among these three persons, friends, this person who is liberated by faith is, in my view, the most excellent and the most sublime among these three.
"And for what reason?
Because, friends, this person’s faculty of faith is predominant.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita:
“Friend Koṭṭhika, there are these three persons found existing in the world.
Which three?
The body-witness, the one attained to vision, and the one liberated by faith.”
“Friends, these three persons are found existing in the world.
Among these three persons, friend, which person do you consider to be more excellent and more sublime?
“Friend Sāriputta, there are these three persons found existing in the world.”
Which three?
The body-witness, the one attained to vision, and the one liberated by faith.
These, friends, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
"Friends, among these three types of persons, the one who is a body-witness—I consider this person to be more excellent and more sublime than the other two.
Why is that? Because, friends, this person’s faculty of concentration is preeminent."
Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world.
Which three?"
“The body-witness, the one attained to view, and the one liberated by faith—
these, friends, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
Among these three persons, friend, which person do you consider to be more excellent and more sublime?”
“Friend Koṭṭhika, there are three kinds of persons found existing in the world.
Which three?
The body-witness, the one attained to view, and the one liberated by faith.”
"Friends, these three persons are found existing in the world.
Among these three persons, friends, the one who has attained through vision—I consider that person to be more excellent and more sublime than the other two.
For what reason?"
“Friends, for this person the faculty of wisdom is predominant.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Samiddha and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika:
“Friends, we have all given our explanations according to our own inspiration.”
"Come, friends, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
We will bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it.
"So be it, friend," the Venerable Samiddha and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Samiddha, and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between him and the Venerable Samiddha and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika.
“Sāriputta, it is not easy to give a categorical answer to this.”
‘This one is more excellent and more sublime than these three persons.
For it is possible, Sāriputta, that this person who is liberated by faith might be practicing for arahantship;
whereas this person who is a body-witness might be a once-returner or a non-returner; and as for this person who has attained through view—[this latter is the most excellent].”
He is either a once-returner or a non-returner.
But here, Sāriputta, it is not easy to declare categorically:
‘This one is more excellent and more sublime than these three persons.’”
For it is possible, Sāriputta, that this person who is a body-witness may be practicing for arahantship;
that this person who is liberated by faith may be a once-returner or a non-returner; and that this person who has attained to view may be a once-returner or a non-returner.
"It is not easy, Sāriputta, to declare categorically:
'This one among these three persons is more excellent and more sublime.
For it is possible, Sāriputta, that this person who has attained to view might be practicing for arahantship."
Whether this person liberated-by-faith is a once-returner or a non-returner, and whether this person who is a body-witness is a once-returner or a non-returner—
it is not easy, Sāriputta, to declare this categorically.
“This one is more excellent and more sublime than these three persons. Thus it was said.
