3. Puggalavagga Gilānasutta (The Sick Person) (AN 3.22, PTS AN i 120) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhadda is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. May the Blessed One go to the Venerable Bhadda out of compassion. “Ānanda, if you go to the bhikkhu Bhadda, who is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill, and speak thus, it will be for his long-term welfare and happiness. “A second time, venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhadda is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. May the Blessed One go to the Venerable Bhadda out of compassion. “A second time, Ānanda, if you go to the bhikkhu Bhadda, who is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill, and speak thus, it will be for his long-term welfare and happiness. “A third time, venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhadda is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. May the Blessed One go to the Venerable Bhadda out of compassion. “Then the Blessed One consented by silence. Then the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and went with a number of bhikkhus to the Venerable Bhadda. When he arrived, he sat down on a prepared seat. The Venerable Bhadda then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Bhadda: “Bhadda, are you bearing up, are you enduring? Do your pains diminish rather than increase? Is there a sign of their diminishing rather than increasing? “Venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not enduring. My pains increase rather than diminish; there is no sign of their diminishing rather than increasing. “Bhadda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) Here, Bhadda, some person dwells pursuing the practice of body-contemplation in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. (2) Some other person dwells pursuing the practice of feeling-contemplation in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. (3) Some other person dwells pursuing the practice of mind-contemplation in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. (4) Some other person dwells pursuing the practice of phenomena-contemplation in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. These, Bhadda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which of these four persons do you consider to be the most excellent and sublime? “Venerable sir, as to these four kinds of persons found existing in the world, it is the person who dwells pursuing the practice of phenomena-contemplation in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, whom I consider to be the most excellent and sublime among them. “Good, good, Bhadda! It is indeed the person who dwells pursuing the practice of phenomena-contemplation in phenomena... whom I consider to be the most excellent and sublime among them. Why is that? Because, Bhadda, this Dhamma is taught through phenomena, based on phenomena, and rooted in phenomena. Therefore, Bhadda, you should train yourself in this way: ‘We will dwell pursuing the practice of phenomena-contemplation in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the Venerable Bhadda with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed. Soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Bhadda died. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:

“Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhadda has died. What is his destination? What is his future bourn? “Bhikkhus, the bhikkhu Bhadda was wise. He practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me in the teaching of the Dhamma. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he has reappeared spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will attain final nibbāna there, never to return from that world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of persons are there who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, have reappeared spontaneously and will attain final nibbāna there, never to return from that world? “There are, Ānanda, these seven kinds of persons who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, have reappeared spontaneously and will attain final nibbāna there, never to return from that world. What seven? (1) Here, Ānanda, some person attains the cessation of perception and feeling while still alive. With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the devas of the Aviha heaven. There he attains final nibbāna; he does not return from that world. (2) Some other person does not attain the cessation of perception and feeling while still alive. With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the devas of the Atappa heaven. There he attains final nibbāna; he does not return from that world. (3) Some other person does not attain the cessation of perception and feeling while still alive. With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the devas of the Sudassa heaven. There he attains final nibbāna; he does not return from that world. (4) Some other person does not attain the cessation of perception and feeling while still alive. “Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of sick persons found existing in the world.
What are the three?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain sick person, whether obtaining suitable food or not obtaining suitable food, [is unable to recover].”
Whether he obtains suitable food or does not obtain suitable food, whether he obtains suitable medicine or does not obtain suitable medicine,
whether he obtains a suitable attendant or does not obtain a suitable attendant, he does not recover from that illness.
But here, monks, a certain sick person— whether he obtains suitable food or does not obtain it...
Whether he obtains suitable food or does not obtain suitable food, whether he obtains suitable medicine or does not obtain suitable medicine,
whether he obtains a suitable attendant or does not obtain a suitable attendant, he recovers from that illness. But here, monks,
a certain sick person recovers only when he obtains suitable food, and not when he does not obtain it.
He recovers from that illness by obtaining suitable medicines rather than not obtaining them, and by obtaining a suitable attendant rather than not obtaining one.
In this regard, monks, as for that sick person who recovers by obtaining suitable food rather than not obtaining it... [and so on].
If one does not obtain suitable medicines, or even if obtaining them, does not obtain a suitable attendant, yet still recovers from that illness—
it was with reference to such a sick person, monks, that I authorized sick food, authorized medicine for the sick,
and authorized an attendant for the sick.
"And furthermore, monks, because of this sick person, other sick persons should also be attended to.
These, monks, are the three types of sick persons existing and found in the world.
In the same way, monks, there are these three types of persons resembling the sick, existing and found in the world."
Which three? Here,
monks, a certain person— whether obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata,
whether obtaining the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata—
He does not enter into the certainty of correctness regarding wholesome states for the sake of hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya.
However, monks, here a certain person— whether obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata,
whether obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining it—
Or, he enters upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states for the sake of hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. But here,
monks, a certain person enters upon the certainty [of rightness] only when he obtains a vision of the Tathāgata and not when he does not obtain it,
and only when he obtains the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata for the sake of hearing it and not when he does not obtain it.
Rightness in wholesome states.
In this regard, monks, that person who, when obtaining the sight of the Tathāgata and not failing to obtain it,
and when obtaining the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and not failing to obtain it, enters upon the certainty of wholesome states—
"Rightness regarding phenomena—this, monks, is the person on account of whom the teaching of the Dhamma has been authorized.

These, monks, are the three types of persons resembling the sick who are found existing in the world."

Saṅkhārasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these three persons found existing in the world.”
Which three?
Here, monks, a certain person performs an afflictive bodily formation, performs an afflictive verbal formation, and performs an afflictive mental formation.
Having performed an afflictive bodily formation, having performed an afflictive verbal formation, and having performed an afflictive mental formation, he is reborn in an afflictive world.
When he has been reborn in a world that is afflicted, afflicted contacts touch him.
Being touched by afflicted contacts, he experiences afflicted feelings that are exclusively painful, just like the beings in hell.
But here, monks, a certain person performs an unafflicted bodily formation, performs an unafflicted verbal formation, and performs an unafflicted mental formation.
Having formed a non-afflictive bodily formation, having formed a non-afflictive verbal formation, and having formed a non-afflictive mental formation, one is reborn in a non-afflictive world.
Being reborn in that non-afflictive world, non-afflictive contacts touch him.
Touched by those non-afflictive contacts, he experiences non-afflictive feeling, which is exclusively pleasant, just like the Subhakiṇha devas.
But here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive;
he performs a verbal formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive; he performs a mental formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive.
Thus, having performed a bodily formation that is both harmful and harmless,
having performed a verbal formation that is both harmful and harmless, and having performed a mental formation that is both harmful and harmless,
one is reborn in a world that is both harmful and harmless.
When he has been reborn in a world that is both harmful and harmless, contacts—both harmful and harmless—touch him.

Being touched by contacts that are both harmful and harmless, he experiences feelings that are both harmful and harmless, a mixture of pleasure and pain, just like humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
These, monks, are the three types of persons found existing in the world.”

“Monks, there is a person who should not be associated with, should not be cultivated, and should not be attended upon.

And who, monks, is the person not to be served, not to be associated with, and not to be waited upon?
Here, monks, a certain person is inferior in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

For what reason?

For us who have attained equality in concentration, there will be talk of concentration, and that talk will proceed among us, and it will be a source of comfort for us.

The Discourse on What is to be Loathed (Jigucchitabbasutta). “Bhikkhus,

Which three?

The Discourse on the Dung-Pit (Gūthabhāṇīsutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these three persons found existing in the world.”
Which three?
The one who speaks dung, the one who speaks flowers, and the one who speaks honey.
And what, monks, is the person who speaks dung?

In this case, monks, a certain person, having been summoned as a witness before an assembly, a council, a gathering of kinsmen, a guild, or the royal court, is asked: "Come now, good man, speak what you know.
Not knowing, he says, "I know"; or knowing, he says, "I do not know"; or not seeing, he says, "I see."
Or, seeing, he says: "I do not see. Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trifling material gain, he speaks a deliberate lie.
This person, monks, is called one who speaks dung.
And what, monks, is the person who speaks like a flower?

Here, monks, a certain person, having been summoned as a witness before an assembly, a council, a gathering of kinsmen, a guild, or the royal court, is asked: "Come now, good man, speak whatever you know."
"Speak! he says. Not knowing, he says, "I do not know"; or knowing, he says, "I know. Not seeing, he says, "I do not see";
or seeing, he says, "I see. Thus, whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he does not speak a deliberate falsehood.
“Monks, this person is called one who speaks like a flower.
And what, monks, is the person who speaks like honey?
Here, monks, a certain person, having abandoned harsh speech, abstains from harsh speech.”
Whatever speech he utters is blameless, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many, and dear to many—such is the kind of speech he speaks.
This person, monks, is called one who speaks like honey.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world.”

The Discourse on the Blind (Andhasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these three persons found existing in the world.”
Which three?
The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed.
And who, monks, is the blind person?
"Here, monks, a certain person does not possess such an eye as that eye by which one might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired;

nor does he possess such an eye as that eye by which one might know wholesome and unwholesome states, know blameworthy and blameless states, know inferior and superior states, or know dark and bright states with their counterparts.
This, monks, is called a blind person."
And what, monks, is the one-eyed person?
Here, monks, a certain person possesses such an eye by which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired;
yet he does not possess such an eye by which he might know wholesome and unwholesome states.

He should know the states that are blameworthy and blameless; he should know the states that are inferior and superior; he should know the states that are dark and bright, along with their counterparts.
This, monks, is called the person with one eye.
And who, monks, is the person with two eyes?
In this case, monks, a certain person possesses such an eye that with such an eye he might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired;
he also possesses such an eye that with such an eye he would know wholesome and unwholesome states,
know blameworthy and blameless states, know inferior and superior states, and know dark and bright states with their counterparts.
"This, monks, is called the person with two eyes.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
And such wealth as that—
And he performs no meritorious deeds;
for the blind man whose sight is destroyed, there is a misfortune in both worlds.
Furthermore, another person is described as the "one-eyed": he is deceitful,
acting according to both what is righteous and what is unrighteous.
He seeks enjoyments by means of theft, fraudulent acts,
and falsehood— both together.
The man who is skilled at accumulating wealth yet remains a consumer of sensual pleasures will,
after departing from here, go to hell.
One with a single eye suffers;
but one with two eyes is declared to be the most excellent of persons.
With wealth acquired through righteousness,

3. Puggalavagga Avakujjasutta (The Upright Discourse,
AN 3.30, PTS AN i 130)
“Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world.
Which three?
The person of inverted wisdom, the person of shallow wisdom, and the person of broad wisdom.”
And who, monks, is the person with downcast wisdom?
Here, monks, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; they proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure.
Seated on that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he still does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Just as, monks, water poured into an overturned pot flows out and does not remain there; so it is with him.
In the same way, monks, here a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Yet, while sitting on that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to the middle, nor does he attend to the end.
Even after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, he does not attend to its middle, and he does not attend to its end.
This, monks, is called the person of downcast wisdom.
And who, monks, is the person of lap-like wisdom?
In this case, monks, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing, and they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Seated on that very seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to the middle, and he attends to the end.
But having risen from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end. It is just as if, monks,
various kinds of snacks were piled up in a man's lap—
sesame seeds, rice, sweetmeats, and jujubes.
Just as one rising from that seat might scatter [the flowers] through a lapse of mindfulness,
even so, monks, here a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the presence of the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing— and they reveal the holy life in its entirety, complete and pure.
Thus, sitting on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end;
yet, having risen from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
This, monks, is called a person of shallow wisdom.
And who, monks, is the person of wide wisdom?
Here, monks, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the monks.

The monks teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Seated on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.

Just as, monks, water poured into an upright jar remains there and does not overflow; so too, monks, whatever wholesome qualities have been fully understood by a bhikkhu through right view are consolidated within him and do not leak away. This is called a bhikkhu who is like an upright jar.
In the same way, monks, here a certain person goes to the monastery frequently to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing, and they reveal the holy life in its full perfection and purity.
Seated on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to the middle, and he attends to the end.
Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
This, monks, is called a person of broad wisdom.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
A man of downcast wisdom,
foolish and lacking insight,
even if he is constantly...
He went into the presence of the bhikkhus. Being such as he was,
he spoke likewise of the beginning, the middle,
and the end of the discourse.
He is unable to grasp it,
for wisdom is not found in him;
such a man possesses only the wisdom of his lap.
It is better that one is called such,
even if it happens constantly,
when one goes into the presence of the monks.
Such as he was at the beginning, in the middle,
and at the end of the discourse,
so he sat upon that seat.
Having mastered the phrasing,
one who has emerged from meditation does not understand it;
for what was grasped is forgotten.
A person of broad wisdom is said to be superior to these,
even if he possesses it only occasionally.
He went into the presence of the monks. Being such as he was,
he spoke of the beginning, the middle,
and the end of the discourse.
Seated upon that seat,
having mastered the phrasing,
he who possesses the most excellent intention retains it in mind.
“A person whose mind is not agitated,
practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma,
may become one who makes an end of suffering.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“Could it be, venerable sir, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that there would be no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit regarding this conscious body, and no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit regarding all external signs;
and that he might enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, upon entering which these underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit do not exist?”
“It may be, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu attains such a state of concentration that there would be no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit regarding this conscious body,
nor any underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit toward any external signs;

and he might dwell having entered upon that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein, for one who dwells having entered upon it, those underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit do not exist.”

“But how, venerable sir, might a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that there would be no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit regarding this conscious body, nor any underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit regarding all external signs;
and that he might enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, upon entering which these underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit do not exist?”
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu thinks thus:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration as this, both in this world with its consciousness...”

"There would be no underlying tendencies of 'I-making,' 'mine-making,' and conceit regarding the body, nor would there be underlying tendencies of 'I-making,' 'mine-making,' and conceit regarding all external signs;

and one would dwell having attained that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein, for one who dwells having attained it, there are no underlying tendencies of 'I-making,' 'mine-making,' and conceit.
And it was with reference to this, Ānanda, that it was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Puṇṇaka* inquiry:
“Having scrutinized the higher and lower worlds in this universe,
he for whom there is no agitation anywhere in the world—
he is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and desireless.”
"He has crossed over birth and old age—so I say.

4. Devadūtavagga Sāriputtasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers. When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how well the Blessed One has stated: ‘There are these five powers. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would further explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, Sāriputta, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied. The Blessed One said this: “Here, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses the power of faith. He places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, Sāriputta, is called the power of faith. Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses the power of energy. He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. This, Sāriputta, is called the power of energy. Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses the power of mindfulness. He is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. This, Sāriputta, is called the power of mindfulness. Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses the power of concentration. When his mind is concentrated, his mental disturbances are stilled, and he attains the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This, Sāriputta, is called the power of concentration. Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses the power of wisdom. He possesses wisdom directed toward arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Sāriputta, is called the power of wisdom. These, Sāriputta, are the five powers. When a noble disciple possesses these five powers, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, heading for enlightenment. Just as, Sāriputta, a great river flowing down from the Himālaya mountains, carrying along its current, would never flow back toward the highlands once it has reached the lowlands, even so, when a noble disciple possesses these five powers, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, heading for enlightenment.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Sāriputta, I might teach the Dhamma in brief, and I might also teach the Dhamma in detail."
“Sāriputta, whether I teach the Dhamma in brief or in detail, those who understand it are rare.
“Now is the time for this, Blessed One; now is the time for this, Sugata.”
“The Blessed One might teach the Dhamma in brief, he might teach the Dhamma in detail, or he might teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail;
there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
“Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves thus:”
‘In this conscious body, there will be no underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit;
externally, toward all signs, there will be no underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit;
and that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom which one enters and dwells in, wherein the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not exist—that liberation of mind...’
‘We shall dwell having attained liberation through wisdom.
It is in this way, Sāriputta, that one should train.
But when, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu has abandoned the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding this conscious body, and...
They do not exist; and externally, regarding all signs, the underlying tendencies of the conceits of "I-making" and "mine-making" do not exist;

and he enters and dwells in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein, for one who has entered and dwells therein, the underlying tendencies of the conceits of "I-making" and "mine-making" do not exist.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.34 4. Devadūtavagga Nidānasutta “Monks, there are these three causes for the arising of unwholesome states. What three? Greed is a cause for the arising of unwholesome states; hatred is a cause for the arising of unwholesome states; delusion is a cause for the arising of unwholesome states. These, monks, are the three causes for the arising of unwholesome states. There are, monks, these three causes for the arising of wholesome states. What three? Non-greed is a cause for the arising of wholesome states; non-hatred is a cause for the arising of wholesome states; non-delusion is a cause for the arising of wholesome states. These, monks, are the three causes for the arising of wholesome states.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma. What are the three? [The text continues as follows:]”
Greed is the cause for the origination of kamma; hatred is the cause for the origination of kamma; delusion is the cause for the origination of kamma.
Monks, whatever kamma is fashioned by greed, born of greed, caused by greed, and originating from greed, that kamma ripens wherever a personal identity (attabhāva) is produced for it.
Wherever that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma—either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
“Monks, whatever action is performed out of hatred, born of hatred, rooted in hatred, originating from hatred—wherever his personal existence is reborn, there that action ripens.
Wherever that action ripens, there he experiences its result: either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
Monks, whatever action is performed out of delusion, born of delusion, rooted in delusion, originating from delusion—wherever his personal existence is reborn, there that action ripens.”
Wherever that karma ripens, there one experiences its result— either in this very life, or upon rebirth,
or in some subsequent period. Just as if, monks, seeds that are unbroken, undecayed, not damaged by wind or heat, fertile, well-stored, and placed in a well-prepared field on good soil,
and the rain-god were to send down a proper shower.
In that way, monks, those seeds would attain growth, increase, and abundance.
Even so, monks, whatever action is fashioned by greed, born of greed, caused by greed, and originating from greed, that action ripens wherever a personal existence (attabhāva) is produced for it.
Wherever that action ripens, there one experiences the result of that action—either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
Whatever action is performed out of hatred...
whatever action is performed out of delusion—born of delusion, rooted in delusion, originating from delusion—that action ripens wherever one’s personal existence (attabhāva) is produced.
Wherever that action ripens, there one experiences its result: either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
“Monks, these three are the causes for the origination of kamma.
Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma. What are the three? [The text continues with the enumeration of the three causes.]”
Non-greed is the cause for the origination of kamma; non-hatred is the cause for the origination of kamma; non-delusion is the cause for the origination of kamma.
Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed out of non-greed, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, and originating from non-greed—that kamma is abandoned when greed has vanished;
it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and rendered incapable of future arising.
It is of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Monks, whatever action is performed out of non-hatred, born of non-hatred, rooted in non-hatred, and originating from non-hatred— that action, when hatred has vanished,
is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and of a nature not to arise again in the future.
“Monks, whatever action is produced by non-delusion, born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, and originating from non-delusion—that action is abandoned when delusion has vanished;
it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Monks, it is just as if there were seeds that are unbroken, unrotted, not damaged by wind or heat, fertile, and well-stored.”
A man might burn them with fire;
having burned them with fire, he might reduce them to ashes;
having reduced them to ashes, he might scatter the ashes in a great wind or carry them away in a swift-flowing river.
“Just as those seeds, monks, would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising in the future; even so, monks,
whatever action is performed out of non-greed, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, and originating from non-greed— that action, when greed has vanished,
is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and rendered non-existent.”
...subject to non-arising in the future.
Whatever action is performed out of non-hatred ...pe...
whatever action is performed out of non-delusion—born of non-delusion, rooted in non-delusion, originating from non-delusion—is abandoned when delusion has vanished ...pe...
...having the nature of not arising in the future.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of kamma:
that born of greed, that born of hatred, and likewise [that born of delusion].
And whatever karma has been performed by one who is cast away through delusion,
whether it be little or much;
Right here is that which is to be felt;
no other basis exists.
Therefore, [abandon] both greed and hatred.
And the wise one born of delusion;
by arousing true knowledge,
a bhikkhu abandons all miserable destinies.”

The Discourse to Hatthaka (Hatthakasutta).
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, on the Cow Path, in the Siṃsapā Grove, seated upon a spread of leaves.
Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, while walking and wandering for exercise, saw the Blessed One sitting on the spread of leaves in the Siṃsapā Grove on the Cow Path.
Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Hatthaka of Āḷavī said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, did the Blessed One sleep comfortably?
“Yes, prince, I slept comfortably.
And among those who sleep comfortably in the world, I am one of them.”
“Venerable sir, it is winter night; it is the season of the intermediate eight days when snow falls; the ground is rough, trampled by cattle hooves;
the leaf-strewn layer is thin; the leaves on the tree are sparse; the saffron robes are cold;
and the Verambha wind blows cold.”
And yet the Blessed One said this:
“In this way, young man, you have slept happily;
and I am one among those who sleep happily in the world.”
“In that case, prince, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, prince? Suppose there were a householder or a householder’s son here who has a gabled upper chamber—plastered inside and out, windless, with bolts fastened and windows shuttered.
Therein is a couch spread with woolen coverlets, embroidered coverlets, and counterpanes, with a choice spread of antelope hide, provided with a canopy above and red bolsters at both ends.”
Suppose, young man, an oil lamp were burning here,
and the four wives were attending to it with agreeable and disagreeable things.
What do you think, young man, would he sleep happily or not?
“And what do you think about this?
“He would sleep happily, Bhante,
and he would be one of those who sleep happily in the world.”
“What do you think, prince?

Would there arise in that householder or householder’s son any fever born of passion, whether physical or mental, by which, being consumed by that fever born of passion, he would sleep in suffering?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Kumāra, that lust by which a householder or a householder’s son, burning with the fevers born of lust, would lie in suffering—
that lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and is subject to non-arising in the future.”
Therefore, I slept happily.
What do you think, prince, would there arise in that householder or householder’s son feverish distress born of hatred? … [and so on] …”
“Are there feverish distresses born of delusion, whether physical or mental, by which, while being burned by those feverish distresses born of delusion, he would sleep in suffering?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”— “Indeed, young man, when that householder or householder’s son is being burned by those feverish distresses born of delusion...”
One might sleep in suffering; that delusion has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, I have slept happily.
Truly, at all times the brahmin who has attained final Nibbāna sleeps in happiness—
he who is not smeared by sensual desires.
Become cooled and free from acquisitions,
having severed all attachments and removed the distress from the heart.
“Peaceful, having attained peace of mind, one dwells happily.
Thus ends the fifth [verse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.36 4.
Devadūtavagga Devadūtasutta (The Discourse on the Divine Messengers)
“Monks, there are these three divine messengers. What are the three? [The Buddha said:]”
In this case, monks, a certain person engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell seize him by his various limbs and present him to King Yama, saying:
“‘Sire, this man is disrespectful toward his mother, disrespectful toward his father, undisciplined toward recluses, undisciplined toward brahmins, and he does not honor his elders in the family.
May Your Majesty inflict punishment upon him.
Then, monks, King Yama questions, interrogates, and cross-examines that person regarding that first divine messenger:”
“Ho there, man! Did you not see the first divine messenger appear among human beings?
He replied:
“I did not see him, venerable sir.”
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:

“Ho there, man! Did you not see among humans a woman or a man who was eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, decrepit with age, bent like a roof-rafter, hunched, supported by a staff, and trembling?”
"Have you ever seen a person walking who is afflicted, whose youth has passed, whose teeth are broken, whose hair is gray, whose body is withered, whose head is bald, who is wrinkled,
and whose limbs are covered with freckles? He replied thus:
‘I saw it, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama said this to him:
‘O man, did it not occur to you—that you were wise, mindful, and mature—[that you should have reflected on this]?’
‘I too am subject to old age and have not transcended it; come now, let me do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind’?
He would say this:
‘I could not, Bhante. I would have been negligent, Bhante.’”
Then, monks, King Yama says to him:
"Ho there, man! Because of negligence you did not do what is good by body, speech, or mind.
Truly, my good man, they will deal with you exactly as one who is negligent deserves."
Moreover, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother,
nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations,
nor by the deities, nor by recluses and brahmins.
‘Now, this evil deed was committed by you; you alone shall experience its result.
Then, monks, after King Yama has questioned, examined, and exhorted him regarding the first divine messenger, he questions, examines, and exhorts him regarding the second divine messenger:
‘Ho there, man! Did you not see the second divine messenger appearing among human beings?’”
He says thus:
"I did not see them, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama says this:
“O man, have you not seen among human beings a woman or a man who is afflicted,
suffering, and gravely ill, lying fouled in their own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some and laid down by others?
He replied thus:
‘I saw it, Bhante,’ he replied.
Then, monks, King Yama said to him:
‘O man, did this not occur to you—being wise, mindful, and mature:’
“Am I also subject to illness and not exempt from illness? Come now, let me do what is good with body, speech, and mind?
He replied:
“I could not, Bhante. I would have been negligent, Bhante.”
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:
“Ho there, man! Because of negligence, you did not do what is good with body, speech, or mind.
Truly, ho there, man, they will deal with you according as you were negligent.”
Moreover, this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother,
nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and blood relations,
nor by the deities, nor by ascetics and brahmins.
"Indeed, you yourself have committed this evil deed; you alone shall experience its result.
Monks, after King Yama has thus interrogated, examined, and exhorted him regarding the second divine messenger, he interrogates, examines, and exhorts him regarding the third divine messenger:
"O man, did you not see the third divine messenger appearing among human beings?"
He says thus:
‘I did not see him, Bhante.
Then, monks, King Yama says this to him:
“O man, have you not seen among human beings a woman or a man dead for one day, or dead for two days, or dead for three days—swollen, discolored, and festering?
He replied:
“I have seen them, Bhante.”
Then, monks, King Yama says to him:
“O man, did it not occur to you—you who were wise, mindful, and mature:
‘I too am subject to death, I have not transcended death; come now, let me do what is wholesome by way of body, speech, and mind’?”
He says this:
“I was not able, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.
To him, monks, King Yama speaks thus:
“O man, through negligence you have not done what is good by way of body, speech, or mind.
Truly, O man, they will deal with you according to your negligence.
Moreover, this evil deed of yours was not committed by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother.”
“Sister, this was not done by your sister, nor by your friends and companions, nor by your kinsmen and blood relatives, nor by the deities, nor by recluses and brahmins;
rather, it was this evil deed that was committed by you yourself. You alone shall experience its result.”
“Monks, when King Yama has thus interrogated, cross-examined, and rebuked him regarding that third divine messenger, he remains silent.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell inflict upon him a torture called the ‘fivefold bondage.
They drive a red-hot iron stake through one hand; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other hand; [they drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot]…”
They drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the second foot; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the middle of the chest.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell, having laid him down, flay him with adzes.
There he experiences feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter; yet he does not die so long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell, seizing him with his feet up and his head down, flay him with axes... [and so on].
“Monks, the wardens of hell yoke that person to a chariot and drive him back and forth across ground that is burning, blazing, and aflame.
(…) Monks, the wardens of hell make that person climb up and down a great mountain of glowing coals that is burning, blazing, and aflame.
(…) Monks, the wardens of hell seize that person by his feet and head, and cast him into a cauldron of molten bronze that is heated, blazing, and aflame. (…)”
There, being cooked in the Boiling Foam, he goes up at one time, down at another, and across at another.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell cast him into the Great Hell.
And furthermore, monks, that Great Hell has four corners and four gates;
it is well-proportioned and measured out in its divisions.
Its perimeter is bounded by an iron wall,
covered over with iron;
its ground is made of iron.
Blazing and endowed with splendor,
it remains at all times, pervading a hundred leagues in every direction.
“Bhikkhus, in the past, this thought occurred to King Yama:
‘It is said, sirs, that those in the world who perform evil deeds are subjected to such various forms of punishment.
Oh, that I might obtain human birth, and that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, might arise in the world, and that I might attend upon that Blessed One!’”
“If the Blessed One were to teach me the Dhamma, and if I were to understand that Dhamma of the Blessed One.
Yet, monks, I do not say this having heard it from another ascetic or brahmin; rather, monks, I say only what has been known by me personally, seen by me personally, and realized by me personally.
Thus urged by the messengers of the gods...
Those young men who are negligent,
those people who have entered an inferior state, will grieve for a long time.
But those virtuous, true persons here who, having been exhorted by the messengers of the gods,
do not become negligent—
Never [revert] from the noble Dhamma;
seeing danger in clinging,
which gives rise to birth and death.
Through non-clinging they are liberated in the destruction of birth and death;
being heedful, they are happy.
They have attained final peace in this very life;
having transcended all enmity and fear,
they have overcome all suffering.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.37 4.
Devadūtavagga (The Chapter on the Messengers of the Gods)
The Discourse on the Four Great Kings (Catumahārājasutta). “Bhikkhus,
on the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers and counselors of the Four Great Kings roam this world, [saying]:”

‘I hope that many people among men are filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in their families; I hope they observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds.
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight, monks, the sons of the Four Great Kings roam this world, [inquiring]:

‘I hope that many people among men are filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in their families; I hope they observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds.’”
Therefore, monks, on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, the Four Great Kings themselves travel through this world, [inquiring]:

"I wonder whether many people among humans are filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in their families; whether they observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds?

Monks, if there are few people among humans who are filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in their families; who observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds...
“Monks, when the Four Great Kings have assembled and are seated together in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, they announce:

‘Sirs, among humans there are few who honor their mother, honor their father, honor the ascetic, honor the brahmin, respect the elders of the family, observe the Uposatha, keep watch on it, and perform meritorious deeds.
Because of this, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas become displeased.”
‘Indeed, sirs, the divine hosts will diminish, and the asura hosts will increase.

But if, monks, there are many among human beings who revere their mothers, revere their fathers, revere ascetics, revere brahmins, honor the elders of the family, observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds—then, monks, the Four Great Kings announce this to the Tāvatiṃsa gods when they have assembled and are seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall: [they report what has occurred].

‘Indeed, sirs, many among humans are filial toward their mothers and fathers, respectful toward recluses and brahmins, honoring those who are senior in their clans; they observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds.
Because of this, monks, the gods of the Thirty-three are uplifted, thinking:
‘Ah, the divine hosts will surely increase, and the hosts of the asuras will diminish!’
“Bhikkhus, once in the past, Sakka, lord of the devas, while exhorting the Tāvatiṃsa devas, on that occasion recited this verse:
‘On the fourteenth and the fifteenth,
and also on the eighth day of the fortnight;’”
One should observe the Uposatha on the fortnight of miracles, perfectly endowed with its eight factors.
‘And whoever among men is like me.

Now, monks, this verse was poorly sung and not well sung, poorly spoken and not well spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas. For what reason? Because it was composed by one who is himself subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and defilement.”
For Sakka, monks, the lord of the devas, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion.
But as for that monk, monks, who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis— of him, monks...
This, monks, is fit for a bhikkhu to say:
“On the fourteenth, on the fifteenth,
and on the eighth day of the fortnight;”
One should observe the Uposatha on the fortnight of miracles, perfectly endowed with its eight factors.
"And that person who is like me—
why is that? Because, monks,
that bhikkhu is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion."
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.38 4.

On the fourteenth and the fifteenth,
and on the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles—
One such as I, a person, should observe the Uposatha complete with its eight factors.
"But that verse, monks, was poorly sung and not well sung by Sakka, the lord of the devas; it was poorly spoken and not well spoken.

And why is that? Because, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, is not yet freed from birth, aging, and death; he is not yet freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not yet freed from suffering, I say."

And why is that? Because, monks, that bhikkhu is completely freed from birth, aging, and death; he is completely freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is completely freed from suffering, I say.
Thus ends the eighth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.39 4. Devadūtavagga Sukhumālasutta “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The delicate person, the delicate in suffering, and the delicate in both. And how, monks, is one a delicate person? Here, monks, someone is well-born on both sides, of pure descent, unblemished back to the seventh generation, with flawless lineage of mother and father, possessing wealth and property, abounding in gold and silver, abundant in bullion and grain, abundant in wealth and grain, abundant in property and possessions—this, monks, is called a delicate person. And how, monks, is one delicate in suffering? Here, monks, someone is afflicted by illness, suffering, gravely ill, pierced by the dart of pain, with little pleasure and much pain, with little happiness and much distress—this, monks, is called delicate in suffering. And how, monks, is one delicate in both? Here, monks, someone is both well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and also afflicted by illness, suffering, gravely ill, pierced by the dart of pain, with little pleasure and much pain, with little happiness and much distress—this, monks, is called delicate in both. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Monks, I was delicate, most delicate, supremely delicate. Monks,
it is said that lotus ponds were constructed by my father in his residence.”
“Bhikkhus, in one place blue lotuses are planted, in another red lotuses, and in another white lotuses, all for my sake.
Yet, bhikkhus, I do not wear Kāsī sandalwood. My turban, bhikkhus, is of Kāsī cloth; my tunic is of Kāsī cloth; my lower garment is of Kāsī cloth; my upper robe is of Kāsī cloth.
And day and night, bhikkhus, a white parasol is held over me.”
‘May cold or heat, grass, dust, or dew not touch him.
Monks, I had three palaces for me: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
During the four months of the rainy season, monks, while being entertained by female musicians in the rainy-season palace, I did not descend to the lower palace.
"Furthermore, monks, whereas in the houses of others food consisting of broken rice with sour gruel is given to the slaves,
laborers, and servants, even so, monks, in my father’s house food consisting of fine rice and meat was given to the slaves, laborers, and servants."
“Bhikkhus, when I was possessed of such supernormal power and such fine appearance, this thought occurred to me:

‘The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to aging and not exempt from aging, sees another who is aged and is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, projecting [his own condition] onto that person, thinking: “I too am subject to aging and not exempt from aging.
Yet, if I—being myself subject to aging and not exempt from aging—were to see another who is aged and be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’”
“Bhikkhus, as I reflected thus, that intoxication with youth which exists in youth was entirely abandoned.

Now, an uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to illness and not exempt from illness, when he sees another who is ill, is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, comparing himself [with that person]:
‘I too am subject to illness and not exempt from illness; yet, while I am myself subject to illness, [I do not reflect on this].’”

‘Having not transcended illness myself, if I were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with health was entirely abandoned. Now, the uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to death and not having transcended death, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, comparing himself to that very person: [“I too am subject to death; I am not exempt from death”]. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to death and not having transcended death, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with life was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to aging and not having transcended aging, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is aged, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to aging; I am not exempt from aging. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to aging and not having transcended aging, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is aged, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with youth was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to decay and not having transcended decay, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is decaying, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to decay; I am not exempt from decay. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to decay and not having transcended decay, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is decaying, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with beauty was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to death and not having transcended death, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to death; I am not exempt from death. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to death and not having transcended death, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with life was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with health was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to aging and not having transcended aging, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is aged, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to aging; I am not exempt from aging. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to aging and not having transcended aging, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is aged, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with youth was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to decay and not having transcended decay, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is decaying, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to decay; I am not exempt from decay. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to decay and not having transcended decay, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is decaying, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with beauty was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to death and not having transcended death, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to death; I am not exempt from death. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to death and not having transcended death, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with life was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with health was entirely abandoned. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with youth was entirely abandoned.
