Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to decay and not having transcended decay, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is decaying, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with beauty was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to death and not having transcended death, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to death; I am not exempt from death. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to death and not having transcended death, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me. Monks, as I reflected thus, my intoxication with life was entirely abandoned. The uninstructed worldling, being himself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, feels repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, comparing himself to that very person: “I too am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness. Thus he reflects: “If I, being myself subject to illness and not having transcended illness, were to feel repelled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, that would not
‘I too am subject to death, I have not transcended death;
and since I myself am subject to death and have not transcended it, it would be unseemly for me to feel repelled, ashamed, or disgusted upon seeing another who has died.
Monks, as I reflected in this way, whatever intoxication with life I had was entirely abandoned.
“Bhikkhus, there are three intoxications.
What three?
Intoxication with youth, intoxication with health, and intoxication with life.”
"Or, bhikkhus, intoxicated by the pride of youth, the uninstructed worldling engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Or, bhikkhus, intoxicated by the pride of health, the uninstructed worldling... [and so on].
"Or, monks, intoxicated by the intoxication of life, the uninstructed worldling engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Or, monks, intoxicated by the intoxication of youth, a monk renounces the training and reverts to the lower life."
"Or, monks, a monk intoxicated by the pride of health...
or, monks, a monk intoxicated by the pride of life, having renounced the training, reverts to the lower life.
[All] are subject to sickness, subject to aging."
Furthermore, those subject to death,
being as they are according to their nature,
ordinary people feel revulsion toward them.
If I were to feel disgust toward living beings who are of such a nature,
it would not be fitting for me.
While dwelling in this way, dwelling thus,
having known the Dhamma that is free from acquisitions, I—
Whatever intoxications there are in health,
in youth, and in life—
I have overcome all such intoxications.
Seeing the safety in renunciation,
as I beheld Nibbāna, enthusiasm arose within me.
I am not capable now of indulging in sensual pleasures;
I shall not turn back.
“Dedicated to the holy life.
Thus [ends] the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.40

4. Devadūtavagga Ādhipateyyasutta (AN 3.40, PTS AN i 147) “Monks, there are these three forms of sovereignty. What three? Sovereignty over the self, sovereignty over others, and sovereignty over both self and others. And what, monks, is sovereignty over the self? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He dwells with a mind devoid of longing, having removed longing from the body. He dwells with a mind devoid of ill will, free from enmity, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. He dwells having abandoned dullness and drowsiness, free from dullness and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending. He dwells having abandoned restlessness and remorse, his mind being inwardly peaceful. He dwells having abandoned doubt, past doubt, not questioning the teachings of the Tathāgata regarding things that are skillful. This, monks, is called sovereignty over the self. And what, monks, is sovereignty over others? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...in the Dhamma... [as above] ...in the Saṅgha... [as above]. He dwells with a mind devoid of longing... [as above] ...he dwells having abandoned doubt, past doubt, not questioning the teachings of the Tathāgata regarding things that are skillful. Furthermore, he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, monks, is called sovereignty over others. And what, monks, is sovereignty over both self and others? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...in the Dhamma... [as above] ...in the Saṅgha... [as above]. He dwells with a mind devoid of longing... [as above] ...he dwells having abandoned doubt, past doubt, not questioning the teachings of the Tathāgata regarding things that are skillful. Furthermore, he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. Moreover, he is learned, possessing the Dhamma, bearing in mind the Dhamma, recollecting the Dhamma, examining the meaning of the Dhamma. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. He dwells with a mind devoid of longing... [as above] ...he dwells having abandoned doubt, past doubt, not questioning the teachings of the Tathāgata regarding things that are skillful. This, monks, is called sovereignty over both self and others. These, monks, are the three forms of sovereignty.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three authorities.
Which three?
Authority over oneself, authority over the world, and authority over the Dhamma.”
And what, monks, is that which has oneself as its authority?
Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
"It is not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness."
I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of lodgings, nor for the sake of this existence or that existence.
Rather, I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, I thought:
"Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned."
‘It would not be fitting for me to seek such sensual pleasures as those for whose sake I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, or even worse.
He reflects thus:
‘My energy will be aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness will be established and unconfused; my body will be tranquil and unagitated; my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed.’
Thus, making oneself alone the master, one abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; one abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; one maintains oneself in purity.
This, monks, is called "having oneself as the master.
And what, monks, is "having the world as the master"?
In this case, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
"It is not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness;
nor for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of lodgings, nor for the sake of becoming this or that state of existence have I gone forth from the home life into homelessness."
"Moreover, I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am submerged in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
Yet, if I, having gone forth in this way, were to think thoughts of sensual desire, or think thoughts of ill will, or think thoughts of cruelty—this world-dwelling is indeed vast.
Moreover, in this vast world-system there are recluses and brahmins who possess supernormal powers, have the divine eye, and are knowers of others' minds.
They see even from afar, they are not seen even when nearby, and they understand the mind with their own minds.
They too would know me thus: [as follows].
‘Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
Now there are deities who possess supernormal power, who have the divine eye, and who know the minds of others.
They see even from afar, they are not seen when nearby, and they know the mind with their own minds.
They might think of me thus:
“See, sirs, this clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, yet he dwells beset by evil, unwholesome states.
He reflects thus:
‘My energy shall be aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused; my body shall be tranquil and unagitated; my mind shall be concentrated and one-pointed.
Taking the world itself as his authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he maintains himself in purity. This, monks, is called having the world as one’s authority.
And what, monks, is the predominance of the Dhamma?
Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
‘It is not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.’
It was not for the sake of alms-food, nor for the sake of lodgings, nor for the sake of becoming this or that state of existence that I went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Rather, I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, I thought:
"Perhaps an end might be discerned to this entire mass of suffering."
“The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
Furthermore, there are my fellow celibates who dwell knowing and seeing.
If I, having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, were to dwell lazy and negligent, that would not be fitting for me.”

Thus he reflects: “My energy will indeed be aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness will be established and unconfused; my body will be tranquil and unagitated; my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed.
Making the Dhamma alone his authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.
This, monks, is called the predominance of the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the three predominances.
There is no such thing as secrecy in the world.
As you are performing an evil deed,
O man, your own self knows whether it is true or false.
It is truly a blessing for you, O Sakka,
that you do not despise yourself,
seeing the evil within yourself while it still exists.
You conceal yourself;
yet the gods and the Tathāgatas see you,
the fool, acting contrary to the way of the world.
Therefore, one who has oneself as the guiding principle,
who is wise, a master of the world, and a meditator;
who has the Dhamma as the guiding principle and lives in accordance with the Dhamma—
The sage who is resolute in truth does not decline.
Having assailed Māra and overcome the Ender,
he who is diligent has touched the destruction of birth.
Thus such is the wise one, the knower of the world,
the sage who is not attached to any phenomena.
The tenth [chapter].
The Fourth Chapter: The Section on the Divine Messengers.
Its summary:
Brahmā, Ānanda, Sāriputta.
The Nidāna, Hatthaka,
the two messengers, the two kings,
and the section on Sukhumāla and Adhipateyya.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.41 5. Cūḷavagga Sammukhībhāvasutta – The Presence of the Three “Monks, there are these three presences. What three? The presence of the Buddha, the presence of the Dhamma, and the presence of the Saṅgha. And what, monks, is the presence of the Buddha? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. When a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Tathāgata. And whatever state arises in dependence on the straight mind is wholesome, not unwholesome. This, monks, is called the presence of the Buddha. And what, monks, is the presence of the Dhamma? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. When a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Dhamma. And whatever state arises in dependence on the straight mind is wholesome, not unwholesome. This, monks, is called the presence of the Dhamma. And what, monks, is the presence of the Saṅgha? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. When a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Saṅgha. And whatever state arises in dependence on the straight mind is wholesome, not unwholesome. This, monks, is called the presence of the Saṅgha. These, monks, are the three presences.”
“Bhikkhus, when three things are present, a clansman endowed with faith generates much merit. Which three? [The Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha].”
“Monks, through the presence of faith, a faithful clansman generates much merit.
Monks, through the presence of things worthy of being given, a faithful clansman generates much merit.
Monks, through the presence of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman generates much merit.”
“Monks, when these three things are present, a faithful clansman generates much merit.
Thus was the first [sutta].
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 3.42.

5. Cūḷavagga: Tiṭhānasutta (AN 3.42, PTS AN i 150) “Bhikkhus, there are these four grounds for the settling of a dispute. What four? A dispute settled by recollection, a dispute settled by investigation of the Dhamma, a dispute settled by majority vote, and a dispute settled by the rule of the majority. These, bhikkhus, are the four grounds for the settling of a dispute.”
“Monks, one who is endowed with faith and is confident should be known by three grounds.
By which three?

He desires to see those possessed of virtue; he desires to hear the true Dhamma; and he dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure-palmed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and rejoicing in sharing what he has.
Monks, by these three grounds a person of faith and confidence is to be known:
he desires to see those who possess virtue and vows,
and he wishes to hear the true Dhamma.
One who has removed the stain of stinginess regarding the discipline—
verily, such a person is called "one endowed with faith. Thus ends the second [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.43 5. Cūḷavagga Atthavasasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these eight benefits of the noble life. What eight? One gains wealth that is not shared with others; one gains a reputation that is not shared with others; one gains a retinue that is not shared with others; one gains a heavenly rebirth that is not shared with others; one gains a state of happiness that is not shared with others; one gains a state of well-being that is not shared with others; one gains a state of fame that is not shared with others; and one gains a state of renown that is not shared with others. These, bhikkhus, are the eight benefits of the noble life.”
“Bhikkhus, seeing three reasons, it is indeed sufficient for one to teach the Dhamma to others.
What are the three?
The one who teaches the Dhamma experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma.
The one who listens to the Dhamma experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma.
Both the one who teaches the Dhamma and the one who listens to the Dhamma experience both the meaning and the Dhamma.
“Monks, seeing these three purposes, it is indeed sufficient to teach the Dhamma to others.
This is the third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.44.

5. Cūḷavagga: Kathāpavattisutta (AN 3.44, PTS AN i 151) “Monks, when a talk on the Dhamma is being given, it is possible that five kinds of persons will attend to it. What five? One who attends to it thinking: ‘I shall hear the Dhamma I have not heard before’; one who attends to it thinking: ‘I shall hear the Dhamma already heard, so as to clarify what I have understood’; one who attends to it thinking: ‘Perhaps I shall get to see the Teacher or those who are like the Teacher’; one who attends to it thinking: ‘Perhaps I shall get to see eminent bhikkhus, elders of great stature, who are learned, heirs of the Dhamma, experts on the Dhamma, experts on the Vinaya, experts on the Mātikā’; and one who attends to it thinking: ‘Perhaps I shall gain some material support. When a talk on the Dhamma is being given, it is possible that these five kinds of persons will attend to it.”
“Monks, conversation proceeds on three grounds.
What three?
The one who teaches the Dhamma experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma.”
“The one who hears the Dhamma experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma.
Both the one who teaches the Dhamma and the one who hears the Dhamma experience both the meaning and the Dhamma.
It is through these three factors, monks, that conversation proceeds.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.45 5.
Cūḷavagga (The Shorter Section)
The Discourse on the Wise (Paṇḍitasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these three things designated by the wise, designated by the true person.”
Which three?
Giving, monks, is prescribed by the wise, prescribed by the virtuous.
The going forth, monks, is prescribed by the wise, prescribed by the virtuous.
“Monks, attending upon one’s mother and father is prescribed by the wise and prescribed by the good.
Monks, these three things are prescribed by the wise and prescribed by the good.
Giving is prescribed by the virtuous.”
Non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control;
service to mother and father,
and to those who are peaceful and lead the holy life.
These are the states that a wise person should cultivate,
a noble one endowed with vision.
“He attains a blissful world.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 3.46.

5. Cūḷavagga Sīlavantasutta (AN 3.46, PTS AN i 151) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is virtuous; the person who is immoral; the person who is both virtuous and immoral; and the person who is neither virtuous nor immoral. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then explained: “Bhikkhus, the person who is virtuous is rare in the world. The person who is immoral is more numerous than that. The person who is both virtuous and immoral is more numerous than those two. But the person who is neither virtuous nor immoral is the rarest of all. [The Buddha continued: “Bhikkhus, just as the blue lotus, the red lotus, or the white lotus, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by it; even so, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, though born in the world and grown in the world, transcends the world and dwells unsoiled by worldly things. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be like the blue lotus, the red lotus, or the white lotus. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”
“Monks, when virtuous renunciants dwell in dependence upon a village or a town,
people there generate much merit on three grounds.
What are those three?
"By body, by speech, and by mind.
Monks, whatever virtuous renunciants dwell in dependence upon a village or a town,
there people generate much merit through these three bases."
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.47 5.
Cūḷavagga (The Short Chapter)
Saṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
Which three?
Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.
These, monks, are the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.”
Seventh: The Discourse on the Characteristics of the Unconditioned.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of the unconditioned that belong to the unconditioned.
“What three?
Arising is not discerned, passing away is not discerned, and alteration while standing is not discerned.
These, monks, are the three unconditioned characteristics of the unconditioned.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.48 5.
Cūḷavagga (The Shorter Section)
Pabbatarājasutta: “Bhikkhus, depending on Himavanta,
the king of mountains, great sal trees grow by way of three kinds of growth.”
By which three?
They grow by means of branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow by means of bark and inner bark; they grow by means of softwood and heartwood.
Supported by the Himalayas, monks, the king of mountains, these great sāl trees grow by these three kinds of growth.
In the same way, monks, by depending on a faithful head of a family, the people within his household prosper in three ways.
In what three?
They prosper in faith, they prosper in virtue, and they prosper in wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, by depending on a clansman endowed with faith, the people within his household grow in these three ways.
Just as a rocky mountain in the wilderness,
in a vast forest,”
Just as those forest trees grow depending upon that tree,
even so it is with one endowed with virtue.
By relying here upon a faithful head of a family,
one's children, wife, and kinsmen flourish.
His ministers, his circle of kinsmen, and those who depend upon him—
these follow the virtue of that virtuous man.
Seeing generosity and good conduct,
the wise practice them for their own ultimate benefit.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
the path leading to a happy destination,
they rejoice in the world of the gods.
“Those who desire sensual pleasures rejoice.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.49.

5. Cūḷavagga Ātappakaraṇīyasutta (AN 3.49, PTS AN i 153) “Monks, when it was said: ‘This Dhamma is for one who exerts himself, not for one who does not exert himself; this Dhamma is for one who is ardent, not for one who is not ardent,’ it is with reference to this that it was said. And how, monks, is the Dhamma for one who exerts himself, not for one who does not exert himself? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute in abandoning unwholesome states and in undertaking wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not neglect the duty of development. It is in this way, monks, that the Dhamma is for one who exerts himself, not for one who does not exert himself. And how, monks, is the Dhamma for one who is ardent, not for one who is not ardent? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, monks, that the Dhamma is for one who is ardent, not for one who is not ardent.”
“Monks, ardent effort should be made for three reasons.
Which three?

Ardent effort should be made for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; [ardent effort should be made for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; ardent effort should be made for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.”
"One should exert effort for the arising of wholesome states;
one should exert effort for the endurance of arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Monks, one should exert effort in these three instances."
Monks, when a monk exerts himself for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
when he exerts himself for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
and when he exerts himself regarding arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening—
He exerts himself for the sake of endurance.
This, monks, is called a monk who is ardent, prudent, and mindful for the right ending of suffering.
Thus ends the tenth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.50 5. Cūḷavagga Mahācorasutta – The Great Robber “Monks, there are these three kinds of great robbers. What three? The one who robs by means of the sword; the one who robs by means of the stick; and the one who robs by means of the Dhamma. And how, monks, does one rob by means of the sword? Here, someone takes from a village or a forest whatever is not given, whether it be much or little, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, by means of the sword. This is called one who robs by means of the sword. And how, monks, does one rob by means of the stick? Here, someone takes from a village or a forest whatever is not given, whether it be much or little, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, by means of the stick. This is called one who robs by means of the stick. And how, monks, does one rob by means of the Dhamma? Here, someone teaches a Dhamma that is unrighteous and contrary to the good; he speaks in praise of such a Dhamma; and those who listen to his teaching, having heard it, practice accordingly. As they practice, they fall away from the true Dhamma and the Discipline. This is called one who robs by means of the Dhamma. These, monks, are the three kinds of great robbers. Of these three, monks, the one who robs by means of the Dhamma is the most blameworthy, the most wicked, and the most difficult to appease.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing three factors, a great thief breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits robbery, and lies in ambush on the road. Which three? [The text continues as follows:]”
"Here, monks, a great thief relies on uneven terrain, relies on dense thickets, and relies on powerful allies.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on uneven terrain?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a river difficult to cross or on mountainous ruggedness."
"In this way, monks, a great thief relies on uneven terrain.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on thickets?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a thicket of grass, or a thicket of trees, or a riverbank, or a dense forest grove."
In this way, monks, a great thief relies on a thicket.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on the powerful?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a king or on royal ministers.
It occurs to him:
"If anyone says anything to me, these kings or royal ministers will explain the meaning to me in my defense.
If anyone says something to him, those kings or royal ministers explain the meaning to him in his defense.
"In this way, monks, a great thief relies on the powerful.
Possessing these three factors, monks, a great thief breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits robbery in solitary dwellings, and lies in ambush on the road.

In the same way, monks, a wicked monk who possesses these three factors maintains himself in a state of injury and ruin; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit."
Which three?
Here, monks, an evil bhikkhu relies on the uneven, relies on the thickets, and relies on the powerful.
And how, monks, does an evil bhikkhu rely on the uneven?
"Here, monks, a wicked monk is possessed of uneven bodily action, he is possessed of uneven verbal action, and he is possessed of uneven mental action.
In this way, monks, a wicked monk relies on what is uneven.
And how, monks, does a wicked monk rely on the thicket?
"In this case, monks, a wicked monk holds wrong view; he is possessed of a view that grasps at extremes.
It is in this way, monks, that a wicked monk relies on a thicket.
And how, monks, does a wicked monk rely on the powerful?
In this case, monks, an evil bhikkhu relies upon a king or a king’s high minister.
It occurs to him:
“If anyone says anything to me, these kings or king’s high ministers will speak up on my behalf and explain the matter.”
“If anyone says anything to him, the kings or royal ministers refute his meaning for him.
It is in this way, monks, that a wicked monk relies on the powerful.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a wicked monk maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he produces much demerit.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.56 6. Brāhmaṇavagga Palokasutta (The Discourse on Disintegration) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who disintegrates and perishes with the body; the person who disintegrates and perishes after death; and the person who disintegrates and perishes here and now. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who disintegrates and perishes with the body? Here, bhikkhus, someone is a killer of living beings, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, one who speaks falsely, one who speaks divisively, one who speaks harshly, and one who indulges in idle chatter. He is full of longing, with a mind full of ill will, holding wrong view, and he possesses the habits of such a person. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, even in hell. But while remaining right here, he is already disintegrating and perishing. This is called a person who disintegrates and perishes with the body. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who disintegrates and perishes after death? Here, bhikkhus, someone is a killer of living beings... [as above] ...and holds wrong view, but he does not possess the habits of such a person. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, even in hell. This is called a person who disintegrates and perishes after death. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who disintegrates and perishes here and now? Here, bhikkhus, someone is a killer of living beings... [as above] ...and holds wrong view, and he possesses the habits of such a person. By means of the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it. This is called a person who disintegrates and perishes here and now. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 3.56, PTS AN i 159) Then a certain wealthy brahmin approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that wealthy brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“In the past, indeed, this world was as if filled with people right up to the Avīci hell; the villages, towns, and royal capitals were so close together that a cock could fly from one to another.
What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why nowadays there is a decline of people, and sparseness is discerned;
why villages have become non-villages, towns have become non-towns, cities have become non-cities, and districts have become non-districts?”
“Brahmin, at present people are stained by unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and beset by false doctrines.
Being stained by unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and beset by false doctrines, they take up sharp weapons and deprive one another of life; thereby many people die.
This, brahmin, is the cause, this is the condition, why there is now a decline and a diminution of human beings.”
It becomes apparent that villages become non-villages, market towns become non-towns, cities become non-cities, and districts become non-districts.
Furthermore, brahmin, at present people are dyed with unrighteous passion, overcome by improper greed, and beset by false doctrine.

Because of that, there is famine, a scarcity of grain, white bones, and subsistence by means of tally-sticks.

Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for three people and becomes a hindrance to three people.
Of which three?
He becomes an obstacle to the merit of the donor; he becomes an obstacle to the gains of the recipients; and furthermore, his own self is already ruined and impaired.
Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift becomes an obstacle-maker for these three and a hinderer of these three.
But as for me, Vaccha, I say this:

Which five factors have been abandoned?
Sensual desire has been abandoned, ill will has been abandoned, sloth and torpor have been abandoned, restlessness and remorse have been abandoned, and doubt has been abandoned.

Then the brahmin Tikaṇṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side after exchanging greetings with the Blessed One.

one who is a philologist and a grammarian, and is unerring in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man.

“Brahmin, the way brahmins define a brahmin who possesses the threefold knowledge is one thing, but in the discipline of the Noble One, one becomes a possessor of the threefold knowledge in quite another way.

“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.

The Blessed One said this:

“Here, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences pleasure with the body.
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as: “Equanimous and mindful, dwelling in happiness.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births... [and so on].
"Four births, five births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
'In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.'"

"Having passed away from there, I arose there. There too, I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experiencer of pleasure and pain, and such the limit of my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
This is the first true knowledge (vijjā) attained by him:
ignorance is destroyed and true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled and light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

ignorance is destroyed and true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled and light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

ignorance is destroyed, true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

By means of these three knowledges,
a brahmin becomes one possessed of the threefold knowledge;
him I call one possessed of the threefold knowledge.
“Not merely reciting and rehearsing.
“In this way, brahmin, one becomes a possessor of the threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One.
