"In this case too, Master Gotama, when it is so, the practice of merit results in multiple future bodies, namely, that which has renunciation as its basis.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava:
“Of these two ways, brahmin, which way do you prefer—the one that requires less exertion and is more fruitful and beneficial?
When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Just as it is with Master Gotama and Master Ānanda.”
"These are my objects of veneration; these are my objects of praise.
A second time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava:
"I do not ask you this, brahmin: [is it the case that...]"
“Who are those you honor, or who are those you praise?
It is in this way, brahmin, that I ask you:
“Of these two ways of practice, brahmin, which one do you prefer as being less troublesome, requiring less exertion, and yielding greater fruit and greater benefit?”
A second time, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Just as Master Gotama is, so too is Master Ānanda. These are worthy of my honor;
these are worthy of my praise.”
A third time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava:
“I do not ask you this, brahmin:
‘Who are those you honor, or who are those you praise?’”
“Thus, brahmin, I ask you this:
‘Of these two ways, brahmin, which way do you prefer—the one that requires less exertion and involves less trouble, yet yields greater fruit and greater benefit?
For a third time, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are,
so these are worthy of my honor and praise.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
When the brahmin Saṅgārava had been asked a question in accordance with the Dhamma for a third time, he faltered and did not answer.
[Thinking], “What if I were to release him?
the Blessed One then said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava:
“What conversation, brahmin, arose today among the royal officers assembled and gathered together in the king’s palace?
“This, Master Gotama, was the conversation that arose today among the royal officers assembled and gathered together in the king’s palace:
‘In the past, it is said, there were fewer bhikkhus who displayed wonders of supernormal power beyond the human state, yet they were more numerous;’”
"But now, there are even more bhikkhus and fewer who display the miracle of supernormal power (iddhipāṭihāriya), which transcends human conditions.
"This, Master Gotama, was the conversation that arose among the king’s men as they were sitting together and assembled in the royal palace today.
"There are, brahmin, these three miracles."
Which three?
The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.
And what, brahmin, is the miracle of psychic power?
“Here, brahmin, a certain person experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains unhindered, as if through space;
and he dives in and out of the earth, as if it were water.”
In water; he walks upon water without breaking the surface, just as on earth; he travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
with his hand he touches and strokes these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
and even as far as the Brahma-world, he exercises mastery with his body.’
This, brahmin, is called the marvel of psychic power.
And what, brahmin, is the marvel of direct communication?
Here, brahmin, a certain person communicates by means of a sign:
‘Such is your mind, such is your intention, such is your thought.
Even if he predicts much, it happens exactly so and not otherwise.
But here, brahmin, some person does not predict by means of signs; rather, having heard the voice of humans, non-humans, or deities, he predicts:
‘Such is your mind, such is your intention, such is your thought.
Even if he predicts much, it happens exactly so and not otherwise.
But here, brahmin, some person does not predict by means of a sign, nor by means of humans or non-humans.

Or having heard the sound of deities, he declares: "Such is your mind, such is your mind, such is your consciousness. Moreover, when one is thinking and pondering, having heard the sound produced by the movement of thought, he declares:
"Your mind is thus, your mind is so, your consciousness is such.
Even if he declares much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
But here, brahmin, a certain person does not indeed predict by means of signs, nor does he predict having heard the voices of humans, non-humans, or deities,
nor does he predict having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought from one who is thinking and deliberating;
rather, having entered upon a concentration free from directed thought and evaluation, he understands the mind with his own mind:
‘Just as these mental formations of this venerable one have been directed, immediately following this state of mind, he will think such-and-such a thought.
Even if he explains much, it happens exactly so and not otherwise.
This, brahmin, is called the miracle of direct declaration (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*).
And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction?
Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus:
“Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to this, do not attend to that; abandon this, and having entered upon this, dwell therein.”
“This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction.
These, brahmin, are the three miracles.
Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle do you consider to be the most excellent and the most sublime?”
“In this regard, Master Gotama, as for this miracle: here someone experiences various kinds of psychic power...
[as far as] he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
This miracle, Master Gotama, is such that whoever performs it, he alone experiences it; whoever performs it, it belongs to him alone.”
"Master Gotama, this miracle of mine appears like a form produced by magic.
Furthermore, Master Gotama, when someone here indicates by means of a sign, saying:
'Your mind is thus, your mind is such, your consciousness is such,' and though he may indicate much, it is exactly so and not otherwise."
"But here, Master Gotama, a certain person does not indeed predict by means of a sign; rather, having heard the sound of humans, or non-humans, or deities, he predicts...
nor does he predict by hearing the sound of humans, or non-humans, or deities; rather, while thinking and pondering, having heard the sound produced by the movement of thought, he predicts..."

Nor does he announce it by hearing the sound of the diffusion of thought while one is thinking and pondering; rather, having entered a concentration free from directed thought and evaluation, he understands the mind with his own mind:
“As this venerable one’s mental formations are directed, such a thought will arise immediately after this consciousness of his. Even if he announces much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
"Master Gotama, this miracle too is such that whoever performs it, he alone experiences it; whoever performs it, it belongs to him alone.
Master Gotama, this miracle of yours also appears to me like a phenomenon associated with illusion.
But as for this miracle, Master Gotama, where someone instructs another thus:"
"‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to the mind in this way, do not attend to it in that way; abandon this, and having entered upon this, dwell therein.
This, Master Gotama, among these three kinds of wonders, is the most excellent and the most sublime.
It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!"
"Excellent indeed is this that has been spoken by Master Gotama! And because of these three miracles, we shall remember Master Gotama as one endowed with them.
For Master Gotama experiences various kinds of psychic power... [as far as] he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma-world;
and Master Gotama, having entered upon a concentration free from directed thought and evaluation, understands with his own mind the minds of others."
‘Just as these mental formations of this venerable one have been directed, immediately following this state of mind, he will think such-and-such a thought.
For Master Gotama instructs thus:
‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to the mind in this way, do not attend to it in that way; abandon this, and having entered upon this, dwell therein.’”
“Certainly, brahmin, I have spoken these words to you out of malice and with intent to provoke you;
nevertheless, I shall answer you.
For I, brahmin, experience various kinds of psychic power... [as before] ...even as far as the Brahma-world, I wield mastery with my body.”
"For I, brahmin, having entered upon a concentration free from directed thought and evaluation, understand by encompassing his mind with my own mind:
'As this venerable one's mental formations are directed, immediately following this consciousness, he will direct such-and-such a thought.
For it is thus, brahmin, that I instruct."
“‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to the mind in this way, do not attend to it in that way; abandon this, and having entered upon this, dwell therein.
“But, Master Gotama, is there even a single other bhikkhu who possesses these three kinds of wonders, apart from Master Gotama?”

“Indeed, brahmin, it is not only one hundred, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred; rather, there are even more than that—those bhikkhus who are endowed with these three marvels.
“But where, Master Gotama, do those bhikkhus dwell at present?
“In this very Saṅgha of bhikkhus, brahmin.”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [even so has this Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama.]”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many lines of reasoning.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
The tenth.
The first chapter, on Brahmins.
Its summary verse:
Two brahmins, Caññatara and Palokavaccha,
and Tikaṇṇa were converted by the wanderer Nibbuta.
"And with a voice like a lute.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.61, Mahāvagga.
The Discourse on the Bases of Sectarian Tenets (Titthāyatanasutta): “Monks,
there are these three bases of sectarian tenets which, when pursued, investigated, and pressed by the wise, even after going as far as possible, result in non-action.”
Which three?
There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view:
"Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past."
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Deity (issaranimmāna).
Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:”
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is without cause or condition.
In this regard, monks, when I approach those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past,’ I say this to them:
“Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past’?
When asked this by me, they admit, “Yes.”
To them I say this:
"In that case, venerable sirs, you will be killers of living beings because of what was done in the past; you will be takers of what is not given because of what was done in the past;
you will be unchaste because of what was done in the past; you will be speakers of falsehood because of what was done in the past."
‘They will be slanderers because of past deeds; they will be harsh-speakers because of past deeds; they will be idle talkers because of past deeds;
they will be covetous because of past deeds; they will be ill-willed because of past deeds;
they will hold wrong views because of past deeds.’”
“Furthermore, monks, for those who regard what was done in the past as essential, there is no desire or effort [to act], nor the thought: ‘This should be done’ or ‘This should not be done.

When what should and should not be done is thus not found to exist in truth and reality, then for those who dwell with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there can be no personal, legitimate discourse on the ascetic life.
This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.”
In this regard, monks, when those recluses and brahmins hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord’ (issaranimmāna), I approach them and say:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view?’”
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord’?
When I ask them this, they acknowledge, ‘Yes.
To them I say:

‘In that case, venerable sirs, you will be killers of living beings because of the creative act of a Supreme Lord; you will be takers of what is not given because of the creative act of a Supreme Lord;
you will be unchaste because of the creative act of a Supreme Lord; you will be speakers of falsehood because of the creative act of a Supreme Lord;
you will be speakers of divisive speech because of the creative act of a Supreme Lord; you will be speakers of harsh speech...’
‘They will become speakers of idle chatter because of the creative power of a supreme deity; they will become covetous because of the creative power of a supreme deity;
they will become ill-willed because of the creative power of a supreme deity; they will hold wrong views because of the creative power of a supreme deity.
But for those who rely on the creative power of a supreme deity as the essential truth, bhikkhus, there is no desire or effort, nor the thought: ‘This should be done’ or ‘This should not be done.’”

But when what ought to be done and what ought not to be done cannot be found in truth and reality, there can be no personal, legitimate discourse on asceticism for those who dwell with muddled mindfulness and without protection.
This, monks, is my second legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views.
In this regard, monks, as for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views:
‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is without cause or condition. Having approached them, I say this:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is without cause or condition”?’”
When they are asked this by me, they admit, "Yes.
I then say to them:
"In that case, venerable sirs, you will be killers of living beings without cause or condition... [and so on] ...you will be holders of wrong view without cause or condition."
"But for those who return to the view that there is no cause or condition, there can be no desire or effort, nor the thought: 'This should be done' or 'This should not be done.

And when what should and should not be done cannot be found as real and true, then for those who dwell with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there can be no personal, legitimate discourse on the ascetic life.
This, monks, is my third legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold such views."
“Monks, these three bases of sectarian tenets, when pursued, investigated, and scrutinized by the wise—even after going to the furthest extent—result in non-action.
But this Dhamma, monks, has been taught by me as one that is unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
And what, monks, is this Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and not censured by wise recluses and brahmins?”
“Monks, ‘These six elements’—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, and irreproachable by wise recluses and brahmins.
Monks, ‘These six bases of contact’—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, and irreproachable by wise recluses and brahmins.
Monks, ‘These eighteen mental explorations’—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, and irreproachable by wise recluses and brahmins.”
"Monks, 'These are the four noble truths'—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Monks, 'These are the six elements'—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus indeed was it said."
And with reference to what was this said?
There are, monks, these six elements:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
“‘These six elements,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me—unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, and irreproachable before wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus, it was with reference to this that it was said.
“‘These six bases of contact,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me—unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, and irreproachable before wise recluses and brahmins.”
Thus indeed it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
There are, monks, these six bases of contact.

"The eye is a sphere of contact, the ear is a sphere of contact, the nose is a sphere of contact, the tongue is a sphere of contact, the body is a sphere of contact, and the mind is a sphere of contact.
These, monks, are the six spheres of contact; this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and beyond criticism by wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
“Bhikkhus, these eighteen mental explorations are the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and beyond censure by wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus it was said.
And with reference to what was this said?
Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for joy, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for grief, and one dwells upon a form that is a basis for equanimity.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so forth].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for joy, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for grief, or one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity.
“‘These eighteen mental explorations, monks, are the Dhamma taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, irreproachable, and not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus, it was with reference to this that it was said.
‘These four noble truths, monks, are the Dhamma taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, irreproachable, and not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.’”
Thus it was said.
And with reference to what was this said?
Monks, the descent into the womb occurs depending upon six elements.

When there is descent [into the womb], there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling.
Now, monks, for one who feels, I declare: "This is suffering," I declare: "This is the origin of suffering," I declare: "This is the cessation of suffering," and I declare:
"This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (…) death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not to get what one desires is suffering.
In short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises.
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;
with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
In this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
“‘These are the four noble truths,’ monks—this Dhamma has been taught by me as unrefuted, undefiled, irreproachable, and uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
The first.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.62 7. Mahāvagga Bhayasutta (The Discourse on Fear) “Monks, there are these three fears that arise in the world. What three? The fear of death, the fear of ill-repute, and the fear of the next world. These are the three fears that arise in the world.

When, monks, a noble disciple has abandoned the fear of death, abandoned the fear of ill-repute, and abandoned the fear of the next world, he is called a noble disciple who has crossed over the flood, gone beyond, and reached the further shore. And how, monks, does a noble disciple abandon the fear of death? Here, monks, a noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly awakened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. To this extent, monks, a noble disciple abandons the fear of death. And how, monks, does a noble disciple abandon the fear of ill-repute? Here, monks, a noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. To this extent, monks, a noble disciple abandons the fear of ill-repute. And how, monks, does a noble disciple abandon the fear of the next world? Here, monks, a noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. To this extent, monks, a noble disciple abandons the fear of the next world. When, monks, a noble disciple has abandoned the fear of death, abandoned the fear of ill-repute, and abandoned the fear of the next world, he is called a noble disciple who has crossed over the flood, gone beyond, and reached the further shore.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three fears that do not exist between mother and son,” so says the uninstructed worldling.
What are the three?
There comes a time, monks, when a great conflagration breaks out.
When that great conflagration has broken out, monks, villages are burned, market towns are burned, and cities are burned.
As the villages, market towns, and cities burn, there a mother does not find her son, nor does a son find his mother.
“Monks, this is the first peril involving mother and son that the uninstructed worldling speaks of.
Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when a great rain-cloud pours down.
When a great rain-cloud has poured down, monks, a great flood arises.”
But when great floods arise, monks, villages are swept away, market towns are swept away, and cities are swept away.
When villages, market towns, and cities are being swept away, there a mother does not find her son, nor does a son find his mother.
This, monks, is the second peril involving the separation of mother and son, which the uninstructed worldling speaks of.
Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when there is fear and turmoil in the wilderness, and the people of the countryside wander about mounted on chariots.

When there is such fear, monks, when there is turmoil in the wilderness and the people of the countryside are wandering about mounted on chariots, there a mother does not find her son, nor does a son find his mother.
This, monks, is what the uninstructed worldling calls the third peril involving the separation of mother and son.
“Monks, these three fears that do not separate mother and son are what the uninstructed worldling speaks of.
Yet, monks, these three fears that actually do separate mother and son are what the uninstructed worldling speaks of as fears that do not separate mother and son.
What are the three?”
There comes a time, monks, when a great conflagration breaks out.
When that great conflagration has broken out, monks, villages are burned, market towns are burned, and cities are burned.
While the villages, market towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time—though it may be rare—when a mother finds her son, or a son finds his mother.
“Monks, this is the first danger that an uninstructed worldling speaks of as a danger involving mother and son, though it is actually a danger not involving mother and son.
Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when a great rain-cloud pours down.
When a great rain-cloud has poured down, monks, a great flood arises.”
But when a great flood occurs, monks, villages are swept away, market towns are swept away, and cities are swept away.
When villages, market towns, and cities are being swept away, there comes a time—though it may be rare—when a mother finds her son, or a son finds his mother.
This, monks, is the second danger that is truly a danger between mother and son, yet the uninstructed worldling speaks of it as a danger between mother and son.
Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when there is danger, a disturbance in the wilderness, and the people of the countryside, mounted on their chariots, wander about.

When such danger exists, monks, when there is a disturbance in the wilderness and the people of the countryside are wandering about mounted on their chariots, there comes a time—though it may be only once in a while—when even a mother loses her son, or a son loses his mother.
This, monks, is the third instance where the uninstructed worldling speaks of a "danger involving mother and son" as being a "danger devoid of mother and son."
“Monks, these three fears that are indeed fears between mother and son are spoken of by the uninstructed worldling as fears not between mother and son.
Monks, there are these three fears that are not between mother and son.
What are the three?”
The fear of aging, the fear of illness, and the fear of death.
Monks, a mother does not obtain this wish for her son as he grows old:
"May I grow old, but may my son not grow old."
Nor does a son, when his mother is growing old, obtain [the wish]:
"May I grow old, but let my mother not grow old.
Monks, a mother does not obtain [the wish] for her son when he is falling ill: [“May I fall ill, but let my son not fall ill”].
‘I am falling ill; may my son not fall ill’;
yet a son, when his mother is falling ill, does not likewise obtain this:
‘I am falling ill; may my mother not fall ill.’
Monks, when a mother is dying, she does not have this wish:
"May I die, but let my son not die";
nor does a son, when his mother is dying, have this wish: [“May I die, but let my mother not die”].
‘I am dying; may my mother not die.
These, monks, are the three fears that do not spare mother and son.
There is, monks, a path, there is a way that leads to the abandoning and the transcending of these three fears involving mother and son, and these three fears that do not spare mother and son.
"And what, monks, is the path and what is the way that leads to the abandoning and the transcending of these three fears involving mother and son, and these three fears not involving mother and son?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

“Monks, this is the path, this is the way that leads to the abandoning and the transcending of these three fears involving mother and son, and these three fears not involving mother and son. Thus was the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.63
7. Mahāvagga: The Discourse on Veṇāgapura (AN 3.63, PTS AN i 180)
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Venāgapura.
The brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura."
Furthermore, this excellent report has spread concerning the venerable Gotama:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having personally realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—through direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Veṇāgapura approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the courteous and amiable conversation, sat down to one side;
some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan.
Some sat down to one side, while others sat down to one side in silence.
Seated to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said this to the Blessed One:
"It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!"
To such an extent, Master Gotama, are your faculties serene, and your complexion is pure and radiant.
Just as a ripe jujube fruit in autumn is pure and radiant,
even so, Master Gotama, are your faculties serene, and your complexion is pure and radiant.
"Just as, Master Gotama, a palmyra fruit recently released from its bond is pure and bright, even so are the faculties of Master Gotama serene, his complexion pure and bright.

Just as, Master Gotama, a bowl made of Jambu-river gold, well-worked by a skilled smith’s apprentice, well-polished at the forge and placed upon a yellow cloth, shines, glows, and radiates; even so are the faculties of Master Gotama serene, his complexion pure and bright."
In the same way, the faculties of Master Gotama are serene, his complexion is pure and radiant. As for those high and luxurious beds, Master Gotama— such as a sofa, a divan, a woolen rug,

a patterned rug, a white woolen rug, a long-haired rug, a short-haired rug, a cotton-down quilt, a quilt of various colors, one with long fleece on both sides, or one with long fleece on only one side—

“Surely Master Gotama must be one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, such high and luxurious beds as those made of kāṭṭissa, of silk, of embroidered cloth, elephant-rug covers, horse-rug covers, chariot-rug covers, antelope skins, fine spreads of kadali-deer hide, with canopies above and red cushions at both ends.”
“Furthermore, brahmin, as for those high and luxurious beds and seats,
such as: a long chair, a sofa, a woolen rug, a patterned cloth, a white woolen cloth, a cotton-down quilt, a multi-layered quilt, a long-haired coverlet, a single-sided long-haired coverlet,

a red silk cloth, a silk cloth embroidered with gems, a golden cloth, a silver cloth, an elephant-back rug, a horse-back rug, a chariot-seat rug, a rug made of antelope hide, and a choice spread of kadali-deer skin.”
It has a canopy and red pillows at both ends.
These are difficult for renunciants to obtain, and even if obtained, they are not allowable.
There are, however, brahmin, these three high and luxurious beds and seats, which I now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
Which three?
The celestial high and luxurious bed, the divine high and luxurious bed, and the noble high and luxurious bed.
These, brahmin, are the three high and luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is that divine high and luxurious bed on which you now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship?
“In this case, brahmin, whatever village or town I am staying near, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I enter that very village or town for alms.
Having returned from the alms round after the meal, I enter the forest itself.”
So, whatever grasses or leaves were there, I gathered them together in one place and sat down, folding my legs crosswise, setting my body erect, and establishing mindfulness before me.

Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.
And with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experienced happiness with the body;
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in happiness who is equanimous and mindful."

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
If, brahmin, while I am in such a state, I walk back and forth, then at that time my walking is divine.
If, brahmin, while I am in such a state, I stand still, then at that time my standing is divine.
“If, brahmin, I sit down while being thus, on that occasion this is my divine seat.
If, brahmin, I lie down while being thus, on that occasion this is my divine high and luxurious bed.
This, brahmin, is the divine high and luxurious bed, which I now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.”
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
Who else could obtain such a divine high and luxurious bed at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, other than Master Gotama?
But what, Master Gotama, is that Brahmā-like high and luxurious bed which you now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship?”
“Here, brahmin, whatever village or town I am depending on for my residence, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I enter that very village or town for alms.
After the meal, returning from the alms round, I enter the edge of the forest.
There, gathering whatever grass or leaves are available, I sit down, cross my legs, set my body erect, and establish mindfulness before me.
Thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, I dwell pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third,
and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to myself, I dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—
vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind accompanied by compassion …pe… with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy … with a mind accompanied by equanimity,
I dwell pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third.
Likewise, fourthly, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as myself, I dwell having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—
vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. If, O Brahmin,
while I am in such a state I walk back and forth, at that time my walking is Brahmā’s walking.
If, Brahmin, being thus, I stand... [as before] ...or sit...
[as before] ...or lie down, on that occasion this high and luxurious bed of mine becomes sublime.
“This, brahmin, is the high and luxurious bed of Brahmā, which I now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
Who else could obtain such a high and luxurious bed of Brahmā at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, other than Master Gotama?”
“But what, Master Gotama, is that noble high and luxurious bed which you, Master Gotama, now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship?
“In this case, brahmin, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I enter the village or town in dependence upon which I am staying for alms.
Having returned from the alms round after the meal, I enter the forest itself.”
Therefore, whatever grass or leaves were there, I gathered them together, sat down cross-legged, set my body erect, and established mindfulness before me.
I knew thus:
"Lust has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising."
“Hatred has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future;
delusion has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
If, brahmin, I am thus disposed when I walk back and forth, on that occasion my walking back and forth is noble.
If, brahmin, being thus, I stand... [as before] ...I sit...
[as before] ...or I lie down, on that occasion this noble high and luxurious bed belongs to me.
“This, brahmin, is the noble high and luxurious bed, which I now obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
Who else could obtain such a noble high and luxurious bed at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, other than Master Gotama?”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama made the Dhamma clear in many ways.”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has elucidated the Dhamma in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.64. 7. Mahāvagga.
The Discourse to Sarabha (Sarabhasutta).
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, a wanderer named Sarabha had recently departed from this Dhamma and Discipline.
He was speaking these words in an assembly at Rājagaha:
“I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans.
And because I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, I have departed from that Dhamma and Discipline.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Those bhikkhus heard Sarabha the wanderer speaking these words in the assembly at Rājagaha:
“I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan;
and having understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan, I have therefore departed from that Dhamma and Discipline.”
Then those bhikkhus, having walked for alms in Rājagaha, returned from their almsround after the meal and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, a wanderer named Sarabha has recently departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
In the assembly at Rājagaha, he speaks these words:
‘I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans.’”
“‘But having understood the Dhamma of the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, it was for this reason that I departed from that Dhamma and Vinaya.
‘It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would go to the wanderers’ park on the bank of the Sippinikā River where the wanderer Sarabha is staying.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.”
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the wanderers’ park on the bank of the Sippinikā River, where the wanderer Sarabha was staying.
Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Sarabha:
“Is it true, Sarabha, that you say this:
‘I have understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans.
And having understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, I have departed from that Dhamma and Vinaya’?”
When this was said, the wanderer Sarabha became silent.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Sarabha:
“Speak, Sarabha; how have you understood the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans?”
“If it is incomplete for you, I shall complete it;
but if it is complete for you, I shall rejoice in it.
A second time, the wanderer Sarabha remained silent.
A third time, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Sarabha:
"Sarabha, since you claim that the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, is known to you, tell us, Sarabha, how is the Dhamma of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, understood by you?
If it should be incomplete for you, I shall complete it."
"But if it is complete for you, I shall offer a blessing.
For a third time, the wanderer Sarabha remained silent.
Then those wanderers said this to the wanderer Sarabha:
“Whatever, friend Sarabha, you might ask of the ascetic Gotama, that very thing the ascetic Gotama offers to you.
Speak, friend Sarabha; how have you understood the Dhamma of the ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans?
If it should be incomplete for you, the ascetic Gotama will fulfill it.”
"But if it is complete, the ascetic Gotama will give you his approval.
When this was said, the wanderer Sarabha sat silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and unable to respond.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the wanderer Sarabha was silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and unable to respond, said this to those wanderers:
“Monks, if anyone were to say this to me:

‘While you claim to be a perfectly awakened Buddha (sammāsambuddha), these things have not been fully awakened to by you,’ I would thoroughly examine, investigate, and cross-examine him regarding that matter.
When he is thus thoroughly examined, investigated, and cross-examined by me, it is impossible—”
It is impossible that he would fall into any one of these three states:
that he would evade one question with another, divert the discussion to an external topic, or display anger, hatred, and resentment;
or that he would sit silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping and head cast down, brooding and speechless—just as...
The wanderer Sarabha:
"Wanderers, if anyone were to say this to me:
'Though you claim to have destroyed the taints, these taints are not yet destroyed,' I would thoroughly examine, investigate, and cross-examine that person on that point."
Thus, indeed, when I am thoroughly questioning him, pursuing him, and cross-examining him,
it is impossible and there is no occasion that he would not fall into one of these three states: either he would prevaricate with one thing for another,
divert the conversation to external matters, or manifest anger, hatred, and resentment, or remain silent.
He will sit down abashed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless,
just like the wanderer Sarabha.
O wanderers, whoever should speak to me in this way:

‘But for whomsoever this Dhamma has been taught, it does not lead that practitioner toward the complete destruction of suffering’—in such a case, I would thoroughly investigate, scrutinize, and press him on that point.
Were he thus thoroughly investigated, scrutinized, and pressed by me, it is impossible and out of the question that he would not fall into one of three states:
either he would evade the matter with something else, or... [he would contradict himself, or he would display anger, hatred, and bitterness].
"How will he turn away from this talk about the external? He will manifest anger, hatred, and resentment;
instead, he will sit silent, abashed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless—just like the wanderer Sarabha."
Then the Blessed One, having let out a lion’s roar three times in the wanderers’ park on the bank of the Sappinī River, departed through the air.
Not long after the Blessed One had left, those wanderers began to revile Sarabha the wanderer from all sides with a torrent of words, saying:
“Friend Sarabha, just as an old jackal in a vast forest might think, ‘I shall roar a lion’s roar,’ yet roars only like a jackal and howls like a jackal;”
In just this way, friend Sarabha, although you intend to roar the lion’s roar apart from the ascetic Gotama, you merely howl like a jackal, you merely screech like a jackal.
Just as, friend Sarabha, a water-fowl intends to cry out with the cry of a man, yet it cries out only with the cry of a water-fowl;
even so, friend Sarabha, although you intend to cry out with the cry of a man apart from the ascetic Gotama, you merely cry out with the cry of a water-fowl.
“Friend Sarabha, just as a bull thinks he should bellow deeply in an empty cow-pen,
even so do you, friend Sarabha, think you should bellow deeply only in the absence of the ascetic Gotama.
Then those wanderers reviled and censured the wanderer Sarabha from all sides with verbal abuse.
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.65 7. Mahāvagga
The Discourse to the Kesiāputtas (Kesamuttisutta).
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks, he arrived at Kesamutta, a market town of the Kālāmas.
The Kālāmas of Kesamutta heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has indeed arrived at Kesamutta."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:
“Such indeed is the Blessed One … it is good to see such Arahants.”
Then the Kālāmas of Kesamutta approached the Blessed One.

Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the polite and friendly conversation, sat down to one side; others [approached] where the Blessed One was...
Having paid homage with joined palms, some sat down to one side; some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side;
and some, remaining silent, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those Kālāmas of Kesamutta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there are some recluses and brahmins who come to Kesamutta.
They illuminate and exalt their own doctrine, while they revile, deride, despise, and disparage the doctrines of others.
Yet, venerable sir, there are also other recluses and brahmins who come to Kesamutta.”
They illuminate and clarify their own doctrine alone, while they revile, deride, despise, and disparage the doctrines of others.
Therefore, Bhante, we have doubt and uncertainty as to this:
“Which of these venerable recluses and brahmins speaks the truth, and which speaks falsehood?”
“Enough, Kālāmas, of being perplexed; enough of being doubtful.
It is precisely at a point that should cause perplexity that doubt has arisen in you.
Come now, Kālāmas: do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures.

"Do not rely on tradition, do not rely on logic, do not rely on reasoned reflection, do not rely on the acceptance of views after contemplation, do not rely on the competence of the speaker, nor think, 'The ascetic is our teacher.
But when you know for yourselves, Kālāmas: [that these things are unwholesome...]"

‘These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,’ then you, Kālāmas, should abandon them.
What do you think, Kālāmas:
when greed arises within a person, does it arise for their benefit or for their harm?”
“For their harm, Bhante. “Furthermore,
Kālāmas, this greedy person, overcome by greed and with mind consumed by it,
kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise.”
“...and encourages [others to do so], which will lead to his harm and suffering for a long time.
“So it is, Bhante.
“What do you think, Kālāmas?”
“Does hatred, arising within a person, arise for his benefit or for his harm?
“For his harm, Bhante.
“But when this person, Kālāmas, is hateful, overcome by hatred, and his mind is possessed by it, he might even take the life of a living being.”
“He kills, he takes what is not given, he commits adultery, he speaks falsehood, and he encourages others to do likewise;
this leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Kālāmas?
When delusion arises within a person, does it arise for their benefit or for their harm?
“For their harm, Bhante.”
“Furthermore, Kālāmas, a person who is deluded, overcome by delusion, and whose mind is consumed by it,
kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise;
this leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?
“Unwholesome, venerable sir.”
“Is it blameworthy or blameless?
“It is blameworthy, venerable sir.
“Is it censured by the wise or praised by the wise?”
“They are censured by the wise, venerable sir.
“When fully undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?
Or how is it in this case?”
“Venerable sir, when they have been undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering;
this is our view in this matter. “In that case, Kālāmas, as for what we said:”
"Come, Kālāmas. Do not go by oral tradition,
do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of scriptures, do not go by logical reasoning, do not go by inferential grounds,
do not go by the result of reflection on appearances, do not go by the acceptance of a view after pondering it, and do not go by the consideration of one's own capability."
"Do not think, 'The recluse is our teacher.
Rather, Kālāmas, when you know for yourselves:

'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,' then, Kālāmas, you should abandon them."
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this:
"Come, Kālāmas, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of scriptures,
do not go by logical reasoning, do not go by inferential grounds, do not go by reflective pondering, and do not go by approval based on reflection on one's own views."
"Because of his venerable appearance, do not think, 'The ascetic is our teacher.
But when you yourselves know:

'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness,' then, Kālāmas, having entered upon them, you should abide in them."
“What do you think, Kālāmas?
When non-greed arises within a person, does it arise for their welfare or for their harm?
“For their welfare, Bhante.”
“However, Kālāmas, this person who is not greedy, who is not overcome by greed, and whose mind is not consumed by it,
neither kills living beings, nor takes what is not given, nor goes to another’s wife, nor speaks falsehoods,
nor even encourages others to do so; this leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time.”

“Yes, venerable sir. “What do you think, Kālāmas? When non-hatred arises within a person, does it arise for his benefit or for his harm? “For his benefit, venerable sir. “… [as before] …” “When non-hatred arises within a person, does it arise for his benefit or for his harm? “For his benefit, venerable sir. “… [as before] …” “When non-delusion arises within a person, does it arise for his benefit or for his harm? “For his benefit, venerable sir. “… [as before] …” “When non-delusion arises within a person, does it arise for his benefit or for his harm? “For his benefit, venerable sir. “… [as before] …” “Therefore, Kālāmas, those things that are wholesome, blameless, praised by the wise, and when undertaken lead to welfare and happiness—these you should undertake and practice.”
“Non-delusion, arising within a person,
arises for his welfare and happiness.”—
“So it is, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?
“Wholesome, venerable sir.
“Are they blameworthy or blameless?”
“Blameless, venerable sir.
“Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?
“They are praised by the wise, venerable sir.”
“Do those things undertaken and practiced lead to welfare and happiness, or not?
Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, those things undertaken and practiced do lead to welfare and happiness.”
“This is how it appears to us in this matter.
“Thus, Kālāmas, as for what we said:
‘Come, you Kālāmas. …’”
Do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures,

do not go by reasoned argument, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval after pondering a view, do not go by the consideration of "he is capable," and do not go by the thought,
"the recluse is our teacher."
“Kālāmas, when you know for yourselves:

‘These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness’—then, Kālāmas, having entered upon them, you should abide therein.
It was with reference to this that it was said.

In this way, Kālāmas, that noble disciple—free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;
likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as himself, he dwells pervading the entire world.
He dwells having pervaded the world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion …pe… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy …pe…
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;

thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Kālāmas, that noble disciple, with a mind thus free from enmity, thus free from ill will, thus undefiled, and thus purified,
has attained four consolations even in this very life.
"If indeed there is another world, and if there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, then I— ”
‘With the breakup of the body, after death, I shall reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world’—
this is the first consolation he has attained.
‘But if there is no other world, and no fruit or result of good and evil deeds, [then at least I have lived well in this life].’
‘Then, in this very life, I maintain myself free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress, and happy’—
this is the second consolation he has attained.
‘If indeed evil is done by the one who acts, yet I harbor no evil intent toward anyone.’
‘But since I am not performing an evil deed, how could suffering touch me?’—this is the third consolation he has attained.
‘If indeed no evil is done by one who acts, then I perceive myself as purified in both respects’—this is the fourth consolation he has attained.
Thus, Kālāmas, that noble disciple is one whose mind is free from enmity, free from ill will, free from corruption, and purified.
“In this very life, these four assurances have been attained by him.
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
For that noble disciple, venerable sir, whose mind is thus free from enmity, whose mind is thus free from ill will, whose mind is thus undefiled, and whose mind is thus purified—”
In this very life, four consolations have been attained by him:
"If indeed there is another world, and if there is the fruit and result of well-done and ill-done deeds,
then, with the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world"— this is his first consolation.
“Breathing in is attained:
‘If indeed there is no other world, and no fruit or result of well-done or ill-done deeds,
then in this very life I maintain myself free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress, and happy.’”
This is the second consolation he has attained.

"If indeed evil is produced by one who acts, yet I do not intend evil toward anyone; and since I have not committed an evil deed, how shall suffering touch me? This is the third consolation he has attained.
"If indeed evil is not produced by one who acts, then I perceive myself to be purified in both respects. This is the fourth consolation he has attained.

“Venerable sir, that noble disciple who possesses such a mind free from enmity, such a mind free from ill will, such a mind free from defilement, and such a purified mind, has attained these four consolations in this very life.
Excellent, venerable sir! …” [as before]
“Venerable sir, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The fifth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66 7. Mahāvagga Sāḷhasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Sāḷha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“Sāḷha, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is intent on the inferior, the person who is intent on the medium, and the person who is intent on the superior. And what, Sāḷha, is the person intent on the inferior? Here, someone dwells pursuing the inferior in body, speech, and mind. This is called the person intent on the inferior. And what, Sāḷha, is the person intent on the medium? Here, someone dwells pursuing the medium in body, speech, and mind. This is called the person intent on the medium. And what, Sāḷha, is the person intent on the superior? Here, someone dwells pursuing the superior in body, speech, and mind. This is called the person intent on the superior. These, Sāḷha, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Sāḷha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Venerable Sāḷha rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. Not long after the Venerable Sāḷha had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and there were a blind turtle which would come up once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, thrust its neck into that yoke with a single hole? “It would be a matter of chance, venerable sir, that the blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, might thrust its neck into that yoke with a single hole. “So too, bhikkhus, it is by chance that one obtains the human state; by chance that the True Dhamma appears; by chance that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One arises in the world; by chance that the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma; by chance that one hears the Dhamma; by chance that one goes forth; by chance that one dwells pursuing the superior in body, speech, and mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell pursuing the superior in body, speech, and mind. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints by non-clinging. And the Venerable Sāḷha attained the unsurpassed security from bondage in this very life. Thus it was that the Venerable Sāḷha acquired his name.
(AN 3.66, PTS AN i 193) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Nandaka was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, and Sāṇa, the grandson of Sekhunī, approached the Venerable Nandaka;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Nandaka, they sat down to one side.
As Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, was sitting there, the Venerable Nandaka said this to him:
“Come now, Sāḷha, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures,
do not go by reasoned argument, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval after pondering a view,
do not go by the consideration of ‘one’s suitability,’ nor because ‘the ascetic is our teacher.’”
“Sāḷha, when you yourselves know: ‘These states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy;
these states are censured by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,’ then, Sāḷha, you should abandon them.”
“What do you think, Sāḷha,
does greed exist?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Sāḷha, I say that covetousness is this very thing.
One who is greedy and covetous, Sāḷha, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsely, and incites others to do likewise; thus it leads to his long-term harm.”
“...for their harm and suffering.
“So it is, Bhante.
“What do you think, Sāḷha?”
“Is there hatred?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Sāḷha, I say that this very thing is ill will.”
“Sāḷha, this person who is corrupt and malevolent kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, and speaks falsehood;
he also encourages others to do likewise. This leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Sāḷha,
does delusion exist?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Sāḷha, I say that this refers to ignorance.
One who is deluded and immersed in ignorance kills living beings, takes what is not given, and commits adultery with the wives of others.”
“He goes about, speaks falsely, and encourages others to do likewise; this leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Sāḷha, are these states wholesome or unwholesome?
“Unwholesome, Bhante.
“Are they blameworthy or blameless?”
“Blameworthy, venerable sir.
“Is it censured by the wise or praised by the wise?
“It is censured by the wise, venerable sir.”
“Do those things undertaken and observed lead to harm and suffering, or not?
Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, those things undertaken and observed do lead to harm and suffering.”
“This is how it appears to us in this matter.
“Thus indeed, Sāḷha, as for what we said:
‘Come, you, Sāḷha, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures...’”

"Do not [judge] by reason of logic, do not by reason of method, do not by reflection on the mode, do not by approval after pondering a view, do not by the appearance of competence, and do not because 'the recluse is our teacher.
When you yourselves know: "Sāḷha," [then you may accept it]."

"These states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy; these states are censured by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering"—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
"Come, Sāḷhas, do not rely on oral tradition, do not rely on lineage, do not rely on hearsay, do not rely on the authority of the Piṭakas..."

"Do not [conclude] on account of reasoning, do not on account of method, do not by means of reflection on modes, do not through approval based on views, do not because of his being of suitable appearance, and do not because 'the ascetic is our teacher.
When you yourselves, Sāḷha, shall know: "

‘These states are wholesome; these states are blameless; these states are praised by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness. Then, Sāḷha, you might enter upon and abide in them.
What do you think, Sāḷha, does non-greed exist?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”
“‘Non-covetousness,’ Sāḷha, is what I mean by this term.
One who is not greedy and is non-covetous does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not go to another’s wife, and does not speak falsehood;
nor does he encourage others to do so. This leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Sāḷha, is there non-hatred?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“‘Non-ill will,’ Sāḷha, is what I say this means.

One who is without hatred and has a mind free from ill will neither kills living beings, nor takes what is not given, nor goes to another’s wife, nor speaks falsehood; nor does he encourage others to do likewise. This is what it is.”
“...for their long-term welfare and happiness.
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Sāḷha?”
“Is there non-delusion?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Sāḷha, it is precisely this that I call ‘true knowledge.’”

“Sāḷha, this one who is undeluded and possessed of true knowledge neither kills living beings, nor takes what is not given, nor goes to another’s wife, nor speaks falsehood, nor encourages others to do likewise; this leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
“So it is, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Sāḷha, are these states wholesome or unwholesome?
“Wholesome, Bhante.
“Are they blameworthy or blameless?”
“Blameless, venerable sir.
“Is it censured by the wise or praised by the wise?
“It is praised by the wise, venerable sir.”
“Do those things undertaken and practiced lead to welfare and happiness, or not?
Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, those things undertaken and practiced do lead to welfare and happiness.”
“This is how it appears to us in this matter.
“Thus indeed, Sāḷha, as for what we said:
‘Come, you, Sāḷha, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the Piṭakas...’”
"Do not [conclude] because of reasoning, do not because of logic, do not by means of an analytical reflection on modes,
do not because of approval through contemplation of views, do not because of the appearance of possibility, and do not because of the thought, 'The ascetic is our teacher.
When you yourselves, Sāḷha, will know— "
‘These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise;

these things, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness for a long time’—it is with reference to this that it was said: ‘Then you, Sāḷha, having attained them, should dwell therein. Thus was it spoken.
