He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus he understands:
“This exists; there is the inferior; there is the superior; there is an escape beyond this realm of perception.

For him who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
He understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus he understands.
‘In the past there was greed; that was unwholesome. That does not exist now; this is wholesome.
In the past there was hatred...
[and so on] ...in the past there was delusion; that was unwholesome. That does not exist now; this is wholesome.’
“Thus, in this very life, free from craving, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, he dwells with a self that has become sublime.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 3.67.

7. Mahāvagga: Kathāvatthusutta (AN 3.67, PTS AN i 197) “Monks, there are these four bases for discussion. What four? Discussion concerning the past, discussion concerning the future, discussion concerning the present, and discussion concerning the self. These, monks, are the four bases for discussion.”
“Monks, there are these three bases for talk.
What are the three?
Monks, one might speak a talk concerning the past time:”
‘Thus it was in the past,’ or,
monks, concerning the future time, one might speak thus:
‘Thus it will be in the future.’
Or now, monks, concerning the present time, one might speak thus:
“Such is the case at present in the present time.
By means of such discourse, monks, a person is to be known as either refined or unrefined.
If, monks, when this person is asked a question, he does not answer categorically a question that should be answered categorically;
does not analyze a question that should be answered by analysis; does not answer with a counter-question a question that should be answered with a counter-question;
and does not set aside a question that should be set aside—being thus, monks, [he is one who speaks untruth].
Such a person is not fit [to be questioned].
But if, monks, when this person is asked a question, he answers a question that requires a categorical answer categorically;
he answers a question that requires an analytical answer analytically; he answers a question that requires a counter-question...
He answers a question by counter-questioning, and he sets aside a question that should be set aside;
it is in this way, monks, that a person is "scratching. By means of his engagement in conversation, monks, a person is to be known as either one who scratches or one who does not scratch.
If, monks, when this person is asked a question, he does not stand firm regarding what is possible and what is impossible, he does not stand firm regarding the formulation,
he does not stand firm regarding the doctrine of "I do not know," and he does not stand firm regarding the practice— being thus, monks,
this person is one who should not be associated with.

But if, monks, when this person is asked a question, he wavers regarding what is possible and what is impossible, he wavers regarding his formulation, he wavers regarding his claim of knowledge, and he wavers regarding the method of practice, then such a person, monks, is one who cannot be argued with.
Monks, whether a person can be argued with or cannot be argued with is to be known by the manner of their discourse.
If, monks, when this person is asked a question, they evade the issue with something else, [turning] outward...
How does he evade? He displays anger, hatred, and resentment; it is in this way, monks, that a person is unfit for conversation.
But if, monks, when this person is asked a question, he does not evade by one thing and another...
He turns the conversation away toward external matters and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment;
it is in this way, monks, that a person is "scratching" (kaccha).
By means of his engagement in conversation, monks, a person is to be known as either "scratching" or "not scratching."
“Monks, if this person, when asked a question, evades it, crushes it, laughs at it, and seizes upon his own lapse, then, monks, such a person is one who should not be spoken to.

But if, monks, this person, when asked a question, does not evade it, does not crush it, does not laugh at it, and does not seize upon his lapse, then, monks, such a person is one who should be spoken to.
By means of his engagement in conversation, monks, a person is to be known as either having a basis or lacking a basis.”
“Monks, one who has not applied the ear lacks a supporting condition; one who has applied the ear possesses a supporting condition.
Possessing a supporting condition, he directly knows one thing, fully understands one thing, abandons one thing, and realizes one thing.
Directly knowing one thing, fully understanding one thing, abandoning one thing, and realizing one thing, he touches right liberation.”
Monks, this is the purpose of discourse;
this is the purpose of consultation;
this is the purpose of the underlying basis.
This is the purpose of lending an ear: namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
Those who speak in opposition, being entrenched and emboldened;
Having resorted to ignoble qualities,
seeking to expose one another’s faults,
they utter ill-spoken words and stumble.
Confusion and defeat;
they take delight in one another—
how could a noble one act thus?
If he should desire to converse,
the wise man, knowing the proper time,
[should speak] that which is connected with the foundation of the Dhamma.
That discourse which concerns the conduct of the noble ones—
let the wise one deliver that discourse,
being neither contentious nor arrogant.
With a mind that is not haughty,
free from fault-finding and without violence,
he is one who does not harbor envy.
One should speak with right understanding;
one should rejoice in well-spoken words and not disparage what is poorly spoken.
One should not train in finding fault,
nor should one seize upon another's lapse;
one should neither revile nor crush another.
One should not utter speech that is confused.
The counsel of the virtuous is indeed for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of confidence.
Thus indeed do the noble ones deliberate;
this is the deliberation of the noble ones.
Having understood this, the wise one—
“One should not be arrogant, O wise one.
Thus [ends] the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.68.

7. Mahāvagga: Aññatitthiyasutta (AN 3.68, PTS AN i 199) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? He does not honor those worthy of honor; he does not respect those worthy of respect; he does not venerate those worthy of veneration; he does not show deference to those worthy of deference; and he does not attend upon those who have attained higher realization. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge.”
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:
‘Friends, there are these three things.
Which three?’”
"Lust, hatred, and delusion—
these, friends, are the three things.
What, friends, is the distinction, what is the difference, and what is the diversity between these three things?"
“If you were asked this, monks, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of these words. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
“Therefore, monks, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, if wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:
‘Friends, there are these three things.
Which three?’”
“Lust, hatred, and delusion—
these, friends, are the three things. What, friends,
is the distinction between these three things, what is their difference in meaning, and what is their diversity?”
Being asked thus, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
“Friend, lust is slightly blameworthy and fades away slowly; hatred is greatly blameworthy and fades away quickly; delusion is greatly blameworthy and fades away slowly.
“But what, friends, is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen lust arises, or why arisen lust leads to increase and expansion?”
‘One should say: “The sign of the beautiful.
For one who attends to the sign of the beautiful in an improper manner, unarisen lust arises, or arisen lust leads to its increase and expansion.
This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition by which unarisen lust arises, or arisen lust leads to its increase and expansion.’”
“But what, friends, is the cause, what is the condition, by which unarisen hatred arises, or arisen hatred leads to increase and expansion?
“One should say: ‘The sign of repulsion.
For one who attends to the sign of repulsion in an improper way, unarisen hatred arises, or arisen hatred leads to increase and expansion.”
“This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition, by which unarisen hatred arises, or arisen hatred leads to its increase and expansion.
“But what, friends, is the cause, what is the condition, by which unarisen delusion arises, or arisen delusion leads to its increase and expansion?
“In this case, it should be said: ‘Inappropriate attention.’”
"For one who attends to it improperly, unarisen delusion arises, or arisen delusion leads to increase and expansion.
This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition by which unarisen delusion arises, or arisen delusion leads to increase and expansion.
"But what, friends, is the cause, what is the condition by which unarisen lust does not arise, and arisen lust is abandoned?"
‘“The sign of the unattractive,” it should be said.
For one who attends thoroughly to the sign of the unattractive, unarisen lust does not arise and arisen lust is abandoned.
This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition, by which unarisen lust does not arise and arisen lust is abandoned.’”
“But what, friends, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby unarisen hatred does not arise and arisen hatred is abandoned?
“‘The liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti),’ it should be said.
For one who attends thoroughly to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, unarisen hatred does not arise and arisen hatred is abandoned.”
“This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition, by which unarisen hatred does not arise and arisen hatred is abandoned.
“But what, friends, is the cause, what is the condition, by which unarisen delusion does not arise and arisen delusion is abandoned?
“‘Appropriate attention,’ it should be said.”
"For one who attends wisely, unarisen delusion does not arise and arisen delusion is abandoned.
This, friends, is the cause, this is the condition, by which unarisen delusion does not arise and arisen delusion is abandoned.
(The eighth.)
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.69 7.

Mahāvagga Akusalamūlasutta (The Discourse on the Roots of the Unwholesome) “Monks, there are these three roots of the unwholesome. What three? Greed as a root of the unwholesome, hatred as a root of the unwholesome, and delusion as a root of the unwholesome. These, monks, are the three roots of the unwholesome.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three roots of unwholesomeness. What are the three? [The text continues with greed, hatred, and delusion.]”
Greed is a root of unwholesomeness, hatred is a root of unwholesomeness, and delusion is a root of unwholesomeness.
Whatever greed there is, bhikkhus, that too is a root of unwholesomeness;
whatever one who is greedy performs by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is unwholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is greedy, overcome by greed, and possessed by a greedy mind inflicts suffering upon another through falsehood—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment, thinking "I am powerful" or "I seek power"—
that too is unwholesome.
In this way, many evil, unwholesome states arise born of greed, caused by greed, originating from greed, and conditioned by greed.
Whatever, monks, is hatred is also a root of the unwholesome;
whatever one who is hateful constructs through body, speech, or mind is also unwholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is corrupted, overcome by hatred, and possessed by a mind of ill will inflicts suffering upon another through falsehood—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment, thinking "I am powerful" or "I seek power"—
that too is unwholesome.
In this way, from hatred as cause, from hatred as source, from hatred as origin, and with hatred as condition, many evil and unwholesome states arise.
Whatever delusion there is, bhikkhus, that too is an unwholesome root;
whatever one who is deluded performs by body, speech, or mind, that too is unwholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is deluded, overcome by delusion, and whose mind is consumed by it, inflicts suffering upon another through falsehood—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment, thinking "I am powerful" or "I seek power"— that too is unwholesome. Thus, from delusion as their source,
from delusion as their origin, from delusion as their arising, and with delusion as their condition, numerous evil and unwholesome states come into being.

“Monks, such a person as this is called one who speaks at an improper time, one who speaks what is untrue, one who speaks what is unbeneficial, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, and one who speaks contrary to the Vinaya.

And why, monks, is such a person called one who speaks at an improper time, one who speaks what is untrue, one who speaks what is unbeneficial, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, and one who speaks contrary to the Vinaya?”

For in this way, monks, such a person inflicts suffering upon another through falsehood—by means of execution, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment—thinking, "I am powerful, I seek power.
Yet when spoken to with what is true, he disregards it and does not acknowledge it;
when spoken to with what is false, he makes no effort to refute it, saying, "This is untrue; this is not factual."

Therefore, such a person is called one who speaks at the wrong time, one who speaks what is untrue, one who speaks what is unbeneficial, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, and one who speaks contrary to the Vinaya.
Such a person, bhikkhus, being overcome by evil, unwholesome states born of greed and with his mind possessed by them, dwells in suffering in this very life—with vexation, despair, and fever.
And with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected for him.
Overcome and possessed by evil, unwholesome states born of hatred... and born of delusion, one dwells in suffering in this very life— with vexation, despair, and fever—
and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

“Just as, monks, a *sāla* tree, a *dhava* tree, or a *phandana* tree that is overgrown and enveloped by three *māluva* creepers meets with misfortune, meets with calamity, meets with misfortune and calamity;
even so, monks, a person such as this—overcome by evil, unwholesome states born of greed, his mind consumed by them—dwells in suffering in this very life, with vexation, distress, and fever.
And with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.”
Overcome and possessed by evil, unwholesome states born of hatred... [and] born of delusion, one dwells in suffering in this very life— with vexation, despair, and fever—
and with the breakup of the body, after death, a miserable destination is to be expected.
"These, monks, are the three roots of unwholesomeness.
There are, monks, these three roots of wholesomeness.
Which three?"
Non-greed is a root of the wholesome, non-hatred is a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion is a root of the wholesome.
Monks, whatever is non-greed is a root of the wholesome;
and whatever one who is not greedy performs by way of body, speech, or mind—that too is wholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is not greedy, not overcome by greed, and whose mind is not consumed by greed does not cause suffering to another through what is untrue—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment— even thinking,
"I am powerful; I seek power"— that too is wholesome.
In this way, many wholesome states arise born of non-greed, with non-greed as their source, with non-greed as their origin, and conditioned by non-greed.
Whatever, monks, is non-hatred—that too is a root of the wholesome;
whatever one who is without hatred performs by way of body, speech, or mind—that too is wholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is not corrupted, not overcome by hatred, and whose mind is not consumed, does not inflict suffering upon another through falsehood—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment— even thinking "I am powerful;
I seek power"— that too is wholesome.
In the same way, from non-hatred as their source, from non-hatred as their origin, from non-hatred as their arising, and from non-hatred as their condition, many wholesome states come into being.
Whatever is non-delusion, monks, that too is a root of the wholesome;
whatever one who is undeluded performs by body, speech, or mind, that too is wholesome.
Furthermore, when one who is undeluded, not overcome by delusion, and whose mind is not consumed by it, does not inflict suffering upon another through falsehood—
whether by killing, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment— even though he might think,
"I am powerful; I seek power"— that too is wholesome.
In the same way, from non-delusion as their source, non-delusion as their cause, non-delusion as their origin, and non-delusion as their condition, many wholesome states arise.

And such a person, monks, is called one who speaks at the proper time, one who speaks truthfully, one who speaks meaningfully, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and one who speaks in accordance with the Vinaya.

Why, monks, is such a person called one who speaks at the proper time, one who speaks truthfully, one who speaks meaningfully, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and one who speaks in accordance with the Vinaya?

For in this way, monks, such a person does not inflict suffering upon another through what is untrue—by means of execution, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment—even thinking, "I am powerful and seek power.
But when spoken to with what is true, he acknowledges it and does not disparage it;
when spoken to with what is untrue, he exerts himself to unravel it.
‘In this way it is untrue; in this way it is not factual.
Therefore, such a person is called one who speaks at the right time, one who speaks what is meaningful, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and one who speaks in accordance with the Vinaya.
For such a person, monks, evil unwholesome states born of greed have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
He dwells in happiness in this very life, free from affliction, anguish, and fever.
He attains final Nibbāna in this very life.
[The same applies to] that born of hatred... [and so on].
He attains final Nibbāna.
Born from delusion...
[and so on] ...he attains final Nibbāna.
"Monks, it is just as if a *sāla* tree, a *dhava* tree, or a *phandana* tree were smothered and enveloped by three *māluvā* creepers.
Then a man might come along carrying a hoe and a basket;
he would cut that *māluvā* creeper at its root, having cut it at the root, he would dig it out, and having dug it out, he would pull out the roots, even down to the size of a lotus stalk."
Suppose one were to cut that māluvā creeper into pieces, having cut it into pieces, one would split them; having split them, one would reduce them to fragments;
having reduced them to fragments, one would dry them in the wind and sun; having dried them in the wind and sun, one would burn them with fire;
having burned them with fire, one would turn them into ash; and having turned them into ash, one would scatter it in a great wind, or...
One might pull it out by the root or wash it away in the swift current of a river.
In this way, monks, that *māluva* creeper would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising again in the future.

Even so, monks, for such a person, evil unwholesome states born of greed are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising again in the future.
He dwells in happiness in this very life, free from affliction, anguish, and fever.
He attains final nibbāna in this very life.
[The same applies to] that born of hatred... [and so on].
Evil, unwholesome states born of delusion have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are no longer subject to future arising.
In this very life, he dwells happily, free from vexation, despair, and fever,
and attains final Nibbāna in this very life.
“These, monks, are the three roots of the wholesome.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.70

7. Mahāvagga: Uposathasutta (AN 3.70, PTS AN i 205) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four kinds of uposatha. What four? The uposatha of fools, the uposatha of worldlings, the uposatha of those who have reached the stream, and the uposatha of the Tathāgatas. And what, monks, is the uposatha of fools? Here, monks, some fool goes to the monastery on the uposatha day and says: ‘Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth; it is the uposatha day. Let the venerable ones perform the uposatha together with me. Then the foolish person performs the uposatha with them. This, monks, is called the uposatha of fools. And what, monks, is the uposatha of worldlings? Here, monks, some worldling goes to the monastery on the uposatha day and says: ‘Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth; it is the uposatha day. Let the venerable ones perform the uposatha together with me. Then the worldling performs the uposatha with them. This, monks, is called the uposatha of worldlings. And what, monks, is the uposatha of those who have reached the stream? Here, monks, one who has reached the stream goes to the monastery on the uposatha day and says: ‘Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth; it is the uposatha day. Let the venerable ones perform the uposatha together with me. Then that person who has reached the stream performs the uposatha with them. This, monks, is called the uposatha of those who have reached the stream. And what, monks, is the uposatha of the Tathāgatas? Here, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, on the uposatha day, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, sits down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he addresses the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus, today is the fifteenth; it is the uposatha day. Let the Saṅgha perform the uposatha together with me. Then the Tathāgata performs the uposatha with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. This, monks, is called the uposatha of the Tathāgatas. These, monks, are the four kinds of uposatha.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s Mother, on that very Uposatha day, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. As Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, was sitting there, the Blessed One said to her:
“Well now, Visākhā, where have you come from so early in the day?
“I am observing the Uposatha today, Bhante,” she replied.
“There are, Visākhā, three kinds of observance days. Which three? The cowherd’s observance day, the Nigaṇṭha’s observance day, and the noble one’s observance day.”
And how, Visākhā, is there a cattle-herder’s uposatha?
Just as, Visākhā, when a cattle-herder has returned the cows to their owners in the evening, he reflects thus:
"Today the cows wandered in such-and-such places and drank water in such-and-such places."
‘Today my cows will graze in such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place, and they will drink water in such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place’—
in the same way, Visākhā, here a certain person observing the Uposatha reflects thus:
‘Today I have eaten this and that kind of solid food, and I have consumed this and that kind of soft food.’
‘Today I shall eat this and that kind of hard food, and I shall consume this and that kind of soft food.
He spends the day with a mind accompanied by covetousness.
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cowherd’s uposatha.
When the Gopālaka Uposatha is observed in this way, Visākhā, it is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, and not of great radiance.
And how, Visākhā, is the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha observed?
There are, Visākhā, those of the ascetic class known as Nigaṇṭhas.
They exhort their disciple thus:
“Come, good man, lay down your rod against all living beings in the eastern direction for more than a hundred leagues;
lay down your rod against all living beings in the western direction for more than a hundred leagues.”
‘Lay down the rod against those living beings in the northern direction more than a hundred leagues away;
lay down the rod against those living beings in the southern direction more than a hundred leagues away.
Thus, they encourage some living beings out of compassion and sympathy, while they do not encourage other living beings out of compassion and sympathy.
On that Uposatha day, they would thus exhort a disciple:
“Come, good man, cast off all your clothes and say:
‘I am nothing belonging to anyone anywhere, nor is there anything of mine anywhere at all.’”
Moreover, his parents know: "This is our son," and he also knows: [this is my mother and this is my father].
‘These are my mother and father.
And his wife and children know of him:
‘This is my husband.’”
He too knows:
"This is my wife and children.
And his slaves, laborers, and servants know it as well.
‘This is our master,’ and he too knows:
‘These are my slaves, laborers, and servants.’
Thus, at the time when they should be encouraged toward truth, they instead encourage them toward false speech.
This, I say, is their false speech.
Then, with the passing of that night, he consumes wealth that has not been given.
This, I say, is his [transgression] regarding taking what is not given.
In this way, Visākhā, the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha is observed.
When the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha is observed in this way, Visākhā, it is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, and not of great radiance.
And how, Visākhā, is there the noble Uposatha?
It is the cleansing, by means of effort, of a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing, by means of effort, of a defiled mind?
“Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:

‘Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

As he recollects the Tathāgata, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, the cleansing of a head that has become defiled is achieved through effort.”
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a head that has become defiled?
By means of soap, by means of clay, by means of water, and by means of a person’s appropriate exertion—thus, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a head that has become defiled.
In the same way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a mind that has become defiled.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:

“The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.”
As he recollects the Tathāgata, his mind becomes serene, gladness arises, and whatever defilements there are in the mind are abandoned.
This, Visākhā, is called:

“A noble disciple observes the Brahmā Uposatha; he dwells together with Brahmā; and with reference to Brahmā, his mind becomes serene, gladness arises, and whatever defilements there are in the mind are abandoned.”
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
There is, Visākhā, the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?
“Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus:
‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.

As he recollects the Dhamma, his mind becomes placid, joy arises, and those defilements of the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, there is the cleansing of a body that has become defiled by means of a purifying agent.”
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a body that has become defiled?
It is by means of a cloth, by means of powder, by means of water, and by means of a person’s appropriate exertion.
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a body that has become defiled.
"In the same way, Visākhā, there is a method for purifying a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there a method for purifying a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma: [text continues]"
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.
As he recollects the Dhamma, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.
This, Visākhā, is called a noble disciple who observes the Uposatha of the Dhamma and dwells together with the Dhamma.
“Taking the Dhamma as his object, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and those defilements of the mind are abandoned.
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
Thus, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.”
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus:

‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing straightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically...’
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing rightly;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples consists of these four pairs of persons, these eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’”
As he recollects the Saṅgha, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in the mind are abandoned.
Just as, Visākhā, the cleansing of a soiled cloth occurs through a specific process:
how, Visākhā, does the cleansing of a soiled cloth occur through a specific process? It is by means of heat, lye, cow dung, water, and the appropriate effort of a person.
"In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a soiled cloth.
Even so, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?"
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well... [as before] ...the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
As he recollects the Saṅgha, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.
“Visākhā, this is called an noble disciple who observes the Uposatha of the Saṅgha, who dwells together with the Saṅgha, and whose mind becomes serene regarding the Saṅgha;
joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in the mind, they are abandoned.
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.”
"Visākhā, for a defiled mind, there is cleansing through effort.
And how, Visākhā, is there cleansing through effort for a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects his own moral virtues—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration."
As he recollects his virtue, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and those defilements of the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a soiled mirror:
how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a soiled mirror?
It depends on oil, it depends on ash, it depends on a wisp of wool, and it depends on the appropriate exertion of a man.
"In this way, Visākhā, the polishing of a tarnished mirror is achieved through effort.
Even so, Visākhā, the cleansing of a defiled mind is achieved through effort.
And how, Visākhā, is the cleansing of a defiled mind achieved through effort?"
“Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects his own virtues—unbroken, [and so forth]... leading to concentration.
As he recollects his virtue, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.

This, Visākhā, is called a noble disciple who observes the Uposatha of virtue; he dwells together with virtue, and by taking virtue as his basis, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.”
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
There is, Visākhā, the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?
"Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the deities:
'There are the Cātumahārājika deities; there are the Tāvatiṃsa deities; there are the Yāma deities; there are the Tusita deities;
there are the Nimmānarati deities; there are the Paranimmitavasavatti deities; there are the Brahmakāyika deities.'"
There are gods even higher than those.
Whatever kind of faith those deities possessed by virtue of which, having passed away from here, they were reborn there—that same kind of faith exists in me as well.
Whatever kind of virtuous conduct those deities possessed by virtue of which, having passed away from here, they were reborn there—that same kind of virtuous conduct exists in me as well.
‘Possessed of such learning as those deities were possessed of when they passed away from here and were reborn there, such learning exists in me too.
Possessed of such generosity as those deities were possessed of when they passed away from here and were reborn there, such generosity exists in me too.
Possessed of such wisdom as those deities were possessed of when they passed away from here and were reborn there, such wisdom exists in me too.’”
As he recollects his own faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom,
as well as those of those deities, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in the mind are abandoned.
Just as, Visākhā, gold that is defiled is purified through a process of refinement.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by means of effort of gold that is defiled?
It is by means of a furnace, salt, red chalk, a pair of tongs, and the appropriate exertion of a person.
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by means of effort of gold that is defiled.
In the same way, Visākhā, there is a method for purifying a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there a method for purifying a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the deities:
“There are the gods of the Four Great Kings; there are the gods of the Thirty-three … [and so on] … there are gods even higher than those.
Possessed of such faith as those deities possessed, who, having passed away from here, were reborn there, such faith exists in me as well.
Possessed of such virtue as those deities possessed …”
‘Those deities who were endowed with learning, generosity, and wisdom have passed away from here and been reborn there; such wisdom as theirs exists in me as well.’”

As he recollects his own faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, as well as those of those deities, his mind becomes serene, joy arises, and whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.

This, Visākhā, is called an “noble disciple who observes the deity-uposatha, who dwells together with the deities, whose mind becomes serene by way of the deities, in whom joy arises, and for whom whatever defilements there were in his mind are abandoned.”
In this way, Visākhā, there is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
That noble disciple reflects thus:

“For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; they lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, they dwell full of sympathy for the welfare of all living beings.”

Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned the taking of life, I dwell abstaining from taking life; with rod laid aside and weapon laid aside, modest, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
By this factor as well, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.

For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of what is not given, abstain from taking what is not given; they take only what is given, expect only what is given, and dwell with their bodies pure and free from theft.

Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned taking what is not given, I abstain from taking what is not given; I take only what is given, I expect only what is given, and I dwell with my self purified by that lack of theft.
By this factor as well, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.
For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned unchastity, live a life of chastity, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.

Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned unchastity, I am one who lives in celibacy, who conducts himself far from it, and who abstains from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
In this respect, too, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.
For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned false speech, abstain from false speech; they are speakers of truth, devoted to truth, steadfast, trustworthy, and reliable to the world.
Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned false speech, I abstain from false speech; I am a speaker of truth, one devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
By this factor as well, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.

For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, distilled liquor, and intoxicants, abstain from the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, distilled liquor, and intoxicants.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned the use of fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, abstain from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
By this factor as well, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.
For as long as life lasts, the Arahants eat but one meal a day, abstaining at night and refraining from eating at improper times.
Today, for this night and this day, I shall eat but one meal, abstaining from food at night and refraining from eating at improper times.
In this respect, too, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.

For as long as life lasts, the Arahants abstain from dancing, singing, instrumental music, watching shows, and from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and from adorning or beautifying themselves with cosmetics.
Today, for this night and this day, I too abstain from dancing, singing, music, watching shows, and the wearing of garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, as well as from adorning and beautifying myself.
In this respect also I imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.

For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats, and make use of low resting places, either a small couch or a grass mat spread upon the ground.

‘Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, I shall abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats; I shall lie down on a low bed, either on a couch or on a spread of grass.
In this way too, Visākhā, one emulates the Arahants in this factor, and the Uposatha will have been observed by me.
It is in this way, Visākhā, that the noble Uposatha takes place.
When the noble Uposatha is observed in this way, Visākhā, it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance.
How great is its fruit, how great its benefit, how great its splendor, and how great its radiance?
Suppose, Visākhā, one were to exercise sovereign lordship and kingship over these sixteen great lands abounding in the seven precious gems, namely: [list follows].
Compared to the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, the [wealth] of the Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāsīs, Kosalas, Vajjis, Mallas, Cetis,
Vaṅgas, Kurus, Pañcālas, Macchas, Sūrasenas, Assakas, Avantis, Gandhāras,
and Kambojas is not worth even a sixteenth part of it.
For what reason?
Because human sovereignty, Visākhā, is miserable compared to celestial happiness.
Those fifty human years, Visākhā, constitute a single day and night for the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Thirty nights of that [human] night make one month;
twelve months of that month make one year.
By that reckoning of years, five hundred celestial years is the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
"It is indeed possible, Visākhā, that here some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha complete in eight factors,
with the breakup of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
It was with reference to this, Visākhā, that it was said:"
“Human sovereignty is miserable when compared with celestial happiness.
Visākhā, what is a hundred years for humans is but a single day and night for the gods of the Thirty-three.
Thirty such nights make a month.”
Twelve months of that [lunar month] make a year.
A thousand celestial years by that reckoning is the lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three.
Now, Visākhā, it is possible that here some woman or man, endowed with the eight factors—
Having observed the Uposatha, with the breakup of the body, after death, one might be reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
It was with reference to this, Visākhā, that it was said:
"Miserable is human sovereignty compared to celestial happiness."
"Visākhā, those two hundred human years are one day and night for the Yāma devas.
Thirty such nights make a month.
Twelve such months make a year."
By that reckoning, two thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Yāma devas.

It is possible, Visākhā, that here some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha complete in eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of the Yāma devas.
It was with reference to this, Visākhā, that it was said:
“Human sovereignty is wretched when compared with celestial happiness.
Visākhā, those four hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Tusita devas.
Thirty such nights make a month.”
Twelve months make a year.
By that reckoning, the lifespan of the Tusita devas is four thousand celestial years.

It is possible, Visākhā, that a certain woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha complete in its eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tusita devas.
"Moreover, Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said:
‘Human sovereignty is meager when compared to celestial happiness.
Visākhā, those eight hundred human years are equal to a single day and night for the Nimmānarati devas."
Thirty nights of that [human] night make one month.
Twelve months of that month make one year.
Eight thousand celestial years of that year is the measure of the lifespan of the Nimmānarati devas.
"It is indeed possible, Visākhā, that here some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha complete in eight factors,
on the dissolution of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas.
It was with reference to this, Visākhā, that it was said:"
“Human kingship is miserable when compared with divine bliss.
Visākhā, those sixteen hundred human years are a single day and night for the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.
Thirty such nights make a month.
Twelve months of that [lunar] reckoning make one year.
Sixteen thousand such celestial years is the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.
Now, Visākhā, it is possible that here some woman or man, endowed with the eight factors—
Having observed the Uposatha, with the breakup of the body, after death, one might be reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.
It was with reference to this, Visākhā, that it was said:
"Miserable is human sovereignty compared to celestial happiness."
One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given,
nor speak falsehoods, nor be a drinker of intoxicants;
one should abstain from unchaste conduct and sexual intercourse.
One should not eat at night, nor at improper times.
One should not wear garlands, nor use perfumes;
one should lie down either on the ground or on a bed spread out.
For this indeed is called the eightfold Uposatha,
proclaimed by the Buddha, the one who has reached the end of suffering.
Both the moon and the sun are beautiful to behold;
They move about, illuminating as far as they reach;
those light-dispelling sky-dwellers shine in the heavens, radiating splendor in every direction.
Whatever wealth exists within this space—
pearls, gems, and excellent beryl;
fine gold, or even refined gold—
Whatever is called "native gold" or "jātarūpa"—
even a sixteenth part of that does not equal a single fraction of the eightfold-upheld Uposatha.
And all the hosts of stars with the radiance of the moon.
Therefore, both woman and man who are virtuous,
having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors;
Having performed meritorious deeds that result in happiness,
the blameless ones go to the heavenly realm.
Thus ends the tenth [verse].
The Seventh Chapter: Mahāvagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
Fear of heretics and the elephant.
Sarabha, Kesamuttiya;
Sāḷha and Kathāvatthu,
and the Tīrthika-mūla-uposatha.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.71 8. Ānanda-vagga Channa Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Channa was sick, afflicted, gravely ill. The Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Channa is sick, afflicted, gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the Venerable Channa out of compassion. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the dwelling of the Venerable Channa. When he arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Channa then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Channa, are you bearing up, are you enduring? Do your pains diminish rather than increase?

Is there any sign of their diminishing rather than increasing? “I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not enduring. My painful feelings are increasing rather than diminishing; there is no sign of their diminishing rather than increasing. “Channa, these seven factors of enlightenment are noble and emancipating; they lead to the complete destruction of suffering. What seven? The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is noble and emancipating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena... energy... rapture... tranquility... concentration... equanimity, which is noble and emancipating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These seven factors of enlightenment are noble and emancipating; they lead to the complete destruction of suffering. “Now, Channa, do you have these seven factors of enlightenment present in yourself? “No, venerable sir, I do not. “Channa, it is your own fault, it is your own failing, that when the Tathāgata has taught the Dhamma thus, you do not understand it. (AN 3.71, PTS AN i 215) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the wanderer Channa approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side. Seated there, the wanderer Channa said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Friend Ānanda, do you also prescribe the abandoning of lust, the abandoning of hatred, and the abandoning of delusion?
"Friend, we indeed prescribe the abandoning of lust, the abandoning of hatred, and the abandoning of delusion."

“But friends, having seen what danger in lust do you prescribe the abandoning of lust? Having seen what danger in hatred do you prescribe the abandoning of hatred? Having seen what danger in delusion do you prescribe the abandoning of delusion?

“Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, with mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both; he experiences mental pain and dejection.

When lust is abandoned, one does not intend for one's own affliction, nor does one intend for the affliction of others, nor does one intend for the affliction of both; one does not experience mental pain or dejection.
For, friend, when one is lustful, overcome by lust, and with mind consumed by it, one engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.
But when lust is abandoned, one does not engage in misconduct by body, nor misconduct by speech, nor misconduct by mind.

"Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, does not understand his own welfare as it really is, does not understand the welfare of others as it really is, and does not understand the welfare of both as it really is.
When lust is abandoned, he understands his own welfare as it really is, understands the welfare of others as it really is, and understands the welfare of both as it really is.
Lust, friends, causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes lack of knowledge; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna."
"Friends, one who is corrupted by hatred...

and one who is deluded by delusion, being overcome and possessed by it, intends for his own harm, intends for the harm of others, and intends for the harm of both; he experiences mental pain and dejection.
When delusion is abandoned, he does not intend for his own harm, nor does he intend for the harm of others, nor does he intend for the harm of both; he does not experience mental pain and dejection."
"Friends, one who is deluded, overcome by delusion, and whose mind is consumed by it, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.
When delusion is abandoned, one does not engage in misconduct by body, nor misconduct by speech, nor misconduct by mind.

Friends, one who is deluded, overcome by delusion, and whose mind is consumed by it, does not understand his own welfare as it really is, nor the welfare of others as it really is, nor the welfare of both as it really is."
When delusion has been abandoned, one understands one’s own welfare as it really is, one understands the welfare of others as it really is, and one understands the welfare of both as it really is.
Delusion, friends, creates darkness, creates lack of vision, creates ignorance; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
It is by seeing this danger in lust that we, friends, proclaim the abandoning of lust.
“Having seen this danger in hatred, we shall prescribe the abandoning of hatred;
having seen this danger in delusion, we shall prescribe the abandoning of delusion.
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?”
“There is, friends, a path; there is a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.
“But what, friends, is that path; what is that way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?
“It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, namely:”
“Right view... [and so on] ... right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.
“Excellent indeed, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.”
“Enough, friend Ānanda, with diligence!
Thus it was said. First.

8. Ānanda-vagga Ājīvakasutta (AN 3.72, PTS AN i 217) At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Potaliputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, having concluded his polite conversation, sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Potaliputta said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there are these various ascetics and brahmins who maintain different views and hold different opinions. Some say thus: ‘The world is eternal. Others say thus: ‘The world is not eternal. Others say thus: ‘The world is finite. Others say thus: ‘The world is infinite. Others say thus: ‘The soul and the body are the same. Others say thus: ‘The soul and the body are different. Others say thus: ‘After death, a Tathāgata exists. Others say thus: ‘After death, a Tathāgata does not exist. Others say thus: ‘After death, a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist. Others say thus: ‘After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist. Now, Master Gotama, when those venerable ones speak thus, do they all speak as they have been taught by the Teacher, or do they speak otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher? “Potaliputta, when those venerable ones speak thus, some speak as they have been taught by the Teacher, and some speak otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher. “But how is it, Master Gotama? When those venerable ones speak thus, which among them speak as they have been taught by the Teacher, and which speak otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher? “Potaliputta, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘the world is eternal’—if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while being in doubt about it—would they be speaking as they have been taught by the Teacher, or would they be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher? “If, Master Gotama, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘the world is eternal’ were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while being in doubt about it, they would be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher. “Potaliputta, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘the world is not eternal’...

[and so on for each of the other views] ...regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’—if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while being in doubt about it—would they be speaking as they have been taught by the Teacher, or would they be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher? “If, Master Gotama, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while being in doubt about it, they would be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher. “Potaliputta, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘the world is eternal’—if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while knowing it to be so, they would be speaking as they have been taught by the Teacher. But if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘the world is eternal’ while being in doubt about it, they would be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher. Potaliputta, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘the world is not eternal’... [and so on for each of the other views] ...regarding those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the view that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’—if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while knowing it to be so, they would be speaking as they have been taught by the Teacher. But if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while not knowing it to be so, or if they were to assert that ‘after death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’ while being in doubt about it, they would be speaking otherwise than what has been taught by the Teacher. “But, Master Gotama, how is it? Do those venerable ones know: ‘This is the world, this is the self; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘This is the world, this is the self; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘This is not the world, this is not the self; after death I shall not become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘This is not the world, this is not the self; after death I shall not become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘This is the world, this is the self; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘This is the world, this is the self; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘This is not the world, this is not the self; after death I shall not become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘This is not the world, this is not the self; after death I shall not become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘I am not, it will not be, what is not mine, it will not be mine’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘I am not, it will not be, what is not mine, it will not be mine. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘I am, it will be, what is mine, it will be mine’? “Potaliputta, I do not say that I know: ‘I am, it will be, what is mine, it will be mine. “But, Master Gotama, do those venerable ones know: ‘I am not, it will not be, what is not mine, it will not be mine’?
