On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then a certain householder who was a disciple of the Ājīvakas approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that householder who was a disciple of the Ājīvakas—
The householder said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, whose Dhamma is well-expounded?
Who in the world have practiced it correctly?"
“Who in the world is well-done?
“In that case, householder, I will question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, householder?”
“Is the Dhamma well-expounded by those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion?
Or how do you regard this matter?
“Venerable sir, the Dhamma is well-expounded by those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion.”
“This is how it appears to me in this matter.
“What do you think, householder?
Those who have practiced for the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion—have they practiced well in the world, or not?”
“And what do you think about this?
“Venerable sir, those who have practiced for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—they have practiced well in the world.
This is how it appears to me in this matter.”
“What do you think, householder?
For those in whom lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising;
for those in whom hatred has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising...”
"For those by whom delusion has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future—
have they not performed well in the world?
Or how do you regard them in this matter?"
“Venerable sir, those in whom lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising;
those in whom hatred has been abandoned …pe… those in whom delusion has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump,
obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising— they are the ones who have done well in the world.”
“This is how it appears to me in this matter.
“In that case, householder, you have declared:
‘Venerable sir, those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—their Dhamma is well-expounded.’”
By you this was declared:
“Those, venerable sir, who have practiced for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—they have practiced well in the world.
By you this was declared:
“Bhante, those for whom lust has been abandoned—cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future;

those for whom hatred has been abandoned... [and] those for whom delusion has been abandoned—cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future—they are the ones who have performed well in the world.”
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
This is indeed not an exaltation of one’s own doctrine, nor a disparagement of the doctrines of others.
The teaching of the Dhamma is presented in its proper sphere; the meaning has been stated, yet the self has not been introduced.”
"Venerable Ānanda, you teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust; you teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of hatred...
[and] for the abandoning of delusion. Venerable Ānanda, your Dhamma is well-expounded.
Venerable Ānanda, you have practiced for the abandoning of lust; you have practiced for the abandoning of hatred... [and] for the abandoning of delusion."
“Venerable sir, you have practiced well in the world.
Venerable Ānanda, your lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising;
your hatred has been abandoned … [and so on] … your delusion has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump.”
Having been rendered non-existent, it is subject to non-arising in the future.
You have performed a good deed for the world.
Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost,
or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms— in the same way,
the Venerable Ānanda has elucidated the Dhamma by means of many lines of reasoning."
“Venerable Ānanda, I go for refuge to that Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the noble Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.73 8. Ānandavagga Mahānāmasakkasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘stream-enterer,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘stream-enterer,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘stream-enterer,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the stream,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the stream,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the stream,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has entered upon the way,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has entered upon the way,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has entered upon the way,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has attained to view,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has attained to view,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has attained to view,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached certainty,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached certainty,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached certainty,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the fruit,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the fruit,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the fruit,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the goal,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the goal,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the goal,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the end,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the end,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the end,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the ultimate,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the ultimate,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What three? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... These are the three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the ultimate,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has reached the finality,’ no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “There are three things, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has reached the finality,’ no longer bound to the nether
(AN 3.73, PTS AN i 219) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had recently recovered from an illness and had not long been free from his sickness.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“For a long time, Bhante, I have understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus:”
‘Knowledge belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
Now, venerable sir, does concentration come first and knowledge afterwards,
or does knowledge come first and concentration afterwards?”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
"The Blessed One has recently recovered from illness; he has not long been rid of his sickness.
And yet this Sakyan Mahānāma asks the Blessed One a question that is exceedingly profound."
"What if I were to lead Mahānāma the Sakyan aside and teach him the Dhamma?
Then the Venerable Ānanda took Mahānāma the Sakyan by the arm, led him aside, and said to him:
"Mahānāma, the Blessed One has spoken of both the virtue of one in training and the virtue of one beyond training."
The Blessed One has spoken of the concentration of one in training, and he has also spoken of the concentration of one beyond training.
The Blessed One has spoken of the wisdom of one in training, and he has also spoken of the wisdom of one beyond training.
And what, Mahānāma, is the virtue of one in training?
"Here, Mahānāma, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha... [as before] ...he trains himself, having undertaken the training rules.
This, Mahānāma, is called the virtue of one in training (sekha-sīla).
And what, Mahānāma, is concentration of one in training?"
"Here, Mahānāma, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, Mahānāma, is called the concentration of one in training (sekha).
And what, Mahānāma, is the wisdom of one in training?"
“Here, Mahānāma, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, Mahānāma, is called the wisdom of one in training.
Now, Mahānāma, that noble disciple, thus perfected in virtue, thus perfected in concentration, and thus perfected in wisdom—”
With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
having entered upon it. In this way, Mahānāma, both the virtue of one in training and the virtue of one beyond training have been described by the Blessed One.
“Concentration of one in training has been spoken of by the Blessed One, and concentration of one beyond training has been spoken of by the Blessed One.
Wisdom of one in training has been spoken of by the Blessed One, and wisdom of one beyond training has been spoken of by the Blessed One.
This is the third.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.74 8. Ānanda-vagga Nigaṇṭha-sutta At Sāvatthī. “Ānanda, there are these three kinds of Nigaṇṭhas. What three? “There is the case where a certain Nigaṇṭha is one who has not done evil deeds in the past, nor does he do them in the present, nor will he do them in the future; he is restrained with the restraint of all evil deeds. This is called a Nigaṇṭha who is ‘tied up on all sides’—bound by the bond of all evil deeds, whether past, future, or present. “Then there is the case where a certain Nigaṇṭha is one who has not done evil deeds in the past, nor does he do them in the present, nor will he do them in the future; he is restrained with the restraint of all evil deeds. However, he has not abandoned the underlying tendency toward lust, aversion, and delusion that underlie past, future, and present evil deeds. This is called a Nigaṇṭha who is ‘tied up on all sides but not completely’—bound by the bond of all evil deeds, whether past, future, or present, but not completely. “Then there is the case where a certain Nigaṇṭha is one who has not done evil deeds in the past, nor does he do them in the present, nor will he do them in the future; he is restrained with the restraint of all evil deeds. He has abandoned the underlying tendency toward lust, aversion, and delusion that underlie past, future, and present evil deeds. He has attained the complete destruction of the taints. This is called a Nigaṇṭha who is ‘freed on all sides’—freed from the bond of all evil deeds, whether past, future, or present. “These, Ānanda, are the three kinds of Nigaṇṭhas.”
(AN 3.74, PTS AN i 220) On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then Abhaya the Licchavi and Paṇḍitakumāra the Licchavi approached the Venerable Ānanda.
Having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there, Abhaya the Licchavi said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, possessing knowledge and vision without remainder, saying: [text continues]"
‘Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously established before me.
Thus he declares the exhaustion of past kamma through asceticism, and the demolition of the bridge by not performing new kamma.

Thus, with the destruction of kamma comes the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering comes the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.
“In this way, there is a transcendence of that purification through the immediate wearing away [of defilements].
Regarding this, venerable sir, what does the Blessed One say?
“Abhaya, there are these three purifications through the wearing away [of defilements] taught by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One—”
These three [knowledges] have been perfectly proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,
for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
What are the three?
"Here, Abhaya, a bhikkhu is virtuous... he trains himself in the training rules he has undertaken.
He does not perform new kamma, and he makes an end of old kamma by experiencing it as it arises.
This wearing away is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise."
“Abhaya, when a bhikkhu is thus perfected in virtue, secluded from sensual pleasures... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He does not perform new kamma, and he makes an end of old kamma by experiencing it as it arises.
This wearing away is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.”

Abhaya, when a bhikkhu is thus perfected in concentration, through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
He does not perform new kamma, and he makes an end of old kamma by experiencing it as it arises.
This wearing away is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
“Abhaya, these three modes of wearing away and purification have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One,
the Perfectly Enlightened One— for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief,
for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.”
When this was said, the Licchavi Paṇḍitakumāra said this to the Licchavi Abhaya:
“But why, friend Abhaya, do you not applaud what has been well-spoken by the Venerable Ānanda as being well-spoken?
“How could I, friend Paṇḍitakumāra, not applaud what has been well-spoken by the Venerable Ānanda as being well-spoken?”
"Even his head would split apart, whoever did not rejoice in what was well-spoken by the Venerable Ānanda as being well-spoken.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.75

8. Ānanda-vagga: Nivesaka-sutta (AN 3.75, PTS AN i 222) “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on building up; the person who is intent on destroying; the person who is intent on both building up and destroying; and the person who is intent on neither building up nor destroying. And how, Ānanda, is one a person intent on building up? Here, Ānanda, a certain person builds up what is unwholesome and does not destroy it; he builds up what is unskillful and does not destroy it; he builds up what is unrighteous and does not destroy it. This, Ānanda, is called a person intent on building up. And how, Ānanda, is one a person intent on destroying? Here, Ānanda, a certain person destroys what is wholesome and does not build it up; he destroys what is skillful and does not build it up; he destroys what is righteous and does not build it up. This, Ānanda, is called a person intent on destroying. And how, Ānanda, is one a person intent on both building up and destroying? Here, Ānanda, a certain person builds up what is unwholesome and does not destroy it; he builds up what is unskillful and does not destroy it; he builds up what is unrighteous and does not destroy it; and he also destroys what is wholesome and does not build it up; he destroys what is skillful and does not build it up; he destroys what is righteous and does not build it up. This, Ānanda, is called a person intent on both building up and destroying. And how, Ānanda, is one a person intent on neither building up nor destroying? Here, Ānanda, a certain person neither builds up what is unwholesome nor fails to destroy it; he neither builds up what is unskillful nor fails to destroy it; he neither builds up what is unrighteous nor fails to destroy it; and he neither destroys what is wholesome nor fails to build it up; he neither destroys what is skillful nor fails to build it up; he neither destroys what is righteous nor fails to build it up. This, Ānanda, is called a person intent on neither building up nor destroying. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:

“Ānanda, those whom you would compassionately regard—whether friends, colleagues, kinsmen, or blood relatives—and who might think they should listen to you, these, Ānanda, you should encourage, settle, and establish in three things.
In which three?”
They should be encouraged, settled, and established in unwavering confidence in the Buddha:

“Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
They should be encouraged, settled, and established in unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:

‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise’—thus should they be encouraged, settled, and established in verified confidence toward the Saṅgha:
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way...’
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing rightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples consists of these four pairs of persons, these eight types of individuals.
This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’”

It may be, Ānanda, that there is a change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—but it is impossible for there to be any change in a noble disciple who possesses verified confidence in the Buddha; such a change is simply not possible.

For indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a noble disciple endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha should be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts. This cannot happen.

It may be, Ānanda, that there could be a change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—but there could never be a change in a noble disciple who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma...
nor in one who possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha. This, indeed, is what constitutes such a change.
“Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a noble disciple endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha should be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts.

Those whom you should have compassion for, Ānanda—whether friends, colleagues, kinsmen, or blood relatives—and those who think they should listen to you, should be encouraged, established, and settled by you, Ānanda, in these three things.
The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.76 8. Ānanda-vagga Paṭhama-bhava-sutta (The First Discourse on Existence) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of existence. What three? Sensual existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of existence. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘existence, existence. In what way, venerable sir, is there existence? “Ānanda, when there is a basis, when there is a source, when there is a cause, when there is a condition for the arising of consciousness, there is existence. When there is no basis, when there is no source, when there is no cause, when there is no condition for the arising of consciousness, there is no existence. And what, Ānanda, is the basis, the source, the cause, the condition for the arising of consciousness? It is name-and-form. When there is name-and-form as a basis, as a source, as a cause, as a condition for the arising of consciousness, there is existence. When there is no name-and-form as a basis, as a source, as a cause, as a condition for the arising of consciousness, there is no existence. And what, Ānanda, is the basis, the source, the cause, the condition for the arising of name-and-form? It is consciousness. When there is consciousness as a basis, as a source, as a cause, as a condition for the arising of name-and-form, there is existence. When there is no consciousness as a basis, as a source, as a cause, as a condition for the arising of name-and-form, there is no existence. Thus, Ānanda, consciousness comes to be with name-and-form as its support; name-and-form comes to be with consciousness as its support. Consciousness and name-and-form are mutually dependent, like two sheaves of reeds leaning against each other.

In this way, Ānanda, one who possesses right view understands things as they really are: ‘This is suffering’; ‘this is the origin of suffering’; ‘this is the cessation of suffering’; ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “This, venerable sir, is called the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the beloved is suffering, not getting what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, venerable sir, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, venerable sir, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, venerable sir, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: it is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it has a noble meaning and a noble phrasing; it is unique, complete, pure, and cleansed. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the teaching, the teaching. In what way, venerable sir, is it the teaching? “Ānanda, this Dhamma has been taught by me through direct knowledge, realized by myself, and made known to others. This, Ānanda, is called the teaching. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the truth, the truth. In what way, venerable sir, is it the truth? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is true, unerring, and not otherwise. This, Ānanda, is called the truth. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the reality, the reality. In what way, venerable sir, is it the reality? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is real, not unreal, not otherwise. This, Ānanda, is called the reality. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma leads to the goal, leads to Nibbāna, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be seen by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be attained by the wise, to be personally experienced, and to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be entered upon by the wise, to be penetrated by the wise, and to be fully understood by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be realized by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be attained by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be lived in accordance with by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be practiced by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be cultivated by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be developed by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be made to arise by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be brought forth by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be established by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be settled by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be maintained by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be preserved by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Dhamma, the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is it the Dhamma? “Ānanda, this Dhamma is to be protected by the wise, each for themselves, and it is to be guarded by the wise, each for themselves. This, Ānanda, is called the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘
(AN 3.76, PTS AN i 223) Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Becoming, becoming,’ it is said, venerable sir.”
“To what extent, venerable sir, does existence come to be?
“If, Ānanda, there were no kamma ripening in the sense-sphere realm, would sense-sphere existence be discerned?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Thus, Ānanda, karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.
For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, consciousness becomes established in a lower realm; in this way there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
(… ) If, Ānanda, there were no karma ripening in the form realm, would a rebirth-existence in the form realm be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Thus, Ānanda, karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.
For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, consciousness becomes established in the intermediate realm; thus there is the production of renewed existence in the future. (…)”
“Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the formless realm, would a formless existence be discerned?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
“Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.”
"When the consciousness of beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving is established in a refined element, thus there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that there is becoming.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.77 8. Ānanda-vagga Dutiyabhava-sutta (The Second Discourse on Existence) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of existence. What three? Sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of existence. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, you have long been one who speaks much about the Dhamma. But since you say, ‘Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief,’ it is for this reason that I will question you. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Ānanda? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [And so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “What do you think, Ānanda? Since consciousness is impermanent, is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Therefore, Ānanda, whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... Whatever perception... Whatever volitional formations... Whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing thus, Ānanda, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. “This, venerable sir, is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s brief statement. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is marvelous, Ānanda! How well you have grasped the meaning of the Tathāgata’s brief statement. Therefore, Ānanda, remember this as the teaching of the Tathāgata, and remember it as spoken by the Tathāgata.”
(AN 3.77, PTS AN i 224) Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, it is said: 'existence, existence.'"
“To what extent, venerable sir, does existence come to be?
“If, Ānanda, there were no karma ripening in the sense-sphere realm, would sense-sphere existence be discerned?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Thus, Ānanda, karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.

For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, volition is established in the inferior element and aspiration is established; thus there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
If, Ānanda, there were no karma ripening in the form element, would a rebirth in the form realm be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Thus, Ānanda, karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.

For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, volition is established and aspiration is established in the intermediate state; thus there is the production of renewed existence in the future.”
“Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the formless realm, would the formless existence be discerned?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
“Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture.”
"For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, volition is established in a refined element and aspiration is established; thus there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that becoming comes to be.
(The seventh.)
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.78 8. Ānanda-vagga Sīlabbata-sutta (The Discourse on Virtue and Observances) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world.

What three? The person who is devoted to virtue and observances, the person who is devoted to learning, and the person who is devoted to solitude. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person devoted to virtue and observances? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is called a person devoted to virtue and observances. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person devoted to learning? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has learned much, retained what he has learned, stored it up; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. This is called a person devoted to learning. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person devoted to solitude? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells alone, withdrawn from the crowd, not frequenting society. This is called a person devoted to solitude. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, is every kind of virtue and observance, every way of life, and every holy life fruitful when it has service as its essence?”
“There is not one-sidedness in this matter, Bhante.
“In that case, Ānanda, analyze it.
“Because, Bhante, for one who practices that rule and observance, that way of life, that holy life, which has attendance as its essence, unwholesome states... [increase].”
Unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; such a practice of virtue and observance, a way of life, a holy life, and a core of service is fruitless.
But, venerable sir, as for that practice of virtue and observance, a way of life, a holy life, and a core of service which one pursues, unwholesome states...
“Unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; such virtue, observance, way of life, holy life, and service is fruitful.
This is what the Venerable Ānanda said.
The Teacher gave his approval.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, Ānanda is a trainee;
yet it is not easy to find anyone who is his equal in wisdom.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.79 8. Ānanda-vagga Gandhajāta-sutta (The Discourse on the Origin of Fragrance) “Bhikkhus, there are these three origins of fragrance. What three? The origin of fragrance that is root-based, the origin of fragrance that is stalk-based, and the origin of fragrance that is blossom-based. These, bhikkhus, are the three origins of fragrance. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these three origins of fragrance…’ Yet, venerable sir, it is even more wonderful and marvelous how the Blessed One, having himself attained the supreme fragrance among human beings, teaches the Dhamma for the attainment of the supreme fragrance. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! Having attained the supreme fragrance among human beings, I teach the Dhamma for the attainment of the supreme fragrance.

For what reason? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata is one whose conduct is fragrant, whose behavior is fragrant, and whose life is fragrant. And how, Ānanda, is the Tathāgata one whose conduct is fragrant? Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata abstains from taking life; he lays down the rod, lays down the weapon, and dwells compassionate and kind toward all living beings. He abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells honestly without thoughts of theft. He abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, parents, brother, sister, or relatives, nor with those who are protected by their Dhamma, nor with those who are married and under the protection of a husband, nor with those who are garlanded in token of betrothal. He abstains from false speech; when summoned to a court or to a gathering, and questioned as a witness, he does not speak in accordance with his knowledge. He abstains from divisive speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide others from those here, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide these from those there. Thus, being a reconciler of those at variance and an encourager of those already at peace, he delights in harmony, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create unity. He abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that go to the heart, courteous, agreeable, and dear to many. He abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, and speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya. He speaks such words as are timely, true, meaningful, and lead to the goal of the holy life. This, Ānanda, is how the Tathāgata is one whose conduct is fragrant. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata avoids sitting on high seats or couches. He observes celibacy, lives apart, and refrains from sexual intercourse, which is the common practice of worldly people. He abstains from eating at improper times; he does not eat after midday, avoiding food outside the prescribed hours. He abstains from attending dances, songs, music, theatrical performances, and the use of garlands, scents, cosmetics, and ornaments. He abstains from using high and luxurious beds and couches. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain, raw meat, women, girls, male and female slaves, goats, sheep, fowl, swine, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and lands. He abstains from going on errands and running messages. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from cheating with scales, metals, or measures. He abstains from accepting bribes, deceiving, defrauding, and trickery. He abstains from wounding, executing, imprisoning, plundering, and harassing. This, Ānanda, is how the Tathāgata is one whose behavior is fragrant. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata abstains from accepting uncooked grain, raw meat, women, girls, male and female slaves, goats, sheep, fowl, swine, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, as well as fields and lands. He abstains from receiving gold and silver, raw grain, raw meat, women, girls, male and female slaves, goats, sheep, fowl, swine, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, fields and lands, servants and messengers, vehicles and carriages, and various kinds of beds, seats, mats, coverlets, blankets, and pillows. He abstains from accepting lamps, scents, garlands, ointments, long robes, long cloaks, and silk garments. He abstains from accepting gold and silver, bullion and coin, fields and lands, male and female slaves, goats, sheep, fowl, swine, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, as well as all manner of goods and chattels. This, Ānanda, is how the Tathāgata is one whose life is fragrant. Because the Tathāgata is one whose conduct is fragrant, whose behavior is fragrant, and whose life is fragrant, therefore, Ānanda, having attained the supreme fragrance among human beings, I teach the Dhamma for the attainment of the supreme fragrance.”
(AN 3.79, PTS AN i 225) Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“There are these three kinds of fragrant substances, venerable sir, whose fragrance travels only with the wind, and not against the wind.”
Which three? The scent of roots, the scent of heartwood, and the scent of flowers—
these, venerable sir, are the three kinds of scents whose fragrance travels only with the wind, not against the wind.
“Is there, venerable sir, any kind of fragrance whose scent travels with the wind, whose scent travels against the wind, and whose scent travels both with and against the wind?
“There is, Ānanda, some kind of fragrance whose scent travels with the wind, whose scent travels against the wind, and whose scent travels both with and against the wind.”
“And what, Bhante, is that kind of fragrant substance whose scent travels with the wind, whose scent travels against the wind, and whose scent travels both with and against the wind?
“In this case, Ānanda, in whatever village or town a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha;
who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct...”
He abstains from false speech; he abstains from taking intoxicants, such as fermented liquor, spirits, and strong drink, which cause heedlessness.

He is virtuous, possessed of wholesome qualities, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess—generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and finding joy in sharing his wealth.
Because of this, recluses and brahmins praise him in all directions, saying:
‘In such-and-such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha;

they abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; they are virtuous and of lovely character.’
He dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts.
Deities also speak his praise:
‘In such-and-such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.’”
“He abstains from taking life... [as before] ...he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness;

he is virtuous, of lovely character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, accessible to requests, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts.
This, Ānanda, is that kind of perfume whose scent travels with the wind, against the wind, and even both with and against the wind.
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind,
nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine;
but the fragrance of the virtuous goes even against the wind.
“The true person blows [his fragrance] in all directions.
Thus was the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.80

8. Ānanda-vagga: Cūḷanikāsutta (AN 3.80, PTS AN i 226) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “It is not easy, Ānanda, for one who has not developed the mind to understand: ‘This is the sphere of one who has developed the mind; this is the range of one who has developed the mind. “But, venerable sir, it is precisely because I have not developed the mind that I say: ‘It would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief... “Ānanda, if you were to develop the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. Since, Ānanda, you have developed the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. If you were to develop the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for six years... five years... four years... three years... two years... one year... seven months... six months... five months... four months... three months... two months... one month... half a month... seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. Since, Ānanda, you have developed the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. [The Venerable Ānanda then repeated the entire sequence of the four foundations of mindfulness as taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going-forth at the hands of the Blessed One; may I receive the full admission. “You have been ordained for a long time, Ānanda, by means of the Tathāgata’s higher knowledge,” the Blessed One said. “Nevertheless, since you have expressed your desire, come, bhikkhu. And that was the Venerable Ānanda’s full admission. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the summary and the exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is the summary of the four foundations of mindfulness? It is: ‘This is suffering’; ‘This is the origin of suffering’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the summary of the four foundations of mindfulness. And what, bhikkhus, is the exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, bhikkhus, is the exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well the Blessed One has stated the summary and the exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness! “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous how well the Tathāgata has stated the summary and the exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. The Cūḷanikāsutta is concluded. The eighth discourse in the Ānanda-vagga. The third chapter is concluded. The first book is concluded. The Aṅguttara Nikāya is concluded. The Aṅguttara Nikāya is completed. May there be well-being. May there be welfare. May there be peace. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be free from enmity. May all beings be free from affliction. May all beings be free from distress. May all beings be free from suffering. May all beings be free from fear. May all beings be free from danger. May all beings be free from calamity. May all beings be free from misfortune. May all beings be free from sorrow. May all beings be free from grief. May all beings be free from lamentation. May all beings be free from despair. May all beings be free from anxiety. May all beings be free from terror.
