Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, I have received it directly from the Blessed One:
'Ānanda, while standing in the Brahma-world, the Blessed One Sikhī’s disciple named Abhibhū made himself known by his voice throughout a thousandfold world-system.'"
“But how far, venerable sir, is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, able to make himself heard with his voice?
“He is a disciple, Ānanda; the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.
A second time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him:
‘Ānanda, the Blessed One Sikhī had a disciple named Abhibhū who, while standing in the Brahma-world, made himself heard by his voice throughout a thousandfold world-system.
But, venerable sir, how far is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, able to make himself heard by his voice?”
“Ānanda, that disciple is one for whom the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.
A third time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from the Blessed One:”
“Ānanda, the Blessed One Sikhī had a disciple named Abhibhū who, standing in the Brahmā world, made himself heard by his voice throughout a thousandfold world-system.
“But, Bhante, how far is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, able to make himself heard by his voice?
“Have you heard, Ānanda, of the small thousandfold world-system?”
“This is the time for that, Blessed One;
this is the time for that, Sugata, that the Blessed One should speak. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Ānanda, as far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance, so far extends a world-system of a thousand worlds.”
In that thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru kings of mountains,
a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas,
a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand [thrones of] the Great Kings, and a thousand...
A thousand worlds of the Cātumahārājika devas, a thousand worlds of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, a thousand worlds of the Yāma devas, a thousand worlds of the Tusita devas,
a thousand worlds of the Nimmānarati devas, a thousand worlds of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas,
and a thousand worlds of the Brahmā realm— this, Ānanda, is called a minor chiliocosm.
To whatever extent, Ānanda, there is a small thousandfold world system, that world is a thousandfold [of that].
This, Ānanda, is called a second-order intermediate thousandfold world system.
To whatever extent, Ānanda, there is a second-order intermediate thousandfold world system, that world is a thousandfold [of that].
“This, Ānanda, is called a trichiliocosm, a great thousandfold world-system.
If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could make himself heard by his voice throughout a trichiliocosm, as far as he might wish.
“But how, Bhante, would the Blessed One make himself heard by his voice throughout a trichiliocosm, as far as he might wish?”
“Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata might pervade the trichiliocosm with radiance.
When those beings perceive that light, then the Tathāgata would utter a sound, make his voice heard.
In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata can make himself understood by his voice throughout the trichiliocosm, or as far as he might wish.”
When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the venerable Udāyī:
"It is indeed a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me,
that my Teacher is so powerful and so majestic."
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"What does it matter to you here, friend Ānanda, if your Teacher is so powerful and so majestic?
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Do not say so, Udāyin; do not say so, Udāyin.

If, Udāyin, Ānanda were to pass away while still not free from lust, by virtue of that confidence in his mind, he would exercise divine sovereignty among the devas seven times, and seven times he would exercise great sovereignty right here in Jambudīpa.
Moreover, Udāyin, Ānanda will attain final Nibbāna in this very life.”
The tenth.
The third chapter, the Ānanda-vagga.
Its summary verse:
Channa the Ājīvaka, Sakka,
the Nigaṇṭha, and Nivesaka;
the two types of existence, and virtue-and-observance—
And the perfume called Cūḷanī.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.81, Chapter 9: The Chapter on Ascetics.
Samaṇasutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things that a recluse should do, which are conducive to being a recluse and constitute the duties of a recluse.”
Which three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom—
these, monks, are the three things that make one a recluse, which belong to a recluse, and which must be done by a recluse.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

'We shall have a fervent desire for undertaking the training in the higher virtue; we shall have a fervent desire for undertaking the training in the higher mind; we shall have a fervent desire for undertaking the training in the higher wisdom.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.82 9.
The Chapter on Ascetics (Samaṇavagga)
The Ass Sutta (AN 3.82, AN 3.81b, PTS AN i 229): “Bhikkhus,
just as a donkey follows closely behind a herd of cattle, thinking:”
‘I too am being tamed, I too am being tamed.
Yet he does not have such a color as cattle do; he does not have such a voice as cattle do; he does not have such a gait as cattle do.
He merely follows right behind the herd of cattle:
‘I too am being tamed; I too am being tamed.
In the same way, monks, here a certain bhikkhu follows closely behind the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, thinking:
‘I too am a bhikkhu; I too am a bhikkhu.’
He does not have such a desire for undertaking the training in higher virtue as other bhikkhus have;
he does not have such a desire for undertaking the training in higher mind as other bhikkhus have;
he does not have such a desire for undertaking the training in higher wisdom as other bhikkhus have.
Thus he followed right behind the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, thinking, "I too am a bhikkhu; I too am a bhikkhu.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:

‘There will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher virtue; there will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher mind; there will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher wisdom.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus is the second [instruction].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.83 9. The Chapter on Recluses (Samaṇavagga) The Discourse on the Field (Khettasutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of fields. What three? The field of merit, the field of misery, and the field of neither-merit-nor-misery. And what, bhikkhus, is the field of merit? Here, someone is virtuous, of good character, one who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is called the field of merit. And what, bhikkhus, is the field of misery? Here, someone is immoral, of bad character, one who takes life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is called the field of misery. And what, bhikkhus, is the field of neither-merit-nor-misery? Here, someone is neither virtuous nor immoral, of neither good nor bad character, one who neither takes life nor takes what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is called the field of neither-merit-nor-misery. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of fields."
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things that must first be done by a householder who is a farmer.
What are the three?
In this case, monks, a householder who is a farmer first thoroughly plows and harrows his field.
Having first thoroughly plowed and harrowed his field, he sows the seeds at the proper time.
Having sown the seeds at the proper time, he brings water to it and carries it away from it at the appropriate season.
“Monks, these are the three things that must first be done by a householder who is a farmer.
In the same way, monks, there are these three things that must first be done by a monk.
What are the three?
The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom—
these, monks, are the three things a monk should do beforehand.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

‘There will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher virtue; there will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher mind; there will be a fervent desire in us to undertake the training in the higher wisdom.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. This is the third [instruction].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.84 9. The Chapter on Ascetics (Samaṇavagga) The Discourse to the Son of the Vajjis (Vajjiputtasutta) “Monks, there are these three kinds of ascetics.

What three? “The ascetic who is like a crow, the ascetic who is like a butcher’s dog, and the ascetic who is like a brahmin. “And how, monks, is one an ascetic who is like a crow? Here, monks, some ascetic goes for alms from family to family, seeking, searching, and picking out here and there, just as a crow goes about seeking, searching, and picking out here and there. This is called an ascetic who is like a crow. “And how, monks, is one an ascetic who is like a butcher’s dog? Here, monks, some ascetic goes for alms with his robes tucked up, his bowl lowered, looking ahead only a plow’s length, with shoulders drooping and head downcast, like a butcher’s dog that has been beaten with a stick or staff. This is called an ascetic who is like a butcher’s dog. “And how, monks, is one an ascetic who is like a brahmin? Here, monks, some ascetic goes for alms with a steady gaze, with a composed mind, not looking at what is lowly, not looking at what is high, but looking straight ahead with a steady gaze. This is called an ascetic who is like a brahmin. “These, monks, are the three kinds of ascetics.”
(AN 3.84, AN 3.83, PTS AN i 230) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then a certain Vajjiputtaka bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that Vajjiputtaka bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, more than one hundred and fifty training rules come up for recitation every half-month."
“Venerable sir, I am not able to train myself in this. “But, bhikkhu,
will you be able to train yourself in the three trainings—
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom?”
“I am able, Bhante, to train in the three trainings—
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
“Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself in these three trainings.”
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
When you, bhikkhu, train in higher virtue, train in higher mind, and train in higher wisdom— then, bhikkhu,
as you train in higher virtue, train in higher mind, and train in higher wisdom...
“As you train, lust will be abandoned, hatred will be abandoned, and delusion will be abandoned.
By abandoning lust, by abandoning hatred, and by abandoning delusion, you will not do what is unwholesome; you will not pursue what is evil.
Then, at a later time, that bhikkhu trained in higher virtue, he trained in higher mind, and he trained in higher wisdom.
As he trained in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom, lust was abandoned, hatred was abandoned, and delusion was abandoned.
Through the abandoning of lust, the abandoning of hatred, and the abandoning of delusion, he did nothing unwholesome and practiced no evil.
This is the fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.85 9.

The Chapter on Ascetics (Samaṇavagga) The Discourse on the Trainee (Sekkhāsutta) “Monks, there are these three trainees. What three? The one in training who is a stream-enterer, the one in training who is a once-returner, and the one in training who is a non-returner. These, monks, are the three trainees.”
(AN 3.85, AN 3.84, PTS AN i 231) Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘A trainee, a trainee.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one a trainee?
“Because he trains, bhikkhu, he is therefore called a trainee. And what does he train in? He trains in the higher virtuous behavior, he trains in the higher mind, and he trains in the higher wisdom.”
He trains in higher virtue, he trains in higher mind, and he trains in higher wisdom.
It is because he trains, monk, that he is called a "learner" (sekha).
Of this learner who is training...
Following the straight path,
there is first the knowledge of destruction,
and immediately after that, final knowledge.
Then for one who is liberated through final knowledge,
such a one possesses this wisdom:
"My liberation is unshakable."
“In the destruction of the fetters of existence.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.86

9. Samaṇavagga First Discourse on Training (Paṭhamasikkhāsutta) “Monks, there are these five trainings for a recluse. What five? Here, monks, a recluse is endowed with faith; he places trust in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the training rules of the Pātimokkha. “He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for use when ill. “He dwells having abandoned the hindrances, those obstructive mental states that weaken wisdom. “He dwells having attained the four jhānas—states of sublime happiness in the present life—which belong to the higher mind and are to be realized by one’s own direct knowledge. “These, monks, are the five trainings for a recluse.”
“Monks, this more than one hundred and fifty training rules comes up for recitation every half-month, wherein clansmen who desire their own welfare train themselves.
Monks, there are these three trainings in which all of this is included. What are the three? [The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.]”
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom— these, monks,
are the three trainings in which all this is fully comprised. Here, monks,
a monk is one who fulfills the training in virtue, but is only moderately accomplished in concentration and moderately accomplished in wisdom.
Therefore, as for those minor and lesser training rules, one may both transgress them and emerge from them.
Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared here an incapacity [to train].

Furthermore, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and appropriate to the holy life, he is constant in virtue and steadfast in virtue; having undertaken them, he trains himself in those training rules.
With the complete destruction of three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills his duties in regard to virtuous behavior, while being only moderate in his practice of concentration and moderate in his practice of wisdom.
Therefore, as for those minor and lesser training rules, one may both commit them and emerge from them.
For what reason?
Because, monks, I have not declared that one is incapable [of progress] on account of these.

Furthermore, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and appropriate to the holy life, he is steady in virtue and firm in virtue; having undertaken them, he trains himself in the training rules.

With the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner who, having come back to this world only once more, makes an end of suffering.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills his duties in regard to virtuous behavior, who fulfills his duties in regard to concentration, and who practices wisdom to a moderate degree.
Thus, regarding those training rules that are minor and secondary, he both commits them and emerges from them.
For what reason?
Because, monks, I have not declared here an incapacity [to train].

But as for those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable to the holy life, he is steady in them and firm in them; having undertaken them, he trains himself in those training rules.
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills virtuous conduct, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom.
Thus, as for those minor and lesser training rules, one may both commit them and emerge from them.
For what reason?
Because, monks, I have not declared here that one is incapable [of progress].

But as for those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable to the holy life—in these he is constant in virtue and firm in virtue; having undertaken them, he trains himself in the training rules.

Through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.
Thus, monks, one who practices partially achieves the partial, while one who practices fully achieves the full.
“Monks, I say that the training rules are indeed not barren.
Thus was the sixth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.87

9. Samaṇavagga The Second Training Discourse (Sikkhāsutta II) “Monks, there are these five trainings for a recluse. What five? ‘I shall abstain from taking life’—this is a training for a recluse. ‘I shall abstain from taking what is not given’—this is a training for a recluse. ‘I shall abstain from sexual misconduct’—this is a training for a recluse. ‘I shall abstain from false speech’—this is a training for a recluse. ‘I shall abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness’—this is a training for a recluse. These, monks, are the five trainings for a recluse.”
“Monks, this more than one hundred and fifty training rules comes up for recitation every half-month, wherein clansmen who desire their own welfare train themselves.
Monks, there are these three trainings wherein all of this is included. What are the three? [The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.]”
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom— these, monks,
are the three trainings in which all this is fully comprised. Here, monks,
a monk is one who fulfills the training in virtue, but is only partial in his practice regarding concentration and partial in his practice regarding wisdom.
Therefore, regarding those training rules that are minor and lesser, one may both transgress them and emerge from them.
For what reason?
Because, monks, I have not declared here an incapacity [to train].

Furthermore, regarding those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable for the holy life, he is constant in virtue and firm in virtue; having undertaken them, he trains himself in those training rules.
With the complete destruction of three fetters, he becomes one who returns at most seven times;
after wandering and transmigrating among gods and humans for seven times at most, he makes an end of suffering.

Thus, with the complete destruction of three fetters, he becomes a "family-to-family" (kolaṅkolo) practitioner; having wandered and transmigrated through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering.
With the complete destruction of three fetters, he becomes a "single-seed" (ekabījī) practitioner; having produced only one more human existence, he makes an end of suffering.

With the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmī); having come back to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills the precepts, is one who fulfills concentration, and is one who practices wisdom to a moderate degree.
He both commits and emerges from those training rules that are minor and lesser. Why is that?
For it was not, monks, that I have declared him to be incapable in this matter.

However, regarding those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable for the holy life—in these he is of constant virtue and established virtue; having undertaken them, he trains himself in the training rules.
With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Thus, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains final nibbāna with exertion.
With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains final nibbāna without exertion.
With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains final nibbāna upon landing.
Thus, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills his duties regarding virtue, who fulfills his duties regarding concentration, and who fulfills his duties regarding wisdom.
As for those training rules that are minor and lesser, he may both commit them and emerge from them.
For what reason?
Because, monks, I have not declared here an incapacity [for enlightenment].

Rather, regarding those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable for the holy life, one is constant in virtue and steadfast in virtue there, undertaking and training oneself in the training rules.

Thus, with the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.

In this way, monks, one who practices partially achieves the partial, and one who practices fully achieves the full. Yet, monks, I say that the training rules are never barren. Thus ends the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.88 9. Samaṇavagga Tatiyasikkhāsutta (The Third Discourse on Training) “Monks, there are these three trainings. What three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. These, monks, are the three trainings. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One:

“But how, venerable sir, is there the training in higher virtue, how is there the training in higher mind, and how is there the training in higher wisdom? “Here, monk, a noble disciple dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This, monk, is called the training in higher virtue. Furthermore, monk, a noble disciple, detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of detachment. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, monk, is called the training in higher mind. Furthermore, monk, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monk, is called the training in higher wisdom. These, monk, are the three trainings.”
“Monks, this more than one hundred and fifty training rules comes up for recitation every half-month, wherein clansmen who desire their own welfare train themselves.
Monks, there are these three trainings wherein all of this is included.
Which three?
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—
these, monks, are the three trainings in which all this is fully comprised.
In this case, monks, a monk is one who fulfills the precepts, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom.
He both commits and emerges from those minor and lesser training rules.
For what reason?
For it is not, monks, that I have declared here an incapacity [to attain the goal]. Rather,

regarding those training rules that pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and are suitable for the holy life— one who is constant in virtue and firm in virtue trains himself by undertaking and practicing those training rules—
he, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.
But failing to reach or penetrate that, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes an attainer of Nibbāna in the interval.
Or, failing to reach or penetrate that, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes an attainer of Nibbāna upon landing.
Or, failing to reach or penetrate that, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes an attainer of Nibbāna without exertion.
But failing to reach or penetrate that, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna with exertion.
Or, failing to reach or penetrate that, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

But failing to fully realize or penetrate that, through the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, one makes an end of suffering.

Or, failing to fully realize or penetrate that, through the total destruction of three fetters, one becomes a "single-seeder" (ekabījī), who produces only one more human existence and then makes an end of suffering.

But failing to reach or penetrate that, with the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes a "family-to-family" (kolaṅkolo) person; having wandered and transmigrated through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering.
Or, failing to reach or penetrate that, with the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes one who has "at most seven more births" (sattakkhattuparamo);
having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans for at most seven times, he makes an end of suffering.
“Thus, monks, one who fulfills completely attains what is complete; one who fulfills partially attains what is partial.
But, monks, I say that the training rules are never barren.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.89 9. The Chapter on Recluses (Samaṇavagga) The First Discourse on the Three Trainings (Paṭhamasikkhattayasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. What three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the three trainings. “Bhikkhus, for one who has completed the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind is the sequel. For one who has completed the training in higher mind, the training in higher wisdom is the sequel. For one who has completed the training in higher wisdom, the destruction of the taints is the sequel. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of these three trainings, he is called a bhikkhu who is accomplished in the trainings, perfected in the trainings, one who has reached the consummation of the holy life. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is accomplished in the trainings, perfected in the trainings, and has reached the consummation of the holy life.

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus accomplished in the trainings, perfected in the trainings, and has reached the consummation of the holy life, he is called a bhikkhu who is a true recluse, a true brahmin, one who has done his task, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, one who is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is a true recluse, a true brahmin, one who has done his task, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus a true recluse, a true brahmin, one who has done his task, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge, he is called a bhikkhu who has crossed over and gone beyond, a bhikkhu who has no more need for further training. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu has crossed over and gone beyond, and has no more need for further training. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has thus crossed over and gone beyond, and has no more need for further training, he is called a bhikkhu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the true goal, one who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge, he is called a bhikkhu who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, a bhikkhu who has attained the ultimate sanctuary, a bhikkhu who has attained the ultimate peace, a bhikkhu who has attained the ultimate Nibbāna. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu has attained the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate sanctuary, the ultimate peace, and the ultimate Nibbāna. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has thus attained the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate sanctuary, the ultimate peace, and the ultimate Nibbāna, he is called a bhikkhu who is a field of merit unsurpassed, a bhikkhu worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an incomparable field of merit for the world. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is a field of merit unsurpassed, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an incomparable field of merit for the world. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus a field of merit unsurpassed, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an incomparable field of merit for the world, he is called a bhikkhu who is a great person, a great man, a great being, a great soul. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is a great person, a great man, a great being, a great soul. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus a great person, a great man, a great being, a great soul, he is called a bhikkhu who is a lion among men, a bull among men, a nāga among men, a thoroughbred among men, a great elephant among men. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is a lion among men, a bull among men, a nāga among men, a thoroughbred among men, a great elephant among men. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus a lion among men, a bull among men, a nāga among men, a thoroughbred among men, a great elephant among men, he is called a bhikkhu who is a conqueror of Mara, a conqueror of the Evil One, a conqueror of Death. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu is a conqueror of Mara, a conqueror of the Evil One, a conqueror of Death. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus a conqueror of Mara, a conqueror of the Evil One, a conqueror of Death, he is called a bhikkhu who has won the battle, a bhikkhu who has conquered in the war, a bhikkhu who has emerged victorious. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu has won the battle, has conquered in the war, and has emerged victorious. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus one who has won the battle, has conquered in the war, and has emerged victorious, he is called a bhikkhu who has reached the end of the journey, a bhikkhu who has finished the task, a bhikkhu who has laid down the burden, a bhikkhu who has reached the true goal, a bhikkhu who has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, it is in this way that a bhikkhu has reached the end of the journey, has finished the task, has laid down the burden, has reached the true goal, has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus one who has reached the end of the journey, has finished the task, has laid down the burden, has reached the true goal, has completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge, he is called a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.

“Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. Which three? [The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. (AN 3.89, AN 3.88, PTS AN i 235)
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
And what, monks, is the training in higher virtue?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous … [as above] … having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
This, monks, is called the training in higher virtue.
And what, monks, is the training in higher mind?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, monks, is called the training in higher mind.
And what, monks, is the training in higher wisdom?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
“This, monks, is called the training in higher wisdom.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.90 9. Samaṇavagga Dutiyasikkhattayasutta (The Second Discourse on the Three Trainings) "Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. What three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the three trainings. "Bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise; for one who possesses the training in higher mind, it is possible that the training in higher wisdom will arise. When the training in higher wisdom has been developed and cultivated, one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Bhikkhus, just as, when the great ocean is stirred up, the waves arise; and when the great ocean is not stirred up, no waves arise; even so, bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise; for one who possesses the training in higher mind, it is possible that the training in higher wisdom will arise. When the training in higher wisdom has been developed and cultivated, one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Bhikkhus, just as, when the great ocean is heated by the heat of the sun, the steam rises; and when the great ocean is not heated by the heat of the sun, no steam rises; even so, bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise... [as above] ...one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Bhikkhus, just as, when the great ocean is struck by the wind, ripples arise; and when the great ocean is not struck by the wind, no ripples arise; even so, bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise... [as above] ...one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Bhikkhus, just as, when the great ocean is struck by the wind, whirlpools arise; and when the great ocean is not struck by the wind, no whirlpools arise; even so, bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise... [as above] ...one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Bhikkhus, just as, when the great ocean is struck by the wind, waves arise; and when the great ocean is not struck by the wind, no waves arise; even so, bhikkhus, for one who possesses the training in higher virtue, it is possible that the training in higher mind will arise; for one who possesses the training in higher mind, it is possible that the training in higher wisdom will arise. When the training in higher wisdom has been developed and cultivated, one attains the destruction of the taints in this very life. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall possess the training in higher virtue; we shall possess the training in higher mind; we shall possess the training in higher wisdom. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves."
“Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. What three? [The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. (AN 3.90, AN 3.89, PTS AN i 235)
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
And what, monks, is the training in higher virtue?
Here, monks, a monk is virtuous... [as before] ...he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training.
This, monks, is called the training in higher virtue.
And what, monks, is the training in higher mind?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, monks, is called the training in higher consciousness.
And what, monks, is the training in higher wisdom?

Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
This, monks, is called the training in higher wisdom.
These, monks, are the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Possessing energy, one should practice higher wisdom;
steadfast, resolute, meditative, mindful,
and with guarded senses, one should live.
As it was before, so it is after;
as it is after, so it was before;
as it is below, so it is above.
As above, so below;
as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Having overcome all directions by means of immeasurable concentration,
they call that the practice of one in training.
And likewise, one whose conduct is completely purified—
he is called a Sambuddha in the world,
a wise one who has reached the end of the path.
With the cessation of consciousness,
for one liberated through the destruction of craving,
there is Nibbāna just like that of a lamp.
“...there is liberation of the mind.

He would think: ‘I will remove this heap of refuse, this great heap of refuse, from its very base. And he would do so. What do you think, monks? On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks, he arrived at a Kosalan town named Saṅkavā.
There, indeed, the Blessed One stayed at Saṅkavā.
Now at that time, a monk named Kassapagotta was a resident of Saṅkavā.
There, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules.

While the Blessed One was thus instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules, the bhikkhu Kassapagotta became impatient and dissatisfied, thinking:
"This ascetic is being too strict."
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Saṅkavā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Rājagaha.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Rājagaha.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, remorse and regret arose in the bhikkhu of the Kassapa clan:
"It is a loss for me, truly it is no gain for me;

it is ill-gotten for me, truly it is not well-gotten for me, that while the bhikkhus were being instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a Dhamma talk connected to the training rules, I felt impatience and resentment."
“This ascetic surely cuts himself too deeply,” he thought.
“What if I were to approach the Blessed One, and having approached him, confess my transgression as a transgression in the presence of the Blessed One?
Then the monk Kassapagotta, having put his lodging in order and taking his bowl and robes, set out for Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages, he approached Rājagaha, Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, and where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the bhikkhu of the Kassapa clan said this to the Blessed One:
“On one occasion, Bhante, the Blessed One was staying at Saṅkavā, a market town of the Kosalans.
There, Bhante, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules.
While the Blessed One was thus instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with that Dhamma talk connected with the training rules, dissatisfaction and resentment arose in me:”
‘This ascetic is indeed cutting himself too deeply.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Saṅkavā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.
(…) Venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, remorse arose within me and I felt regret:
“It is indeed a loss for me, truly no gain for me;

it is ill-gained by me, truly not well-gained by me, that while the bhikkhus were instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening me with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules, I felt only impatience and resentment, thinking:
‘This ascetic is being too strict.’”
"What if I were now to approach the Blessed One? Having approached, I shall confess my transgression as a transgression in the presence of the Blessed One.

"A transgression, venerable sir, has overcome me—foolish as I was, deluded as I was, and unskilled as I was—in that while the Blessed One was instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules..."
“While he was gladdening me, I felt impatience and dissatisfaction, thinking:
‘This ascetic is indeed too strict.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression, for the sake of future restraint.”
“Truly, Kassapa, a transgression has overcome you, as befitted one who is foolish, deluded, and unskilled,
in that while the monks were instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening you with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules,
you felt impatience and resentment toward me.
‘This ascetic is indeed cutting himself too deeply.
But since you, Kassapa, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.

For this, Kassapa, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future.
If, Kassapa, an elder bhikkhu is not desirous of training, does not speak in praise of undertaking the training,
does not encourage other bhikkhus who are not desirous of training to undertake the training,
and does not speak at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other bhikkhus who are desirous of training— I say of such an elder, Kassapa, [that he is like a rotten tree].
I do not speak in praise of that bhikkhu.
Why is that? Because other bhikkhus might associate with him, thinking, "The Teacher speaks in praise of him," and those who associate with him... [would follow suit].
“They would fall into conformity with his view; those who fall into conformity with his view would, for a long time, lead to their harm and suffering.
Therefore, Kassapa, I do not praise such an elder bhikkhu.
And if he is a middle-ranking bhikkhu... [and so on].
"Furthermore, Kassapa, if a newly ordained bhikkhu is not desirous of training, does not speak in praise of undertaking the training,
does not encourage other bhikkhus who are not desirous of training to undertake the training,
and does not speak at the proper time, in accordance with fact and truth, in praise of those other bhikkhus who are desirous of training— for such a newly ordained one, Kassapa, I [do not praise]..."
I do not speak in praise of that bhikkhu.
Why is that? Because other bhikkhus might associate with him, thinking, "The Teacher speaks in his praise," and those who associate with him...
They would fall into conformity with his view; and for those who fall into conformity with his view, that would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
Therefore, Kassapa, I do not speak in praise of such a new bhikkhu.
But even if he is an elder bhikkhu, Kassapa, who is desirous of training and speaks in praise of undertaking the training, and others—
Those monks who are not desirous of training, he encourages them in the training;
and those other monks who are desirous of training, he speaks their praise at the proper time, truthfully and accurately. It is for such an elder monk, Kassapa, that I speak praise. And why is that?
"Thinking, 'The Teacher speaks in praise of him,' other bhikkhus might associate with him;
those who associate with him might follow his example; and those who follow his example would find it to their long-term welfare and happiness.
Therefore, Kassapa, I speak in praise of such an elder bhikkhu."
If, Kassapa, a middle-ranking bhikkhu is desirous of training …pe… or if,
Kassapa, even a newly ordained bhikkhu is desirous of training, speaks in praise of undertaking the training,
encourages other bhikkhus who are not desirous of training to undertake the training, and [encourages] those other bhikkhus who are desirous of training …pe… [to remain so].
"I speak of the praise of such a new bhikkhu, Kassapa, at the proper time, in a way that is factual and true.
And for what reason?
Because other bhikkhus might associate with him, thinking, 'The Teacher himself speaks his praise,' and those who associate with him..."
“They might fall into conformity with his view; those who fall into conformity with his view would find that it leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
Therefore, Kassapa, I speak in praise of such a new bhikkhu.

Loṇakapallavagga Accāyikasutta (The Discourse on Urgent Matters) “Monks, there are these three urgent matters. What three? The urgent matter of aging, the urgent matter of illness, and the urgent matter of death. These, monks, are the three urgent matters.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three urgent duties for a householder who is a farmer. Which three? [The text continues as follows:]”
In this case, monks, a householder who is a farmer very quickly makes his field well-plowed and well-rolled.
Having very quickly made his field well-plowed and well-rolled, he very quickly sows the seeds.
Having very quickly sown the seeds, he very quickly brings water to it and also carries it away.
“Monks, these are the three urgent tasks for a householder who is a farmer.
Yet, monks, that householder farmer has neither such psychic power nor such majesty as to say:
‘May my crops sprout this very day; may they become full of grain tomorrow; may they ripen the day after tomorrow!’”
Then, monks, there comes a time when those crops of that farmer-householder, being subject to the change of seasons, sprout, become full-bodied, and ripen.
In the same way, monks, there are these three urgent duties for a bhikkhu.
What are the three?
The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom—
these, monks, are the three urgent duties of a monk.
For such a monk, monks, there is neither psychic power nor majesty [to prevent his death].
"May my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging this very day, or tomorrow, or the day after.
Then, monks, there comes a time when that monk’s mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging as he trains in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

‘I will have intense desire for undertaking the training in the higher virtue; I will have intense desire for undertaking the training in the higher mind; I will have intense desire for undertaking the training in the higher wisdom.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus ends the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.93 10. Loṇakapallavagga Pavivekasutta (Solitude) “Monks, there are these three kinds of solitude. What three? The solitude of body, the solitude of mind, and the solitude of views. And what, monks, is the solitude of body? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells alone, secluded, withdrawn from society, not frequenting the company of householders or renunciants, delighting in seclusion, finding joy in seclusion, and making solitude his resort. This is called the solitude of body. And what, monks, is the solitude of mind? Here, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust, removed hatred, and eliminated delusion; he is liberated by non-clinging through the destruction of craving. This is called the solitude of mind. And what, monks, is the solitude of views? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who has destroyed the taints, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This is called the solitude of views. These, monks, are the three kinds of solitude.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of seclusion that wanderers of other sects prescribe.
What are the three?
Seclusion in robes, seclusion in almsfood, and seclusion in lodgings.
In this regard, monks, the wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in robes as follows:
they wear hemp garments, they wear flaxen garments, they wear shrouds from cemeteries, they wear rag-robes, and they wear *tirīṭa* grass garments.
They wear [robes made of] deerskins; they wear garments made from the skins of black antelopes; they wear garments of kusa grass; they wear garments of bark;
they wear garments of wood-shavings; they wear garments of human hair; they wear garments of horse-hair;
they wear garments of owls' wings.
“Monks, this is what the wanderers of other sects prescribe regarding seclusion in robes.
Furthermore, monks, this is what the wanderers of other sects prescribe regarding seclusion in almsfood:
they become eaters of greens, eaters of millet, eaters of wild rice, or eaters of coarse grain.”
They eat fallen grains, they eat husks, they eat rice-scum, they eat oil-cakes, they eat grass, they eat cow-dung;
they subsist on forest roots and fruits, living on windfallen fruit.
This, monks, is what the wanderers of other sects prescribe regarding seclusion in alms-gathering.

In this regard, monks, the wanderers of other sects prescribe these dwellings for seclusion: the forest, the foot of a tree, a cemetery, a wilderness thicket, an open space, a heap of straw, and a granary.
These, monks, are the dwellings that the wanderers of other sects prescribe for seclusion.
Monks, these three kinds of seclusion are prescribed by the wanderers of other sects.
"Furthermore, monks, there are these three kinds of seclusion for a monk in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the three?
Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, and immorality has been abandoned by him; he is secluded from that."
He possesses right view, and wrong view has been abandoned by him, and he is secluded from it;
he is one whose taints are destroyed, and his taints have been abandoned, and he is secluded from them.
When, monks, a monk is virtuous, and immorality has been abandoned by him, and he is secluded from it;
He possesses right view, and wrong view has been abandoned by him, and he is secluded from it;
he is one whose taints are destroyed, and his taints have been abandoned, and he is secluded from them.
This, monks, is called a monk who has reached the pinnacle, reached the essence, who is pure and established in the essence.
“Monks, it is just as if a householder farmer had a well-ripened field of rice.
That farmer would have the rice harvested very quickly;
having had it harvested very quickly, he would have it gathered very quickly.”
Having had it gathered quickly, he should have it carried away quickly.
Having had it carried away quickly, he should have it made into a heap quickly.
Having had it made into a heap quickly, he should have it trampled quickly.
Having had it threshed very quickly, he should have the straw removed very quickly.
Having had the straw removed very quickly, he should have the chaff removed very quickly.
Having had the chaff removed very quickly, he should have it winnowed very quickly.
Having had it winnowed very quickly, he would have it brought in very quickly.
Having had it brought in very quickly, he would have it pounded very quickly.
Having had it pounded very quickly, he would have the husks removed very quickly.
“Monks, in this way those grains of the householder farmer have reached the top, reached the essence, are pure, and established in the essence.
In the same way, monks, when a monk is virtuous and has abandoned immorality, he is thereby secluded from it;
when he possesses right view and has abandoned wrong view, he is thereby secluded from it.”
“He is one whose taints are destroyed, his taints have been abandoned, and he is secluded from them.
This, monks, is called a monk who has reached the pinnacle, reached the essence, who is pure and established in the essence.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.94 10. Loṇakapallavagga Saradasutta “Bhikkhus, just as in autumn, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, ascending in the heavens, dispels all darkness from space with its radiance and glory;

so too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has arrived at the fruit, one who has reached the fruit, a noble one who dwells in the fruit. What four? “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, bhikkhus, he is one who has arrived at the fruit, one who has reached the fruit, a noble one who dwells in the fruit.”

“Bhikkhus, just as in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun, rising into the heavens, dispels all the darkness spread across the firmament and shines, blazes, and radiates;

even so, bhikkhus, when the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arises in a noble disciple, with the arising of that vision, three fetters are abandoned in that noble disciple: [sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, and sīlabbataparāmāsa].”
Personal-existence view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Furthermore, he sets out by means of two qualities: covetousness and ill will.

Being secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“Bhikkhus, if at that time a noble disciple were to pass away, there is no fetter by which that noble disciple would be bound to return again to this world.
The third.

“Bhikkhus, there are these three assemblies.
Which three?
An assembly led by the foremost, a divided assembly, and a harmonious assembly.”
And what, bhikkhus, is an assembly that has the foremost members? Here, bhikkhus,
in whatever assembly the elder bhikkhus are not luxurious or lax, do not take pleasure in backsliding,
but lead the way in seclusion and arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, the reaching of the unreached, and the realization of the unrealized.
For the realization of what has not been realized, for the actualization of what has not yet been actualized, later generations follow in the footsteps of those who have seen.

They, too, do not become luxurious or lax; they lay down the burden of falling away, take the lead in seclusion, and arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the actualization of what has not yet been actualized.
This, monks, is called an assembly that has a leader.
And what, monks, is a divided assembly?

Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus live having fallen into quarrels, having fallen into strife, having entered into disputes, stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue—this, monks, is called a divided assembly.
And what, monks, is a harmonious assembly?

“Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus dwell in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of affection— this, monks, is called a harmonious assembly.
At whatever time, monks, the bhikkhus dwell in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, like milk and water mixed,
looking upon one another with eyes of affection— at that time, monks, the bhikkhus generate much merit.”
“Monks, on that occasion the monks dwell in the divine abode, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

In one who is gladdened, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
Monks, it is just as when rain falls in thick drops upon a mountain above, and that water flows down according to the slope.”
As it flows along, it fills the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies; the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies being filled, fill the small pools;
the small pools being filled, fill the large pools; the large pools being filled, fill the small streams;
the small streams being filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers being filled—
They fill the ocean. In the same way, monks, at whatever time the monks dwell in concord, in harmony, without dispute, like milk and water mixed,
looking upon one another with eyes of affection— at that time, monks, the monks generate much merit.
“Bhikkhus, on that occasion the bhikkhus dwell in the divine abiding, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
These, bhikkhus, are the three assemblies.”
The Fourth.

The First Discourse on the Noble Steed (Paṭhamaājānīyasutta):
“Bhikkhus, endowed with three factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What three? [Text follows].”
Which three?
Here, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.
Endowed with these three factors, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of the king, a possession for the king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
With which three?
Here, monks, a monk is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with beauty? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous;
he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is endowed with beauty.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with strength?

Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is endowed with strength.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with speed?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."
“He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’;
he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a monk is possessed of speed.”

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus was the fifth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.97
