Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.98 10. The Chapter on the Lump of Salt The Third Discourse on the Thoroughbred “Monks, there are these three kinds of thoroughbreds among horses. What three? The thoroughbred that, when struck by a whip, exerts itself; the thoroughbred that, when struck by a whip, exerts itself and does not turn back;

and the thoroughbred that, when struck by a whip, exerts itself, turns back, and does not stop until it has reached its goal. These, monks, are the three kinds of thoroughbreds among horses. In the same way, monks, there are these three kinds of thoroughbreds among human beings. What three? The thoroughbred that, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself; the thoroughbred that, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself and does not turn back; and the thoroughbred that, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself, turns back, and does not stop until he has reached his goal. And how, monks, is one a thoroughbred among human beings who, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself, turns back, and does not stop until he has reached his goal? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, and leading to concentration. This, monks, is how one is a thoroughbred among human beings who, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself, turns back, and does not stop until he has reached his goal. Just as, monks, the thoroughbred horse that, when struck by a whip, exerts itself, turns back, and does not stop until it has reached its goal, is called a ‘thoroughbred’ among horses; so too, monks, the thoroughbred person among human beings who, when struck by a blow of the rod, exerts himself, turns back, and does not stop until he has reached his goal, is called a ‘thoroughbred’ among human beings. These, monks, are the three kinds of thoroughbreds among human beings.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of three factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.
Which three?
Here, bhikkhus, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.
“Monks, possessed of these three factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, possessed of three qualities, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the three? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”
In this case, monks, a monk is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with beauty? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous;
he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with beauty.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with strength?

Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with strength.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with speed?

Here, monks, through the destruction of the taints, a monk dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
"In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with speed.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of offerings... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
This was the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.99 10. The Chapter on the Lump of Salt The Discourse on the Book “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? “The person who is like a book, the person who is like a lump of salt, and the person who is like a great ocean. “And how, monks, is one a person like a book?

Here, monks, a certain person is well-born on both sides, of pure descent, unblemished back to the seventh paternal generation, with flawless lineage of birth and motherhood, possessing wealth, grain, silver, and gold, abundant property and possessions, with many vehicles, many servants and laborers, and many wives, concubines, and maidservants. Yet he is not learned; he does not know the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, and which reveals the holy life in its fulfillment and complete purity. He does not understand it as it really is. This, monks, is called a person like a book. “And how, monks, is one a person like a lump of salt? Here, monks, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...with many wives, concubines, and maidservants. He is learned; he knows the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, and which reveals the holy life in its fulfillment and complete purity. He understands it as it really is. However, whatever wholesome qualities he has acquired, they are few; those unwholesome qualities are many. Just as if, monks, a man were to put a small lump of salt into a small cup of water: would the small cup of water become salty and undrinkable because of that small lump of salt? “Yes, venerable sir. “Just so, monks, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...He is learned... He understands it as it really is. However, whatever wholesome qualities he has acquired, they are few; those unwholesome qualities are many. This, monks, is called a person like a lump of salt. “And how, monks, is one a person like a great ocean? Here, monks, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...He is learned; he knows the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, and which reveals the holy life in its fulfillment and complete purity. He understands it as it really is. Whatever wholesome qualities he has acquired, they are many; those unwholesome qualities are few. Just as if, monks, a man were to put a small lump of salt into the great ocean: would the great ocean become salty and undrinkable because of that small lump of salt? “No, venerable sir. Why is that? Because the great ocean is deep, vast, and immeasurable. “Just so, monks, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...He is learned... He understands it as it really is. Whatever wholesome qualities he has acquired, they are many; those unwholesome qualities are few. This, monks, is called a person like a great ocean. “These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Monks, even a new cloth is ill-colored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value;
monks, even a middle-aged cloth is ill-colored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value. (AN 3.99, AN 3.97–98, PTS AN i 246)
“Monks, even an old rag is discolored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value.
Monks, they either use an old rag to wipe a cooking pot or throw it away on a rubbish heap.
In the same way, monks, even if a monk is new, if he is immoral and of evil character...”
This, I say, is his ugliness.
Just as that cloth, monks, is ugly, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And for those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example, it leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
This, I say, is due to his painful contact.
Just as that cloth, monks, is painful to the touch, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift yields neither great fruit nor great benefit.
This, I say, is because of his lack of worth.
Just as that cloth, monks, is of little value, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And if, monks, a monk is of middle standing... [and so on].
“Monks, even if a monk is an elder who is immoral and of evil character, I say this is his ugliness.
Just as a cloth is ugly, monks, so too, I say, is this person.
And those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example—for them that results in harm and suffering for a long time.”
I say this is because of his painful contact.
Just as that cloth, monks, is painful to the touch, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And for those to whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift is not of great fruit or great benefit.
I say this is because of his worthlessness.
Just as that cloth, monks, is worthless, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And yet, monks, such an elder monk speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha.
The monks said this to him:
“What is the use of what you, a fool and an incompetent person, have to say?
Do you really think that you, too, ought to speak?”
Thus, being angry and displeased, he utters such speech that the Saṅgha suspends him, like a cloth thrown onto a heap of refuse.
Monks, even a new Kāsī cloth is beautiful, pleasant to the touch, and expensive;
monks, even a middle-aged Kāsī cloth is beautiful, pleasant to the touch, and expensive.
“Monks, even a worn-out cloth from Kāsī is beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value.
Even a worn-out cloth from Kāsī is used as a wrapping for jewels or placed inside a perfume casket.
In the same way, monks, if a monk is new but virtuous and of good character, I declare this to be his ‘golden quality.’”
“Just as, monks, that Kāsī cloth is beautiful in color, so too, monks, do I describe this person.
And for those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
This, I say, is due to his pleasant touch.”
“Just as, monks, a cloth from Kāsī is pleasant to the touch, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And for those to whom he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift becomes of great fruit and great benefit.
This, I say, is due to his high worth.”
"Just as, monks, a cloth from Kāsī is of great value, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
Whether he be a junior monk, monks...
or even an elder monk, monks... I describe such a person."
And when such an elder bhikkhu speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the bhikkhus say to him:
“Be quiet, venerable sirs; the elder bhikkhu is speaking on the Dhamma and the Vinaya.”
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
'We shall be like fine Kāsī cloth, not like hempen cloth.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100 10.
The Chapter on the Salt-Crystal (Loṇakapallavagga)
Loṇakapallasutta: “Bhikkhus, suppose someone were to say this: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when developed, leads so much to revulsion as the salt-cellar.
(AN 3.100, AN 3.99, PTS AN i 249) “Whoever, bhikkhus, should speak thus:”

“Bhikkhus, if it were the case that ‘in whatever way this person performs an action, in that very way he experiences its result,’ then, such being the case, there would be no living of the holy life, and no opportunity would be discerned for the complete ending of suffering.
But, bhikkhus, if one were to say:
‘In whatever way this person performs an action to be experienced in a certain manner, in that very way he experiences its ripening’—”
When this is so, monks, there is the living of the holy life, and an opportunity is seen for the complete ending of suffering.
Here, monks, a certain person has committed even a trifling evil deed, and it leads him to hell.

But here, monks, another person has committed exactly the same kind of trifling evil deed, yet it is to be experienced in this very life; not even a slight [result] is perceived, let alone a great one.
“Monks, what kind of person, when they have committed even a slight evil deed, is led by it to hell?

Here, monks, a certain person is one who has not developed the body, has not developed virtue, has not developed the mind, and has not developed wisdom; they are limited, of small self, and dwelling in suffering.
It is for such a person, monks, that even a slight evil deed committed leads them to hell.”
“Monks, what kind of person experiences such a trifling evil deed as something to be felt in this very life, so that not even a speck appears, let alone more?
Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom; he is unshaken, great, and dwells in the immeasurable.
For such a person, monks, such a trifling evil deed committed becomes something to be felt in this very life, so that not even a speck appears, let alone more.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a lump of salt into a small water-pot containing a little water.
What do you think, bhikkhus,
would that small amount of water become salty and undrinkable because of that lump of salt?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“And why is that? “Because, venerable sir, that little water in the water-pot would become salty and undrinkable by means of that lump of salt.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a lump of salt into the river Ganges.
What do you think, bhikkhus,
would the river Ganges become salty and undrinkable because of that lump of salt?”
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because that great body of water in the river Ganges would not become salty from that single lump of salt; it would remain drinkable.”
“In the same way, monks, here some person has committed even a trifling evil deed, and it leads him to hell.

But here, monks, for another person, that very same kind of trifling evil deed committed becomes something to be experienced in this very life; not even a speck [of suffering] appears, let alone much more.
For what kind of person, monks, does even a trifling evil deed committed lead him to hell?

“Here, monks, a certain person has not developed the body, has not developed virtue, has not developed the mind, and has not developed wisdom; he is limited, small-minded, and dwells in a state of suffering.
For such a person, monks, even a trifling evil deed committed leads him to hell.
But for what kind of person, monks, does an exactly similar trifling evil deed committed become experienced in this very life, so that not even a slight [result] appears, let alone a great one?”
“Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom; he is not limited, he is great, and he dwells in the immeasurable.
For such a person, monks, even a trifling evil deed committed becomes experienced in this very life; it does not appear as even a speck, so what need to speak of more?
Here, monks, a certain person goes to prison for half a kahāpaṇa, or goes to prison for a kahāpaṇa, or goes to prison for a hundred kahāpaṇas.”
"Here, monks, a certain person does not go to prison for half a kahāpaṇa, nor does he go to prison for a kahāpaṇa, nor does he go to prison for a hundred kahāpaṇas.
And what kind of person, monks, goes to prison for half a kahāpaṇa, goes to prison for a kahāpaṇa, and goes to prison for a hundred kahāpaṇas?
Here, monks, a certain person is poor, having little wealth and few possessions."
“Monks, such a person as this goes to imprisonment for half a kahāpaṇa, goes to imprisonment for a kahāpaṇa, and even goes to imprisonment for a hundred kahāpaṇas.
But what kind of person, monks, does not go to imprisonment for half a kahāpaṇa, does not go to imprisonment for a kahāpaṇa, and does not go to imprisonment for a hundred kahāpaṇas?
Here, monks, someone is wealthy, possessing great riches and great wealth.”
“Monks, such a person does not go to imprisonment for half a kahāpaṇa coin, nor does he go to imprisonment for one kahāpaṇa coin, nor does he go to imprisonment for even a hundred kahāpaṇa coins.
In the same way, monks, here some individual has committed a trifling evil deed,
yet it leads him to hell.”
“Here, monks, for a certain person, even such a trifling evil deed committed becomes to be experienced in this very life, so that not even a slight [retribution] appears, let alone a great deal.
Of what sort of person, monks, is a trifling evil deed committed led by him to hell?
Here, monks, a certain person is undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom; he is limited, of small self, and one who dwells in suffering.”
“Monks, for such a person as this, even a trifling evil deed committed leads him to hell.
Monks, for what kind of person does an exactly similar trifling evil deed committed become to be experienced in this very life, so that not even a speck appears, let alone more?
Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom; he is unconfined, vast, and dwells in the immeasurable.”
“Monks, for such a person as this, even a trifling evil deed committed is experienced in the present life; not even a speck appears, let alone anything more.
Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom; he is not limited, but is great and dwells in the immeasurable.
For such a person as this, monks, even a trifling evil deed committed is experienced in the present life; not even a speck appears, let alone anything more.”
“Just as, monks, a butcher or a butcher’s assistant, when some sheep steal what has not been given,
is able to kill them, bind them, fine them, or deal with them as the situation requires;
yet when other sheep steal what has not been given, he is not able to kill them, bind them, fine them, or deal with them as the situation requires.”
"Monks, what kind of person is one whom a butcher or a sheep-slaughterer is able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit when that person takes a sheep without it being given?
Here, monks, someone is poor, having little property and few possessions.
It is such a person, monks, whom a butcher or a sheep-slaughterer is able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit when he takes a sheep without it being given."
“Monks, of what sort is a sheep-herder or a sheep-slaughterer who is unable to kill, bind, fine, or do as he pleases with another who is taking a sheep that has not been given?
Here, monks, someone is wealthy, possessing great wealth and great possessions—either a king or a royal minister.
It is with such a person, monks, that a sheep-herder or a sheep-slaughterer is unable to kill, bind, fine, or do as he pleases when taking a sheep that has not been given.”
On the contrary, he begs him with palms joined:
“Give me, dear sir, either a ram or the price for a ram.
In the same way, monks, here some person has committed even such a trifling evil deed that it leads him to hell.

"Furthermore, monks, there is the case where a certain person has committed exactly such a trifling evil deed that it is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a speck [of its result] appears, much less more.
Of what kind of person, monks, is even a trifling evil deed committed led to hell?
Here, monks, a certain person is undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, undeveloped in wisdom—limited, small-minded, dwelling in suffering."
“Monks, even a trifling evil deed committed by such a person leads him to hell.
Monks, for what kind of person does an exactly similar trifling evil deed committed become to be experienced in this very life, so that not even a speck [of its result] appears, let alone more?
Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom; he is unshrinking, great-souled, and dwells in the immeasurable.”
“Monks, for such a person as this, even a trifling evil deed committed will be experienced in this very life; it does not appear as even a grain of [future] consequence, let alone more.
Monks, if one were to say:

‘In whatever way this person performs a deed, in that very way he experiences its result,’ then, monks, there would be no living of the holy life, and no opportunity would be seen for the complete ending of suffering.”
"But, bhikkhus, if someone were to say:
'In whatever way this person performs a deed to be experienced, in that very way he experiences its result'—
if this were so, bhikkhus, there would be a living of the holy life, and an opportunity would be discerned for the complete ending of suffering."
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.101 10.

The Discourse on the Gold-Washer (Paṁsudhovakasutta):
“Bhikkhus, there are gross impurities in gold: dirt, sand, gravel, and pebbles.
Then a goldsmith or his apprentice pours it into a basin and washes, rinses, and cleanses it.
When that has been discarded and eliminated, there remain among the gold certain middle-grade impurities: fine grit and coarse sand.
The goldsmith or his apprentice washes, rinses, and cleanses that as well.
When that has been discarded and eliminated, there remain subtle impurities associated with the gold: fine grit and black specks.
Then a goldsmith or his apprentice washes it, rinses it, and cleanses it thoroughly.
When that has been discarded and eliminated, only golden sand remains.
Then a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice, having placed that gold in a crucible, blows upon it, fans it, and purifies it by blowing.

While that gold is being blown, fanned, and purified, its impurities have not yet been removed; it is neither soft nor workable, nor is it radiant but brittle, and it does not properly serve for work.
There comes a time, monks, when the goldsmith or the goldsmith’s apprentice blows upon, fans, and purifies that gold.
That gold, when beaten, refined, and polished, becomes free from dross; it becomes soft, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and it properly serves for its intended purpose.
Whatever kind of ornament one desires—whether a flat band, a bracelet, a neck-ornament, or a golden garland—it fulfills that purpose.
In the same way, monks, there are gross defilements in a monk who is devoted to the higher mind.
Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct— a wise bhikkhu of steadfast nature abandons them,
dispels them, brings them to an end, and renders them non-existent.
When these have been abandoned and brought to an end, there exist for that bhikkhu devoted to higher mind states those things associated with the middle [level].
The defilements are sensual thought, thought of ill will, and thought of cruelty;
a mindful and steadfast monk abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
When they have been abandoned and brought to an end, there remain for that monk devoted to higher consciousness subtle [defilements] associated with pleasure.
The defilements are thoughts of relatives, thoughts of the country, and thoughts associated with not being despised.
A mindful and steadfast monk abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
When they have been abandoned and brought to an end, thereafter only thoughts of the Dhamma will remain.

Thus there is concentration that is neither peaceful nor sublime, not attained through tranquility, not reached through unification, and characterized by being restrained and suppressed by volitional effort.
There comes a time, monks, when that mind becomes inwardly settled, composed, unified, and concentrated;
that concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility, reached through unification, and is not characterized by being restrained and suppressed by volitional effort.

Whatever state is to be realized through direct knowledge, toward the realization of that state he inclines his mind; in each and every case, he attains the capability of being a witness, provided there is a suitable basis.
If he so desires: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power: being one, may I become many;
being many, may I become one; may I appear and disappear; may I pass through walls, fences, and mountains..."
I could go unhindered, just as in the air; I could dive in and out of the earth, just as in water;
I could walk on water without breaking the surface, just as on earth; I could travel cross-legged through the air, just like a winged bird;
and I could even touch these two, the moon and the sun, so powerful and majestic with such great supernormal might.

‘I would touch and stroke it with my hand; I would wield power with my body even as far as the Brahma-world,’ he attains the capacity for realization in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.

If he should wish: ‘With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near’—he attains the capacity for realization in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.
In each and every instance, he attains the capacity for realization whenever there is a suitable basis.

If he so desires: "May I, by encompassing the mind with my own mind, understand the minds of other beings and other persons—may I understand a mind affected by lust as a mind affected by lust," [he attains it].
One should know a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust;
one should know a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred,
or a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred.
One should know a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," and one should know a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion";
one should know a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
Or he should understand a scattered mind as "a scattered mind";
he should understand an exalted mind as "an exalted mind," and he should understand a non-exalted mind as "a non-exalted mind."
One should understand a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind,
or one should understand an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind;
one should understand a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind.
‘May I know an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind;
may I know a liberated mind as a liberated mind,
and may I know an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’”
In each and every instance, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.
If he so desires: "May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births..."
“Thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
‘There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.’”
‘Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here’—thus he would recollect his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details.’
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.

If he so desires: "May I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their kamma"—he attains this.
One would understand beings thus: "Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. Or these..."
"But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook actions based on right view— on the dissolution of the body, after death,
they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the purified divine eye...
‘May I, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and may I understand how beings fare according to their kamma,’ then he attains the capability for realization in each and every case, whenever there is an appropriate occasion.

Thus, if he wishes: "May I, through the destruction of the taints, dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom," he attains the capacity to be a witness in each and every case, provided there is a suitable basis.
Tenth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.102 10.

Loṇakapallavagga Nimittasutta: The Discourse on the Sign “Monks, there are these three signs. What three? The sign of form, the sign of sound, and the sign of mind-objects. These, monks, are the three signs.”
“Monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs: from time to time he should attend to the sign of concentration;
from time to time he should attend to the sign of exertion; from time to time he should attend to the sign of equanimity.”
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would tend toward indolence.
If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would tend toward agitation.”

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not be rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind attends from time to time to the sign of concentration,
from time to time to the sign of exertion, and from time to time to the sign of equanimity...”
He attends to it; that mind becomes pliant, wieldy, radiant, and not brittle, and it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
Just as, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice might prepare a furnace and [place] the furnace...
Having bound it, one would heat it in a furnace; having heated it in the furnace, one would take the gold with tongs and cast it into the furnace;
having cast it into the furnace, one would blow upon it from time to time, sprinkle it with water from time to time, and look on at it with equanimity from time to time.
“Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to heat that gold exclusively with fire, it is possible that the gold would burn away.
Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to sprinkle that gold exclusively with water, it is possible that the gold would go out.
Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to simply ignore that gold, it is possible that the gold would not reach full maturity.”
But when, monks, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice repeatedly heats that gold,
repeatedly sprinkles it with water, and repeatedly observes it, then that gold becomes soft, workable, radiant, and not brittle; it is properly fit for working.
Whatever kind of ornament he might desire—whether a band, an earring, a neck-ornament, or a golden garland—it serves his purpose.
In the same way, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs:
from time to time he should attend to the sign of concentration; from time to time he should attend to the sign of exertion; and from time to time he should attend to the sign of equanimity.
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would tend toward indolence.
If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would tend toward agitation.”

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind attends from time to time to the sign of concentration,
from time to time to the sign of exertion, and from time to time to the sign of equanimity...”
He attends to it; that mind becomes pliant, wieldy, radiant, and not brittle, and it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

And whatever state realizable by direct knowledge his mind inclines toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge, he attains the capacity to be a witness therein, in each respective case, provided there is a suitable basis.
Thus, if he should wish: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power...
[the six direct knowledges should be expanded here] ...having realized for myself with direct knowledge the destruction of the taints, may I abide therein," [he attains it].
"In each and every case, one attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
The fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Lump of Salt, is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Urgent business, seclusion,
autumn, and the three assemblies.
The thoroughbred horse, the cloth,
salt, and washing the signs—
thus ends the second fiftieth section.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.103 11. Sambodhavagga Pubbeva sambodha Sutta: Before Enlightenment “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me: ‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of form? Then, bhikkhus, through careful attention, there took place in me a breakthrough by wisdom: ‘The gratification in the case of form is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment. ‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of feeling? ... [as above] ... ‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of perception? ... [as above] ... ‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of volitional formations? ... [as above] ... ‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of consciousness? Then, bhikkhus, through careful attention, there took place in me a breakthrough by wisdom: ‘The gratification in the case of consciousness is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: ‘But, venerable sir, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of form? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of feeling? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of perception? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of volitional formations? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of consciousness? ‘The gratification in the case of form, bhikkhu, is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment. The gratification in the case of feeling is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment. The gratification in the case of perception is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment. The gratification in the case of volitional formations is their pleasure; the danger is their suffering; the escape is their relinquishment. The gratification in the case of consciousness is its pleasure; the danger is its suffering; the escape is its relinquishment.’”
“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me:
‘What now in the world is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape?’”
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon the world—this is the gratification in the world.
That the world is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the world."
‘The subduing of desire and lust for the world, the abandoning of desire and lust for the world— this is the escape from the world. Monks,
as long as I did not directly know, according to reality, the gratification of the world as gratification, the danger of the world as danger,
and the escape from the world as escape, for that long, monks, I did not claim in this world with its devas, Māras, and...
“...among the generation with its brahmas, its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

But from the time, monks, that I had thus directly known the world as it really is— with its gratification as gratification, its danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape— then, monks, in this world with its devas...
In this world with its Māras and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
“Unshakable is my liberation; this is the final birth; now there is no further becoming.
Thus it was said. First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.104

11. Sambodhavagga First Discourse on Gratification (Paṭhama-assāda-sutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? They are the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever gratification there is in relation to these five aggregates subject to clinging, that is the gratification in them. Whatever danger there is in relation to these five aggregates subject to clinging, that is the danger in them. Whatever escape there is from these five aggregates subject to clinging, that is the escape from them. And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in the case of form? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form—this is the gratification in form. And what is the danger in form? Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form. And what is the escape from form? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form. In the case of feeling... In the case of perception... In the case of volitional formations... In the case of consciousness: whatever gratification there is in relation to consciousness, that is the gratification in it. Whatever danger there is in relation to consciousness, that is the danger in it. Whatever escape there is from consciousness, that is the escape from it. And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in the case of consciousness? Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. And what is the danger in consciousness? Consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. And what is the escape from consciousness? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness. When a noble disciple has seen thus as it really is with correct wisdom, he here develops dispassion toward form, dispassion toward feeling, dispassion toward perception, dispassion toward volitional formations, and dispassion toward consciousness. Through dispassion, his mind becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, it is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’”
“Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the gratification in the world. Whatever gratification there is in the world, that I discovered.
To whatever extent there is gratification in the world, that has been clearly seen by me with wisdom.
Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the danger in the world. Whatever danger there is in the world, that I discovered.”
Whatever peril there is in the world, that has been well seen by me with wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for escape from the world; I attained that which is the escape from the world.
Whatever escape there is in the world, that has been well seen by me with wisdom.

“Bhikkhus, as long as I did not directly know, as they really are, the gratification in the world as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape, I did not, bhikkhus, claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when I directly knew, as they really are, the gratification in the world as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape, then, bhikkhus,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.”
But when, monks, I had directly known the world’s gratification as gratification, its danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape,
exactly as they truly are, then, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās,
among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
"And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my final birth; now there is no further becoming. This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.105 11.

Sambodhavagga The Second Discourse on Gratification (Dutiya-assāda-sutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these three gratifications in the noble life. What three? The gratification of seeing the Noble Ones, the gratification of hearing the True Dhamma, and the gratification of practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the three gratifications in the noble life.”
“Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in the world, beings would not become infatuated with the world.
But because there is gratification in the world, beings become infatuated with the world. (AN 3.105, AN 3.102a, PTS AN i 260)
If, monks, there were no danger in the world, beings would not become disenchanted with the world.
But because there is danger in the world, monks, beings become disenchanted with the world.
If, monks, there were no escape from the world, beings would not escape from the world.
But because, monks, there is an escape from the world, therefore beings escape from the world. And as long as beings, monks,
have not directly known, as they really are, the gratification of the world as gratification, the danger of the world as danger, and the escape from the world as escape, for so long, monks,
beings do not escape from this world with its devas, its Māras, and its...
They dwelt with a mind that had escaped, was detached, and was utterly liberated from the world including the Brahmās, the generation of recluses and brahmins, and gods and humans,
having made it free of boundaries. But when, monks, beings [perceive] the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape from the world...
When they had directly known escape as it really is, then, monks, beings— along with the world of devas, Māras, and Brahmās,
and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans— became escaped, detached, and utterly liberated,
dwelling with a mind for which the boundaries of the realm of death were transcended.”
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.106.
11. Sambodhavagga (The Chapter on Full Enlightenment).
The Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta):

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the gratification in the world as gratification, the danger in the world as danger, and the escape from the world as escape; [they do not understand these things as they really are].”
“Bhikkhus, those recluses or brahmins are not, in my view, truly recluses among recluses or truly brahmins among brahmins;
nor do those venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life, enter and dwell in the goal of the recluse’s state or the goal of the brahmin’s state.”
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand, as they really are, the gratification of the world as gratification, the danger of the world as danger, and the escape from the world as escape—
those ascetics or brahmins, monks, are reckoned among the ascetics and reckoned among the brahmins;
and those venerable ones, in this very life, have attained the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood."
“Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I dwell having attained it.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.107

11. “Monks, in the discipline of the Noble One, this is weeping: namely, singing.
Monks, in the discipline of the Noble One, this is madness: namely, dancing.
Monks, in the discipline of the Noble One, this is childishness: namely, excessive laughing with bared teeth.”
"Therefore, monks, there should be a demolition of the bridge to song, a demolition of the bridge to dance; it is enough for you who are delighted by the Dhamma to merely smile.
Thus was the fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.108

11. Sambodhavagga Atittisutta (AN 3.108, AN 3.104, PTS AN i 261) “Monks, there are these five things that do not lead to satisfaction for one who is unsatisfied. What five? Sensual pleasures are not satisfying for one who is unsatisfied with sensual pleasures; forms are not satisfying for one who is unsatisfied with forms; sounds are not satisfying for one who is unsatisfied with sounds; odors are not satisfying for one who is unsatisfied with odors; tastes are not satisfying for one who is unsatisfied with tastes. These, monks, are the five things that do not lead to satisfaction for one who is unsatisfied.”
“Bhikkhus, there is no satiety from indulging in three things. Which three?
There is no satiety, bhikkhus, from indulging in sleep.”
“Monks, there is no satisfaction in indulging in the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors.
Monks, there is no satisfaction in engaging in sexual intercourse.
Monks, there is no satisfaction in indulging in these three things.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.109 11.
Sambodhavagga (The Chapter on Full Enlightenment)
The Discourse on the Unprotected (Arakkhitasutta).
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [saluted] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, when the mind is unprotected, bodily action is unprotected, verbal action is unprotected, and mental action is unprotected.

For one whose bodily action is unprotected, whose verbal action is unprotected, and whose mental action is unprotected, bodily action becomes defiled, verbal action becomes defiled, and mental action becomes defiled.”

For one whose bodily action is impure, whose verbal action is impure, and whose mental action is impure, the bodily action becomes putrid, the verbal action becomes putrid, and the mental action becomes putrid.
For one whose bodily action is putrid, whose verbal action is putrid, and whose mental action is putrid, there is no auspicious death, nor a blessed passing away.
Householder, it is just as if, in a gabled house that is poorly roofed, the peak is unprotected, the rafters are unprotected, and the walls are unprotected.
The rafters become leaky, the rafters become rotten, and the walls become leaky;
the rafters become rotten, the rafters become rotten, and the walls become rotten.
In the same way, householder, when the mind is unprotected, bodily action is unprotected, verbal action is unprotected, and mental action is unprotected.

For one whose bodily action is unprotected, whose verbal action is unprotected, and whose mental action is unprotected, their bodily action becomes corrupted, their verbal action becomes corrupted, and their mental action becomes corrupted.

For one whose bodily action is corrupted, whose verbal action is corrupted, and whose mental action is corrupted, their bodily action becomes putrid, their verbal action becomes putrid, and their mental action becomes putrid.
For one whose bodily action is rotten, whose verbal action is rotten, and whose mental action is rotten, there is neither a auspicious death nor an auspicious passing away.
Householder, when the mind is guarded, bodily action is guarded, verbal action is guarded, and mental action is guarded.

For one whose bodily action is guarded, whose verbal action is guarded, and whose mental action is guarded, their bodily action remains untainted, their verbal action remains untainted, and their mental action remains untainted.

For one whose bodily action is untainted, whose verbal action is untainted, and whose mental action is untainted, their bodily action is not putrid, their verbal action is not putrid, and their mental action is not putrid.
For one whose bodily action is not putrid, whose verbal action is not putrid, and whose mental action is not putrid, there is a blessed death and a blessed passing away.
Just as, householder, in a peaked house with a good roof, the peak is protected, the rafters are protected, and the walls are protected;
The roof-peak is not leaking, the rafters are not leaking, and the walls are not leaking;
the roof-peak is not rotten, the rafters are not rotten, and the walls are not rotten.
In the same way, householder, when the mind is guarded, bodily action is guarded, verbal action is guarded, and mental action is guarded.
For one whose bodily action is guarded, whose verbal action is guarded, and whose mental action is guarded, bodily action is untainted, verbal action is untainted, and mental action is untainted.

For one whose bodily action is untainted, whose verbal action is untainted, and whose mental action is untainted, bodily action is not putrid, verbal action is not putrid, and mental action is not putrid.
“For one whose bodily action is not corrupt, whose verbal action is not corrupt, and whose mental action is not corrupt, there is a fortunate death and a fortunate passing away.
The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.110

11. Sambodhavagga Byāpannasutta (AN 3.110, AN 3.106, PTS AN i 262) “Bhikkhus, there are these three persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is full of ill will, the person who is corrupt, and the person who is insane. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one who is full of ill will? Here, bhikkhus, a person has a mind full of ill will toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his relatives, and his kinsmen; he harbors thoughts of harm, thoughts of injury, and thoughts of death toward them. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is full of ill will. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one who is corrupt? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter. He is greedy, malicious, and holds wrong view. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is corrupt. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one who is insane? Here, bhikkhus, a person’s mind is deranged, his faculties are disordered, and he wanders about babbling incoherently. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is insane. These, bhikkhus, are the three persons found existing in the world.”
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, when the mind is corrupted, bodily action is also corrupted, verbal action is also corrupted, and mental action is also corrupted.
For one whose bodily action is corrupted, whose verbal action is corrupted, and whose mental action is corrupted, there is neither a fortunate death nor a fortunate passing away.”
“Just as, householder, in a gabled house that is poorly roofed, the peak collapses, the rafters collapse, and the walls collapse;
even so, householder, when the mind has collapsed, bodily action collapses, verbal action collapses, and mental action collapses.
For one whose bodily action has collapsed, whose verbal action has collapsed, and whose mental action has collapsed, there is no auspicious death, nor a fortunate passing away.”
“Householder, when the mind is free from malice, bodily action is also free from malice, verbal action is also free from malice, and mental action is also free from malice.
For one whose bodily action, verbal action, and mental action are free from malice, there is a fortunate death and a fortunate passing away.
Just as, householder, in a peaked house with a well-thatched roof, the peak is free from decay, the rafters are free from decay, and the walls are free from decay;”

“In the same way, householder, when the mind is uncorrupted, bodily action is also uncorrupted, verbal action is also uncorrupted, and mental action is also uncorrupted. For one whose bodily action is uncorrupted...
[and so on] ...for one whose mental action is uncorrupted, there is a fortunate death and a fortunate passing away.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.111 11. Sambodhavagga Paṭhamanidānasutta (The First Discourse on the Origin) “Bhikkhus, there are these three origins of things. What three? The origin of things through craving, the origin of things through views, and the origin of things through ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the three origins of things. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the origin of things through craving?

“Contact, bhikkhu, is the cause, contact is the condition, for the origin of things through craving. “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the origin of things through views? “The underlying tendency to views, bhikkhu, is the cause, the underlying tendency to views is the condition, for the origin of things through views. “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the origin of things through ignorance? “Lack of wisdom, bhikkhu, is the cause, lack of wisdom is the condition, for the origin of things through ignorance. “Bhikkhus, when one does not understand and does not penetrate the gratification in contact as it really is, the danger in contact as it really is, and the escape from contact as it really is, then contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the origin of things through craving. When one does not understand and does not penetrate the gratification in views as it really is, the danger in views as it really is, and the escape from views as it really is, then the underlying tendency to views is the cause, the underlying tendency to views is the condition, for the origin of things through views. When one does not understand and does not penetrate the gratification in ignorance as it really is, the danger in ignorance as it really is, and the escape from ignorance as it really is, then lack of wisdom is the cause, lack of wisdom is the condition, for the origin of things through ignorance. But, bhikkhus, when one understands and penetrates the gratification in contact as it really is, the danger in contact as it really is, and the escape from contact as it really is, then contact is abandoned. When one understands and penetrates the gratification in views as it really is, the danger in views as it really is, and the escape from views as it really is, then the underlying tendency to views is abandoned. When one understands and penetrates the gratification in ignorance as it really is, the danger in ignorance as it really is, and the escape from ignorance as it really is, then lack of wisdom is abandoned. With the abandoning of craving, the origin of things through craving is abandoned. With the abandoning of the underlying tendency to views, the origin of things through views is abandoned. With the abandoning of ignorance, the origin of things through ignorance is abandoned. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has abandoned the origin of things through craving, the origin of things through views, and the origin of things through ignorance, he is called a noble disciple who has cut off craving, stripped off the fetter, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma. What are the three? [Text continues]”
Greed is the cause for the origination of kamma; hatred is the cause for the origination of kamma; delusion is the cause for the origination of kamma.

Whatever kamma, monks, is fashioned by greed, born of greed, caused by greed, and originated from greed—that kamma is unwholesome, that kamma is blameworthy, that kamma has suffering as its result, and that kamma leads to the further origination of kamma.
...it does not lead to the cessation of karma.

Monks, whatever action is performed out of hatred, born of hatred, rooted in hatred, originating from hatred—that action is unwholesome, that action is blameworthy, that action has suffering as its result; that action leads to the further arising of karma.
it does not lead to the cessation of karma.

Monks, whatever action is produced by delusion, born of delusion, rooted in delusion, and originating from delusion—that action is unwholesome, that action is blameworthy, that action has a painful result; such action leads to the accumulation of karma.
...it does not lead to the cessation of karma.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of karmas.
There are, monks, these three causes for the origination of karmas.
Which three?
Non-greed is a cause for the origination of kamma; non-hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma; non-delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed out of non-greed, born of non-greed, having non-greed as its cause, and originating from non-greed—that [is wholesome].
That action is wholesome; that action is blameless; that action has a pleasant result;
that action leads to the cessation of action, not to the origination of action.
Monks, whatever action is performed out of non-hatred, born of non-hatred, with non-hatred as its source, and with non-hatred as its origin—that action...
That action is wholesome, that action is blameless, that action has a pleasant result;
that action leads to the cessation of karma, not to the origination of karma.
Monks, whatever action is performed out of non-delusion, born of non-delusion, with non-delusion as its source, and with non-delusion as its origin—that action...
“That action is wholesome; that action is blameless; that action has a pleasant result;
that action leads to the cessation of action, not to the origination of action.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of actions.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.112 11.
Sambodhavagga (The Chapter on Full Enlightenment)
The Second Discourse on Origins (Dutiyanidānasutta): “Monks,
there are these three origins for the arising of kamma.”
Which three?
Monks, desire arises based on phenomena that were objects of desire and lust in the past;
monks, desire arises based on phenomena that will be objects of desire and lust in the future.
“Bhikkhus, desire arises with reference to things in the present that are objects for desire and lust.
And how, bhikkhus, does desire arise with reference to things in the past that are objects for desire and lust?
Bhikkhus, with reference to things in the past that are objects for desire and lust, one thinks over them and reflects upon them with the mind.”
When one reflects upon and examines with the mind those phenomena pertaining to the past that are objects of desire and lust, desire arises.
Being possessed by desire, one becomes fettered by those phenomena.
Monks, I call this a fetter: whatever mental passion there is.
"Thus, monks, desire arises with reference to things in the past that are objects for desire and lust.
And how, monks, does desire arise with reference to things in the future that are objects for desire and lust?
With reference to things in the future that are objects for desire and lust, one reflects upon them and examines them with the mind."
When one reflects upon and examines with the mind those future phenomena that are the basis for desire and lust, desire arises.
Once desire has arisen, one becomes bound by those phenomena.
Monks, I call this a fetter: whatever infatuation there is of the mind.
"Thus, monks, desire arises with reference to things that are objects for desire and lust in the future.
And how, monks, does desire arise with reference to things that are objects for desire and lust in the present?
Monks, with reference to things that are objects for desire and lust in the present, one reflects upon them and examines them with the mind."
When one reflects upon and examines with the mind those phenomena in the present that are objects for desire and lust, desire arises.
Once desire has arisen, one becomes bound by those phenomena.
Monks, I call this "fetter": it is the passion of the mind.
"Thus, monks, desire arises with reference to phenomena that are objects for desire and lust in the present.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of kamma.
There are, monks, these three causes for the origination of kamma."
Which three?
Monks, desire does not arise with reference to things that were objects of desire and lust in the past;
monks, desire does not arise with reference to things that will be objects of desire and lust in the future.
“Bhikkhus, desire does not arise with reference to things in the present that are objects of desire and lust.
And how, bhikkhus, does desire not arise with reference to things in the past that are objects of desire and lust?
One understands the future result of those things in the past that are objects of desire and lust.”
Having understood the future result, he turns away from it.
Having turned away from it and having penetrated it with the mind, he sees by piercing through it with wisdom.
In this way, monks, desire does not arise with reference to things in the past that are a basis for desire and lust.
And how, monks, does desire not arise with reference to things that are objects for desire in the future?
One understands the future result of those things that are objects for desire in the future.
Having understood the future result, one turns away from them.
Having turned away from that, having pierced it with the mind, he sees by penetrating it with wisdom.
Thus, monks, desire does not arise in reference to things in the future that are objects for desire and lust.
And how, monks, does desire not arise in reference to things in the present that are objects for desire and lust?
Monks, one understands the future result of present phenomena that are objects of desire and lust;
having understood the future result, one turns away from them; having turned away from them and penetrated them with the mind, one sees by piercing through them with wisdom.
"In this way, monks, desire does not arise with reference to things in the present that are a basis for desire and lust.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of kamma.
The Tenth.
The First Chapter: On Full Enlightenment.
Its summary verse:
First, two on gratification;
The "Ascetic" [chapter] has five on crying;
two on "Not Satiated" are stated;
and there are two others on "Causes."

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.113 12. Āpāyika-vagga Āpāyika-sutta (The Discourse on Those Bound for the States of Deprivation) “Monks, there are these three persons who are bound for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, having no other destination. What three? The person who destroys life; the person who takes what is not given; and the person who engages in sexual misconduct. These, monks, are the three persons who are bound for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, having no other destination. Monks, there are these three persons who are bound for heaven, bound for the celestial realms, having no other destination. What three? The person who abstains from destroying life; the person who abstains from taking what is not given; and the person who abstains from sexual misconduct. These, monks, are the three persons who are bound for heaven, bound for the celestial realms, having no other destination.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three who, without abandoning this, are destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell. Which three? [The text continues with the three types of individuals.]”
One who is not celibate but claims to be celibate;
one who groundlessly accuses another who leads a pure celibate life of uncelibacy;
and one who holds such a doctrine and view as this: "There is no fault in sensual pleasures"—the latter falls into a state of being drunk with sensual pleasures.
“Monks, these three are destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell, and cannot escape them without abandoning this [wrong view].
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.114

12. Āpāyikavagga Dullabhasutta (AN 3.114, AN 3.112, PTS AN i 266) “Monks, it is rare to encounter a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; it is rare to hear the True Dhamma; it is rare to obtain a human birth; it is rare to obtain the arising of the opportune moment; it is rare to obtain the arising of the favorable season. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “It is not easy, Bhante, to obtain a human birth; it is not easy to obtain the arising of the opportune moment; it is not easy to obtain the arising of the favorable season. “It is even rarer than that, monk, to obtain a human birth; it is even rarer to obtain the arising of the opportune moment; it is even rarer to obtain the arising of the favorable season. For what reason? Because, monk, beings are for the most part destined for states of deprivation, bound for states of deprivation, with states of deprivation as their destination, having states of deprivation as their final end. But those who are not so are few. It is because of this, monk, that it is rare to obtain a human birth; it is rare to obtain the arising of the opportune moment; it is rare to obtain the arising of the favorable season. “Monks, it is rare to encounter a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; it is rare to hear the True Dhamma; it is rare to obtain a human birth; it is rare to obtain the arising of the opportune moment; it is rare to obtain the arising of the favorable season. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be those who encounter a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; we shall be those who hear the True Dhamma; we shall be those who obtain a human birth; we shall be those who obtain the arising of the opportune moment; we shall be those who obtain the arising of the favorable season. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
“Monks, the manifestation of three things is rare in the world. Which three?

The manifestation of a Tathāgata, an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha is rare in the world; the manifestation of the Dhamma proclaimed by a Tathāgata is rare in the world; and the manifestation of a person who is a true hearer of the Tathāgata is rare in the world.”
"A person who teaches the Dhamma and Vinaya is rare in the world; a person who is grateful and appreciative is rare in the world.
Indeed, monks, the appearance of these three is rare in the world.
This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.115 12.

Āpāyika Vagga Appameyya Sutta The Incomparable “Monks, there are these three things that are incomparable. What three? The immeasurable mind, the immeasurable liberation, and the immeasurable attainment of concentration. These, monks, are the three things that are incomparable.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three persons found existing in the world. Which three? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
One who is easily measured, one who is difficult to measure, and one who is immeasurable.
And what, monks, is the person who is easily measured?

Here, monks, a certain person is restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties.
“Monks, this is called the person who is easy to measure.
And what, monks, is the person who is difficult to measure?

Here, monks, a certain person is not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not talkative, not loose-tongued; he is established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and with sense faculties restrained.”
“Monks, this person is called one who is difficult to measure.
And what, monks, is the person who is immeasurable?
Here, monks, a monk is an arahant whose taints are destroyed.”
“Monks, this person is called immeasurable.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world.
This was the third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.116 12.

Āpāyika Vagga Āneñja Sutta (The Imperturbable) “Monks, there are these three kinds of imperturbability. What three? The imperturbability of the form realm, the imperturbability of the formless realm, and the imperturbability of the cessation of perception and feeling. These, monks, are the three kinds of imperturbability.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three persons found existing in the world. Which three? [Text continues with the description of the three types of individuals.]”

In this case, monks, a certain person, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking, "Space is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.

He relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it; established therein, intent upon it, dwelling frequently therein, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn into the company of the devas who have attained the base of infinite space.
“Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the gods who have reached the base of infinite space is twenty thousand eons.

Therein, an ordinary person, having remained for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those gods, goes to hell, goes to the animal realm, and goes to the sphere of hungry ghosts.
But the Blessed One’s disciple, having remained there for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those gods, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.”
“This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, in their destination and rebirth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.”

Thus he relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it; established therein, intent upon it, and dwelling frequently therein, he passes away without falling away from that state and is reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
The lifespan of the gods who have reached the base of infinite consciousness, monks, is forty thousand eons.

In that regard, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, goes even to hell, goes to the animal realm, and goes to the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).

But the Blessed One’s disciple, having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, in their destination and rebirth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.

Thus one relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it; established therein, intent upon it, and dwelling frequently therein, one passes away without falling away and is reborn into the company of the gods who have attained the base of nothingness.
The lifespan of the gods who have attained the base of nothingness, monks, is sixty thousand eons.

In that regard, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained for the full span of his life and having exhausted the entire measure of the lifespan of those gods, goes even to hell, goes to the animal realm, and goes to the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).

But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for the full span of his life and having exhausted the entire measure of the lifespan of those gods, attains final nibbāna (parinibbāyati) in that very same existence.
“This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, in their destination and rebirth.
These, monks, are the three types of persons found existing in the world.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.117 12.

Āpāyikavagga Vipattisampadāsutta (The Discourse on Failure and Success) "Bhikkhus, there are these three failures. What three? Failure in morality, failure in concentration, and failure in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the three failures. "Bhikkhus, there are these three successes. What three? Success in morality, success in concentration, and success in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the three successes."
“Bhikkhus, there are these three failures. Which three? [The text continues:]”
Failure in virtue, failure in mind, and failure in view.
And what, monks, is failure in virtue?
Here, monks, a certain person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter.
This, monks, is called failure in virtue.
And what, monks, is failure in mind?
Here, monks, a certain person is covetous and possesses a mind of ill will.
This, monks, is called failure of mind.
And what, monks, is failure of view?
Here, monks, a certain person holds wrong view and possesses a perverted perspective:
‘There is no giving, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge.’
‘Having realized the world for themselves through direct higher knowledge, they make it known.
This, monks, is called failure in view.
Or else, monks, it is because of failure in virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
“Monks, it is because of failure in mind that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or in hell;
or it is because of failure in view, monks, that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or in hell.
These, monks, are the three failures.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three accomplishments.
What three?
Accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in mind, and accomplishment in view.”
And what, monks, is the accomplishment of virtue? Here, monks,
a certain person abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from malicious speech, [abstains from harsh speech...]
He abstains from harsh speech; he abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called accomplishment in virtue.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in mind?
"Here, monks, someone is free from covetousness and possesses a mind without ill will.
This, monks, is called the perfection of mind.
And what, monks, is the perfection of view?"
In this case, monks, a certain person possesses right view and has an unperverted perspective:
"There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done;
there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; and there are beings who arise spontaneously."
‘There are in the world recluses and brahmins who have gone the right way and practiced rightly, who,
having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
This, monks, is called accomplishment in view.
“Monks, it is because of perfection in virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Or, monks, it is because of perfection in mind that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Or, monks, it is because of perfection in view that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
“These, monks, are the three accomplishments.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.118

12. Āpāyikavagga Apaṇṇakasutta (AN 3.118, AN 3.116, PTS AN i 270) “Monks, this Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. It is not something that can be said: ‘Only after a certain time will it be known. This Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.
