Just as, monks, a man might have a friend and companion who is a gambler, a frequenter of gambling dens, addicted to gambling. Whatever wealth that man might acquire through his own efforts, his friend the gambler would take away from him. Then the other man, having acquired some wealth through his own efforts, would think: ‘I have a friend and companion who is a gambler, a frequenter of gambling dens, addicted to gambling. Whatever wealth I acquire through my own efforts, he takes it away from me. Suppose I were to give him some of my wealth? He would give him some of his wealth. Then the gambler, having received that wealth, would think: ‘This man has a friend and companion who is a gambler, a frequenter of gambling dens, addicted to gambling. Whatever wealth he acquires through his own efforts, I take it away from him. Suppose I were to give him some of my wealth? He would give him some of his wealth. In the same way, monks, this Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. It is not something that can be said: ‘Only after a certain time will it be known. This Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be those for whom this Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise; we will not be those for whom this Dhamma is not directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three failures.
What three?
Failure in virtue, failure in mind, and failure in view.”
And what, monks, is failure in virtue?
Here, monks, a certain person destroys life... [and so on] ...he utters idle chatter.
This, monks, is called failure in virtue.
And what, monks, is failure of mind?
Here, monks, a certain person is covetous and has a mind of ill will.
This, monks, is called failure of mind.
And what, monks, is failure in view?
Here, monks, a certain person holds wrong view and has a perverted perspective:

"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice... [as before] ...there are no ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known."
This, monks, is called failure in view.

It is on account of failure in virtue, monks, or on account of failure in view, monks, that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.

Just as, monks, a die that is loaded [to fall one way] is thrown upwards, however it falls, it falls exactly as it was intended; so too, monks, it is on account of failure in virtue or on account of failure in view that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
In the same way, monks, it is due to failure in virtue that beings... [as before] ...are reborn.
These, monks, are the three failures.
There are, monks, these three accomplishments.
Which three?
Accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in mind, and accomplishment in view.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in virtue?
“Here, monks, a certain person abstains from taking life … [as before] … This,
monks, is called accomplishment in virtue.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in mind?”
"Here, monks, someone is free from covetousness and possesses a mind devoid of ill will.
This, monks, is called the perfection of mind.
And what, monks, is the perfection of view?"
"Here, monks, a certain person possesses right view and has an unperverted perspective:
'There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed... [as far as] those who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known.
This, monks, is called the accomplishment of view."
"Monks, it is because of perfection in virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
Or it is because of perfection in mind... or because of perfection in view, monks, that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world."
“Just as, monks, an unerring jewel, when thrown upward, lands wherever it falls, and lands only where it is well-placed;
even so, monks, it is through the cause of perfection in virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world;
or through the cause of perfection in mind... or through the cause of perfection in view, beings [reappear in a happy destination].”
With the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the three accomplishments.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.119 12. Āpāyikavagga Kammantasutta “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who acts for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others; the person who acts for the welfare of others but not for his own welfare; and the person who acts both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person who acts for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others? Here, monks, someone has undertaken and practiced the practice of giving, but he does not encourage others to undertake and practice the practice of giving. He has undertaken and practiced the practice of virtue, but he does not encourage others to undertake and practice the practice of virtue. He has undertaken and practiced the practice of liberality, but he does not encourage others to undertake and practice the practice of liberality. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person who acts for the welfare of others but not for his own welfare? Here, monks, someone does not himself undertake and practice the practice of giving, but he encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of giving. He does not himself undertake and practice the practice of virtue, but he encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of virtue. He does not himself undertake and practice the practice of liberality, but he encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of liberality. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts for the welfare of others but not for his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person who acts both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others? Here, monks, someone himself undertakes and practices the practice of giving and also encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of giving. He himself undertakes and practices the practice of virtue and also encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of virtue. He himself undertakes and practices the practice of liberality and also encourages others to undertake and practice the practice of liberality. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three failures. Which three? [The text continues as follows:]”
Failure in action, failure in livelihood, and failure in view.
And what, monks, is failure in action?
Here, monks, a certain person is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...he is a speaker of idle chatter.
This, monks, is called failure in one’s work.
And what, monks, is failure in livelihood?
Here, monks, a certain person has wrong livelihood; he makes his living by wrong livelihood.
This, monks, is called failure in livelihood.
And what, monks, is failure in view?
Here, monks, a certain person holds wrong view and has a perverted perspective:
‘There is no gift, there is no offering … [and so on] … those who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
This, monks, is called failure in view.
These, monks, are the three failures.
“Monks, there are these three accomplishments.
What three?
Accomplishment in action, accomplishment in livelihood, and accomplishment in view.”
And what, monks, is the perfection of action?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life... [and so on] ...abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called the perfection of action.
And what, monks, is the perfection of livelihood?
Here, monks, a certain person has right livelihood; he makes his living by means of right livelihood.
This, monks, is called the perfection of livelihood.
And what, monks, is the accomplishment of view?
Here, monks, a certain person possesses right view and has an undistorted perspective:
"There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed... [as far as] those who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known."
“Monks, this is called accomplishment in view.
These, monks, are the three accomplishments.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.120 12. Āpāyikavagga First Discourse on Purity (Paṭhamasoceyyasutta) “Monks, there are these three kinds of purity. What three? Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. These, monks, are the three kinds of purity. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is there purity of body? How is there purity of speech? And how is there purity of mind? “Here, monk, a noble disciple abstains from taking life; he lays down the rod and the sword, dwells with kindness and compassion for all living beings; this, monk, is called purity of body. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells honestly without thoughts of theft;

this too, monk, is called purity of body. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from unchastity; he lives apart, aloof from sensuality, refraining from sexual intercourse; this too, monk, is called purity of body. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truthfully, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, and does not deceive anyone in the world; this too, monk, is called purity of speech. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from divisive speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide those people from these, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide these people from those; thus he is one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of unity, who enjoys concord, a speaker of words that create concord; this too, monk, is called purity of speech. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that go to the heart, courteous, and dear to many; this too, monk, is called purity of speech. Furthermore, monk, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth treasuring, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial; this too, monk, is called purity of speech. Furthermore, monk, he is free from covetousness; he does not covet the wealth and property of others, thinking, ‘May what belongs to others be mine!’; this too, monk, is called purity of mind. Furthermore, monk, he is free from ill will and malevolence; his mind is devoid of hate, full of loving-kindness, and he dwells with a mind of boundless benevolence toward all living beings; this too, monk, is called purity of mind. Furthermore, monk, he holds right view; he possesses a perspective that is straight and free from crookedness; this too, monk, is called purity of mind. “This, monk, is how there is purity of body; this is how there is purity of speech; and this is how there is purity of mind. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Purity is the essence of the Dhamma. “It is because purity is indeed the essence of the Dhamma, monk, that it has been so stated by me. For, monk, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past maintained purity, they all did so through these very three kinds of purity. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will maintain purity, they all will do so through these very three kinds of purity. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present maintain purity, they all do so through these very three kinds of purity. Therefore, monk, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall maintain purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. “Yes, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One. And the Blessed One said this further: “Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind— These are the three purities taught by the One Well-Gone. By means of these three purities, one is purified in the world; Having attained purity, one does not come to grief. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, that monk rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind— These are the three purities taught by the One Well-Gone. By means of these three purities, one is purified in the world; Having attained purity, one does not come to grief. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. This is the first discourse on purity in the Section on the State of Woe in the Third Book of the Numerical Discourses.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three purities.
Which three?
Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
And what, monks, is purity of body?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
This, monks, is called purity of body.
And what, monks, is purity of speech?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called purity of speech.
And what, monks, is purity of mind?
Here, monks, a certain person is not covetous, has a mind free from ill will, and possesses right view.
“Monks, this is called purity of mind.
These, monks, are the three purities.
The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.121 12.

Āpāyikavagga Dutiyasoceyyasutta (The Second Discourse on Purity) "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of purity. What three? Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of purity."
“Bhikkhus, there are these three purities. What three? [The purity of body, speech, and mind. (AN 3.121, AN 3.119, PTS AN i 272) “Bhikkhus, there are these three purities. Which three?”
Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
And what, monks, is purity of body?
Here, monks, a monk abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from unchaste conduct.
This, monks, is called purity of body.
And what, monks, is purity of speech?
Here, monks, a monk abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called purity of speech.
And what, monks, is purity of mind?
Here, monks, a monk, when sensual desire is present within him, knows: ‘There is sensual desire in me.’
He understands; or, when sensual desire is absent within him, he understands: ‘There is no sensual desire within me.

He understands how the arising of unarisen sensual desire comes about, and he understands how the abandonment of arisen sensual desire comes about, and he understands how the abandoned sensual desire does not arise again in the future.
There is non-arising in the future, and he understands that;
or, when ill will is present within him, he understands: ‘Ill will is present within me’;
or, when ill will is not present within him, he understands: ‘Ill will is not present within me’; and how there comes to be the non-arising of unarisen [ill will]...
There is the arising of ill will, and he understands that; he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen ill will;
and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of abandoned ill will in the future.
Or, when sloth and torpor are present within him, he understands: "Sloth and torpor are present within me"; when they are not present...
Or, when there is no sloth and torpor within him, he understands: "There is no sloth and torpor within me.
He understands how the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor comes about; he understands how the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor comes about;
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned sloth and torpor will come about in the future.
When restlessness and remorse are present within him, he understands: "There is restlessness and remorse in me";
when restlessness and remorse are not present within him, he understands: "There is no restlessness and remorse in me";
and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse.
He understands how the abandonment of arisen restlessness and remorse comes about, and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned restlessness and remorse occurs in the future.
Or, when doubt is present within him, he understands: "There is doubt within me"; when it is absent...
Or, when doubt is present within him, he understands: ‘Doubt is present within me’;
he understands how the arising of unarisen doubt comes to be; he understands how the abandoning of arisen doubt comes to be;
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned doubt will come to be in the future.
This, monks, is called purity of mind.
These, monks, are the three purities:
purity of body and purity of speech.
The mind-purification that is free from taints—
pure and endowed with purity—
they call the washing away of evil.
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.122 12.
Āpāyika Vagga (The Chapter on Those Bound for States of Misery)
Moneyyasutta: “Monks, there are these three kinds of sagacity.”
Which three?
Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
And what, monks, is purity of body?
"Here, monks, a monk abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from unchaste conduct.
This, monks, is called bodily integrity.
And what, monks, is verbal integrity?"
“Here, monks, a monk abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called verbal integrity.
And what, monks, is mental integrity?”

"Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
This, monks, is called mental refinement.
These, monks, are the three kinds of refinement."
The sage of body, the sage of speech,
the sage of mind, free from taints;
the sage perfected in sagacity—
"They say it abandons everything.
Tenth. The second chapter, the Chapter on Those Bound for States of Misery, is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The one bound for the states of loss, the rare, the immeasurable,
and the failure and success regarding the imperturbable.
Undisputed action,
two kinds of purity, and sagehood—
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.123.
13. Kusināra Chapter:
The Discourse on Kusinārā (AN 3.123, AN 3.121, PTS AN i 274)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Baliharaṇa Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!"
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells depending upon a certain village or town.”
A householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for a meal on the following day.
If he so desires, monks, the bhikkhu accepts.
Then, at the end of that night, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he goes to where that [householder]...
He approaches the residence of a householder or a householder’s son; having approached, he sits down on a prepared seat.
Then that householder or householder’s son, with his own hands, satisfies and serves him with excellent hard food and soft food.
It occurs to him:
"It would be excellent indeed if this householder or householder’s son were to satisfy and serve me with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft.
It occurs to him:
"Oh, may this householder or householder’s son continue to satisfy and serve me with his own hands with such choice food, both hard and soft, even in the future!"
Thus, being tied to that alms-food, infatuated with it, and clinging to it, he consumes it without seeing its danger and without wisdom regarding the escape from it.
Therein, he entertains thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
I say, monks, that what is given to such a monk does not bear great fruit.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that monk dwells heedlessly.
But here, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.
A householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for a meal on the following day.
If he so desires, monks, the bhikkhu accepts.
At the end of that night, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, he goes to where that [householder]...
He approaches the residence of a householder or a householder’s son; having approached, he sits down on a prepared seat.
Then that householder or householder’s son, with his own hands, satisfies and serves him with excellent hard food and soft food.
It does not occur to him:
"It would be good indeed if this householder or householder’s son were to satisfy me with his own hands with excellent food, both hard and soft, and provide me with hospitality.
Nor does he think:
"Oh, may this householder or householder’s son satisfy me with his own hands with such excellent food, both hard and soft, and provide me with hospitality, even in the future!"
Thus, he consumes that almsfood unattached, uninfatuated, and unclinging, seeing the danger in it and possessing wisdom regarding escape.
Therein, he applies thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty.
I say, monks, that what is given to such a monk yields great fruit.
And why is that? Because, monks, a monk dwells diligently. Thus ends the first [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.124 13. Kusināra Chapter Discourse on Quarreling “Monks, there are these three kinds of quarrels. What three? Quarrels arising from lust, quarrels arising from hatred, and quarrels arising from delusion. These, monks, are the three kinds of quarrels. These three kinds of quarrels, monks, lead to the decline and disappearance of true Dhamma. How so? Quarrels arising from lust lead to the decline and disappearance of true Dhamma; quarrels arising from hatred lead to the decline and disappearance of true Dhamma; quarrels arising from delusion lead to the decline and disappearance of true Dhamma. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not engage in quarrels arising from lust. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. You should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not engage in quarrels arising from hatred. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. You should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not engage in quarrels arising from delusion. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, in whatever direction monks dwell having become engaged in quarrels, engaged in strife, fallen into disputes, and wounding one another with the weapons of the tongue—
that direction, bhikkhus, is not pleasant for me even to take it into account.”
How much more so to go!
I reach this conclusion:
"Surely those venerable ones have abandoned three qualities and frequently practiced three qualities."
Which three qualities did they abandon?
Thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty—
these are the three qualities they abandoned.
Which three things did they cultivate extensively?
Sensual thought, ill will, and harmful thought—
these three things they cultivated extensively.
“Bhikkhus, in whatever direction monks dwell having fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes,
stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue— even to merely direct my attention to that direction,
bhikkhus, is not comfortable for me, let alone going there.”
I reach this conclusion:
"Surely those venerable ones have abandoned these three things and have frequently practiced these three things.
But in whatever direction, monks, the bhikkhus are in harmony, living in mutual agreement, without dispute, like milk mixed with water...
They dwell looking upon one another with eyes of affection; monks, even to go toward that quarter is pleasant for me, let alone to attend to it.
Here I reach my conclusion:
“Surely those venerable ones have abandoned three things and cultivated three things.
Which three things did they abandon?
Sensual thought, ill will, and harmful thought.”
They abandoned these three qualities.
Which three qualities did they cultivate extensively?
Thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty.
These three qualities they cultivated extensively.
In whatever direction, monks, the bhikkhus dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together,
looking upon one another with eyes of love— in that direction, monks, it is safe for me to go.
How much less could they even bring them to mind!
I am certain of this:
"Those venerable ones have surely abandoned these three qualities and have frequently practiced these three qualities."
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.125 13. Kusināravagga
Gotamakacetiyasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī at the Gotamaka Shrine.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus.
"Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, I teach the Dhamma through direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge.
Monks, I teach the Dhamma with its basis, not without its basis.”
“Monks, I teach a Dhamma that is accompanied by wonders, not one devoid of wonders. Monks,
when I teach the Dhamma through direct knowledge and not without direct knowledge, when I teach the Dhamma with its causes and not without its causes,
when I teach a Dhamma accompanied by wonders and not devoid of wonders, it is to be practiced.”
“There is exhortation for you, and there is instruction to be carried out.
And it is enough for you, monks, to be contented, enough to be joyful, enough to be glad, thinking:
‘The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing the good way.’”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the thousandfold world-system trembled.
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.126 13. Kusināra Chapter
The Discourse to Bharaṇḍu Kālāma (AN 3.126, AN 3.124, PTS AN i 276).
On one occasion, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, the Blessed One arrived at Kapilavatthu.
Mahānāma the Sakyan heard: “The Blessed One, it is said, has arrived at Kapilavatthu.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. As Mahānāma the Sakyan was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Go, Mahānāma, and find a suitable lodging in Kapilavatthu where we might stay for one night today.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” Mahānāma the Sakyan replied to the Blessed One.
Having entered Kapilavatthu and wandered throughout the entire city, he did not see any suitable lodging in Kapilavatthu where the Blessed One might stay for one night.
Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, there is no such lodging in Kapilavatthu where the Blessed One might stay for one night today.
Venerable sir, this Bharaṇḍu Kālāma was formerly a fellow celibate practitioner with the Blessed One."
“May the Blessed One stay for one night tonight in this hermitage.
“Go, Mahānāma, prepare a seat.
“Very well, Bhante,” Mahānāma the Sakyan replied to the Blessed One, and he went to where Bharandu the Kālāma was.
He approached the hermitage; having approached, he prepared a seat, set out water for washing the feet, and went to where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"The seat is prepared, venerable sir, and water has been set out for washing the feet."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems timely.
Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of Bharandu Kālāma; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet.
Then it occurred to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
"It is not the right time today to attend upon the Blessed One.
The Blessed One is weary."
"Today I shall attend upon the Blessed One," he said, and having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he departed.

Then, at the end of that night, Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. As Mahānāma the Sakyan was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Mahānāma, there are these three teachers found existing in the world."
Which three? Here,
Mahānāma, a certain teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures,
but does not proclaim the full understanding of forms, nor does he proclaim the full understanding of feelings.
But here, Mahānāma, some teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, proclaims the full understanding of forms,

yet does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings. But here, Mahānāma, some teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, proclaims the full understanding of forms, and proclaims the full understanding of feelings.
“Mahānāma, these three teachers are found existing in the world.
Mahānāma, do these three teachers have one goal, or do they have different goals?
When this was said, Bharaṇḍu Kālāma said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“‘One,’ Mahānāma, say.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“‘Many,’ Mahānāma, say.”
A second time, Bharaṇḍu Kālāma said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“Say ‘one,’ Mahānāma.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“Do not say ‘many,’ Mahānāma;
say ‘one,’” [the Blessed One said]. For a third time, Bharaṇḍu Kālāma said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“Say ‘one,’ Mahānāma.”
A third time the Blessed One said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“Say ‘different,’ Mahānāma.
Then it occurred to Bharaṇḍu Kālāma:
“It seems that the ascetic Gotama has been rebuffed up to three times by Mahānāma the Sakyan, who is of great influence.
What if I were to depart from Kapilavatthu? Then Bharaṇḍu Kālāma departed from Kapilavatthu.
From the time he departed from Kapilavatthu, he remained thus departed and did not return again.
This is the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.127
13. Kusinārā Chapter:
The Discourse to Hatthaka (AN 3.127, AN 3.125, PTS AN i 278)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the young deva Hatthaka, in the late night, having illuminated the entirety of Jeta’s Grove with his surpassing beauty, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, thinking, “I shall stand before the Blessed One,” he simply sank down, he simply subsided, and he was unable to remain steady.
Just as if ghee or oil were poured onto sand, it would simply sink and soak away and not remain stable;
even so, Hatthaka the deva-son,
thinking, "I will stand before the Blessed One," simply sank and soaked away and was unable to remain stable.
Then the Blessed One said this to the young deva Hatthaka:
“Manifest a gross body-form, Hatthaka.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Hatthaka the young deva replied to the Blessed One. Having manifested a gross body-form and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
As the young deva Hatthaka was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Hatthaka, those qualities that were active when you were formerly a human being—are they still active now?
“Venerable sir, those very qualities that were active when I was formerly a human being are still active in me now.”
"Venerable sir, those qualities that were not active in me when I was formerly a human being are now active in me.
Just as the Blessed One now dwells surrounded by bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, and followers of other sects and their disciples,
even so, venerable sir, do I dwell surrounded by sons of the gods."
"Venerable sir, even from afar, sons of the gods come into the presence of the deva-son Hatthaka, thinking, 'We shall hear the Dhamma.
Venerable sir, I have died unsatiated and insatiable for three things. Which three?"
"Venerable sir, I have passed away unsatiated and insatiable for the sight of the Blessed One;
I have passed away unsatiated and insatiable for hearing the true Dhamma;
I have passed away unsatiated and insatiable for attending upon the Saṅgha."
"Venerable sir, it was while still unsatiated and insatiable for these three things that I passed away:
'I have never yet found my fill of beholding the Blessed One.'"
For the sake of serving the Saṅgha and for hearing the true Dhamma,
one who trains in the higher virtue—
Delighting in hearing the true Dhamma,
unsated in three things,
Hatthaka has gone to Aviha.
The Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.128 13. Kusināra Chapter
The Bitter Sutta (Kaṭuviyasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Bārāṇasī for alms.

While walking for alms at Goyogapilakkha, the Blessed One saw a certain bhikkhu who was relishing what is empty and relishing what is external, unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained senses.
Having seen that bhikkhu, he said this to him:
“Do not, monk, make yourself bitter.
Indeed, monk, it is impossible that flies would not swarm around and settle upon you when you have made yourself bitter and are soaked with the stench of raw flesh.
Then that monk, having been exhorted by the Blessed One with this advice, was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency.
Then, having walked for alms in Bārāṇasī and returned from the alms round after his meal, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In this case, bhikkhus, in the morning, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, I entered Bārāṇasī for alms.

While walking for alms at Goyogapilakkha, bhikkhus, I saw a certain bhikkhu who was devoid of inner enjoyment and devoid of outer enjoyment, unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties.”
Seeing him, I said this to that bhikkhu:
“Do not, bhikkhu, make yourself bitter.
Indeed, bhikkhu, it is impossible that flies would not swarm around and settle upon you if you have made yourself bitter and are drenched with the stench of raw flesh.”
"Then, monks, that bhikkhu, having been exhorted by me with this exhortation, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
"What, Bhante, is 'bitterness'?"
“What is the raw stench?
What is the fly?
“Covetousness, monk, is the pungent [stench];”
Ill will is a putrid smell;
evil, unwholesome thoughts are flies.
That flies should not swarm around and settle upon one who has made oneself bitter and is soaked with the putrid smell—such a thing is impossible.
One who has not guarded the eye and ear,
and whose sense faculties are unrestrained—
flies will swarm around him.
His intentions are based on passion.
The bhikkhu, steeped in raw stench, is bitter.
One remains far from Nibbāna,
sharing only in distress,
whether in the village or in the forest.
Having failed to attain tranquility for himself,
the foolish and dull-witted man is surrounded by flies.
And those who are endowed with virtue,
who delight in wisdom and tranquility—
being peaceful, they sleep happily.
“Having driven away the flies.
The sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.129
13. Kusinārā Chapter:
The First Discourse to Anuruddha (AN 3.129, AN 3.127, PTS AN i 281)

Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Anuruddha said this to the Blessed One:

"Here, Bhante, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see for the most part women being reborn, after the breakup of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell."
“Bhante, endowed with how many qualities does a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, arise in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell?
“Anuruddha, endowed with three qualities, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, arises in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Which three? [The Buddha then enumerates them.]”
In this case, Anuruddha, in the morning a woman dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess;
at midday she dwells at home with a mind obsessed by envy;
and in the evening she dwells at home with a mind obsessed by sensual lust.
“Anuruddha, possessed of these three qualities, women, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Thus was the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.130

13. Kusinārā Chapter The Second Discourse to Anuruddha (AN 3.130, AN 3.128, PTS AN i 281) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Upavattana, the sal grove of the Mallas. There the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the Venerable Anuruddha and say to him: ‘The Teacher calls you, friend Anuruddha. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, and he went to the Venerable Anuruddha and said: “The Teacher calls you, friend Anuruddha. “Yes, friend,” the Venerable Anuruddha replied, and he went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Anuruddha, how many kinds of persons do you see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus? “Venerable sir, I see four kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. What four? There is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. There is the person who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, venerable sir, are the four kinds of persons that I see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good that you see these four kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For, Anuruddha, these are indeed the four kinds of persons seen in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Furthermore, Anuruddha, how many kinds of persons do you see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus? “Venerable sir, I see eight kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. What eight? There is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; and further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who has attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, having realized for himself with direct knowledge that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom which is free from taints. These, venerable sir, are the eight kinds of persons that I see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good that you see these eight kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For, Anuruddha, these are indeed the eight kinds of persons seen in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Furthermore, Anuruddha, how many kinds of persons do you see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus? “Venerable sir, I see sixteen kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. What sixteen? There is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; and further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who has attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, having realized for himself with direct knowledge that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom which is free from taints.

And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, has reappeared spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will attain final Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the utter destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, is a once-returner who, after coming back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the utter destruction of three fetters, is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, and destined to awaken. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of the family-to-family [among the devas], who after passing from family to family among devas and humans, will make an end of suffering. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of the seven-times-at-most, who after wandering and transmigrating among devas and humans seven times at most, will make an end of suffering. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of the attainer of non-percipient beings, who after passing away from here, will be reborn in a non-percipient realm and will dwell there for the full lifespan. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of the attainer of the realm of nothingness, who after passing away from here, will be reborn in the realm of nothingness and will dwell there for the full lifespan. And further, there is the person who dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, and who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of the attainer of the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, who after passing away from here, will be reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and will dwell there for the full lifespan. These, venerable sir, are the sixteen kinds of persons that I see in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good that you see these sixteen kinds of persons in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For, Anuruddha, these are indeed the sixteen kinds of persons seen in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then the Venerable Anuruddha rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, raising his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘These, Anuruddha, are the sixteen kinds of persons seen in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Having said this, the Venerable Anuruddha paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on his right, departed. Then, not long after the Venerable Anuruddha had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of four qualities, it is fitting for him to enter and dwell
Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Anuruddha said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Here, friend Sāriputta, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I survey a thousandfold world system."
“Yet, friend Anuruddha, although my energy is aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness is established and unconfused, my body is tranquil and untroubled, and my mind is concentrated and one-pointed,
nevertheless my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
“Friend Anuruddha, as for what you think thus:”
‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I survey a thousandfold world-system’—this is conceit in you.
And when it occurs to you, friend Anuruddha:
‘My energy is aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness is established and unconfused, my body is tranquil and unagitated, my mind is concentrated and one-pointed’—this is restlessness in you.
“Furthermore, friend Anuruddha, when you think:
‘Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging,’ this is remorse on your part.
It would be well if the Venerable Anuruddha, having abandoned these three things and having not given attention to these three things, were to direct his mind toward the deathless element.”
Then, at a later time, the Venerable Anuruddha, having abandoned these three things and having not given attention to these three things, directed his mind toward the deathless element.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Anuruddha, before long,
attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And so, the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the Arahants.
The Eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.131 13. Kusināra Chapter
Paṭicchannasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these three things bring about concealment, not disclosure.”
Which three?
Monks, women bring success when they are concealed, not when they are exposed;
monks, the mantras of the brahmins bring success when they are concealed, not when they are exposed.
“Monks, wrong view, when concealed, brings [bad results], not when disclosed.
These three things, monks, bring [bad results] when concealed, not when disclosed.
These three things, monks, shine forth when disclosed, not when concealed.”
Which three?
The lunar disk, monks, shines when it is uncovered, not when it is covered;
the solar disk, monks, shines when it is uncovered, not when it is covered.
“Monks, the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines forth when it is open, not when it is concealed.
These three things, monks, shine forth when they are open, not when they are concealed.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

“Bhikkhus, there are these three persons found existing in the world. Which three? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
A person like a carving on stone, a person like a carving in earth, and a person like a carving in water.
And who, monks, is the person like a carving on stone?
Here, monks, a certain person is prone to anger frequently.
And that anger of his persists for a long time. Just as, monks,
a scratch on a stone is not quickly destroyed by wind or water but remains for a long duration,
even so, monks, a certain person here frequently becomes angry.
And that anger of his persists for a long time.
This, monks, is called the person who is like a scratch on stone.
And what, monks, is the person who is like a scratch on earth?
In this case, monks, a certain person frequently becomes angry, yet that anger of his does not persist for a long time.

Just as a line drawn on the earth is quickly obliterated by wind or water and does not remain for long; so too, monks, a certain person frequently becomes angry, yet that anger of his does not persist for a long time. This is called a person who is like a line on the earth.
In the same way, monks, here a certain person frequently becomes angry,
yet that anger of his does not persist for a long time. This, monks,
is called the person who is like a scratch on the earth.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is like a line drawn in water?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, even when spoken to harshly, spoken to roughly, or spoken to unpleasantly, remains reconciled, remains harmonious, and remains friendly.
Just as, bhikkhus, a line drawn in water quickly vanishes and does not remain for long; such is the person who is like a line drawn in water."

"In the same way, monks, here a certain person, even when addressed with harshness, addressed with roughness, or addressed with what is unpleasant, remains composed, remains harmonious, and remains friendly.
This, monks, is called the person who is like a line drawn on water.
These, monks, are the three persons existing and found in the world."
The tenth.
The third chapter, the Kusinārā Chapter.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
The quarrel at Kusinārā,
Gotama, Bharandu, Hatthaka;
the bitter words, the two Anuruddhas.
“Ten things you have concealed by writing.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.133 14.
The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga)
The Discourse on the Warrior (Yodhājīvasutta): “Bhikkhus,
possessing three qualities, a warrior is worthy of a king, an enjoyer of a king’s wealth, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.”
Which three?
Here, monks, a warrior is one who shoots from afar, one who shoots without missing the mark, and one who pierces a great body.
Endowed with these three factors, monks, a warrior is worthy of a king, an enjoyer of a king’s wealth, and is indeed reckoned as a limb of the king.
"In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is worthy of offerings …pe… an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the three?
Here, monks, a monk is one who shoots from afar, one who shoots without missing the mark, and one who pierces a great body."
And how, monks, is a monk one who shoots far?
Here, monks, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—all form [he regards as it really is with correct wisdom].
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all feeling, [one regards] thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever perception there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all perception is seen thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
‘This is my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all formations, [one sees]: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is seen thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
‘This is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who shoots far.
And how, monks, is a monk one who shoots at the unerring mark?
In this case, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
In this way, monks, a monk is one who shoots at the unerring mark.
And how, monks, is a monk a splitter of the great body?
Here, monks, a monk splits the great mass of ignorance.
"In this way, monks, a monk is one who splits apart a great body.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.134 14.

Yodhājīva-vagga Parisā-sutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four assemblies. What four? The assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of ascetics. These, bhikkhus, are the four assemblies.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three assemblies. Which three? [Text continues as in AN 3.134 and AN 3.132].”
“The assembly trained in the removal of chaff, the assembly trained in cross-examination, and the assembly trained in as much as is necessary—
these, monks, are the three assemblies. This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.135 14.
Yodhājīva-vagga Mitta-sutta (The Friend)
“Bhikkhus, a friend endowed with three factors should be cultivated.
With which three? (…)”
“He gives what is hard to give; he does what is hard to do;
he endures what is hard to endure—it is with these three qualities, monks, that a friend should be cultivated.
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.136 14.

Yodhājīva-vagga Uppāda Sutta: Arising “Monks, there are these three kinds of arising. What three? The arising of suffering, the arising of formations, and the arising of consciousness. These, monks, are the three kinds of arising.”
“Whether, monks, Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena—
that all conditioned things are impermanent.”
The Tathāgata fully awakens to this and realizes it.
Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes plain:
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.”
Whether, monks, Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena—that all conditioned things are suffering.
This the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully realizes.
Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and clarifies:
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering.
Whether Tathāgatas arise, O monks, or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena.
"All phenomena are non-self.
The Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it.
Having awakened to it and realized it, he declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes plain [this truth]:”
“All phenomena are non-self.
This is the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.137

14. Yodhājīva-vagga Kesakambala-sutta (AN 3.137, AN 3.135, PTS AN i 286) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of ascetics who wear hair-cloth. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic wears hair-cloth made from human hair; he is called ‘one who wears hair-cloth. (2) Some ascetic wears hair-cloth made from horse-hair; he is called ‘one who wears hair-cloth. (3) Some ascetic wears hair-cloth made from cow-hair; he is called ‘one who wears hair-cloth. (4) Some ascetic wears hair-cloth made from the feathers of owls; he is called ‘one who wears hair-cloth. (5) Some ascetic wears hair-cloth made from a mixture of those; he is called ‘one who wears hair-cloth. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of ascetics who wear hair-cloth.”
“Monks, just as among all woven garments, a hair-cloth is declared to be the lowest;
a hair-cloth, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch— just so, monks,
among all the doctrines of the various ascetics and brahmins, the doctrine of Makkhali is declared to be the lowest.”
“Bhikkhus, the foolish man Makkhali speaks thus and holds this view:
‘There is no kamma, there is no action, there is no energy.
Even those Blessed Ones who were Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past, bhikkhus, were all proponents of kamma, proponents of action, and proponents of energy.”
“Bhikkhus, the worthless man Makkhali Tepiṭaka opposes [the truth], saying:
‘There is no action, there is no deed, there is no effort.
And those who will arise in the future time as Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, those Blessed Ones too will be proponents of action, proponents of deeds, and proponents of effort.”
“Bhikkhus, the misguided man Makkhali Tepiṭaka opposes [the truth], saying:
‘There is no action, there is no deed, there is no effort.
But I too, bhikkhus, at present, being an Arahant and a Perfectly Enlightened One, am one who speaks of action, who speaks of deeds, and who speaks of effort.”
“Monks, that foolish man Makkhali also opposes me, saying:
‘There is no action, there is no deed, there is no effort.
Monks, it is just as if a net were cast at the mouth of a river for the harm, suffering, ruin, and destruction of many fish.”
“In exactly this way, bhikkhus, the wretched man Makkhali is like a human missile that has appeared in the world for the harm, suffering, ruin, and disaster of many beings.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.138

14. Yodhājīva Vagga: The Discourse on Accomplishment (Sampadā Sutta) “Monks, there are these four accomplishments of a warrior. What four? The accomplishment of armor, the accomplishment of weapons, the accomplishment of strategy, and the accomplishment of battle. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of armor of a warrior? Here, monks, when a warrior has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the training rules of the precepts. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of armor of a warrior. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of weapons of a warrior? Here, monks, a warrior is skilled in many kinds of weapons: the sword, the spear, the club, the bow, and the arrow. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of weapons of a warrior. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of strategy of a warrior? Here, monks, a warrior knows the right time for marching out, the right time for halting, the right time for attacking, the right time for retreating, and the right time for encamping. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of strategy of a warrior. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of battle of a warrior? Here, monks, when a warrior has gone into battle, he does not lose heart, he does not tremble, he does not become cowed, and he does not turn back. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of battle of a warrior. These, monks, are the four accomplishments of a warrior. Just so, monks, there are these four accomplishments of a noble disciple. What four? The accomplishment of armor, the accomplishment of weapons, the accomplishment of strategy, and the accomplishment of battle. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of armor of a noble disciple? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of armor of a noble disciple. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of weapons of a noble disciple? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses the four bases of power (iddhipāda): the basis of power consisting of concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; the basis of power consisting of concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; the basis of power consisting of concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; and the basis of power consisting of concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of weapons of a noble disciple. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of strategy of a noble disciple? Here, monks, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of strategy of a noble disciple. And what, monks, is the accomplishment of battle of a noble disciple? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attains final nibbāna in the interval; or, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attains final nibbāna upon landing; or, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attains final nibbāna without exertion; or, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attains final nibbāna with exertion; or, having abandoned the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of battle of a noble disciple. These, monks, are the four accomplishments of a noble disciple.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three accomplishments.
Which three?
Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, and accomplishment in wisdom.”
“Monks, these indeed are the three accomplishments.
Thus [ends] the sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.139

14. The Chapter on Warriors: The Discourse on Growth (Yodhājīva-vagga Vuddhi-sutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of growth. What four? The growth of wealth, the growth of cattle, the growth of grain, and the growth of wisdom. These, monks, are the four kinds of growth. “What, monks, is the growth of wealth? Here, monks, a noble son, having acquired wealth by energetic effort, right action, and right livelihood, increases that wealth through careful management. This, monks, is called the growth of wealth. “What, monks, is the growth of cattle? Here, monks, a noble son acquires cattle—cows and bulls, calves and heifers, and young oxen—and he causes them to breed and multiply. This, monks, is called the growth of cattle. “What, monks, is the growth of grain? Here, monks, a noble son acquires fields of grain—rice, millet, beans, sesame, and pulses—and they yield abundant crops. This, monks, is called the growth of grain. “What, monks, is the growth of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble son hears the Dhamma not heard before, or he develops the Dhamma already heard, or he gains confidence in the Dhamma not yet gained. By means of this, his unarisen wholesome qualities arise, and arisen wholesome qualities increase, expand, and reach fulfillment. This, monks, is called the growth of wisdom. “These, monks, are the four kinds of growth. “Monks, of these four kinds of growth, the growth of wisdom is supreme. Why is that? Because, monks, when the growth of wisdom has been achieved, the growth of grain is achieved; when the growth of grain has been achieved, the growth of cattle is achieved; and when the growth of cattle has been achieved, the growth of wealth is achieved. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall strive for the growth of wisdom. It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of growth. What three?
Growth in faith, growth in virtue, and growth in wisdom.”
“Monks, these indeed are the three kinds of growth.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.140
14. The Chapter on Warriors:
The Discourse on the Wild Colt (Assakhaḷuṅkasutta) (AN 3.140, AN 3.137, PTS AN i 287)
“Monks, I will teach you about three kinds of wild colts and three kinds of wild men.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of wild colts?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain wild colt is endowed with speed, but not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain wild colt is endowed with speed and endowed with beauty, but not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wild colt is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
These, monks, are the three kinds of wild colts."
"And what, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of human wild colts?
Here, bhikkhus, one kind of human wild colt is endowed with speed, but not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
Then, bhikkhus, another kind of human wild colt is endowed with both speed and beauty, but not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth."
"But here, monks, a certain person who is like a wild colt is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with height and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a wild colt endowed with speed, yet not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with height and girth?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’"
This, I say, is his speed.

this, I say, is not his beauty.
Furthermore, he does not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his lack of physical stature and girth.
Thus, monks, the wild colt of a man possesses speed, but is not possessed of beauty, nor is he possessed of physical stature and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a wild colt endowed with speed and endowed with beauty, but not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned on the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he answers and does not falter;
this, I say, is praise for him.
Yet, he is not a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his lack of excellence in height and girth.
Thus, monks, a wild colt of a man is endowed with speed and endowed with beauty, but not endowed with excellence in height and girth.
And how, monks, is a wild colt of a man endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with excellence in height and girth?
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ …pe… he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned regarding the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he answers and does not falter.”
This, I say, is his excellence of complexion.
Furthermore, he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his excellence of stature and proportion.
"In this way, monks, a person who is like a wild colt is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with height and girth.
These, monks, are the three persons who are like wild colts.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.141 14. Yodhājīva-vagga Assaparassa-sutta (The Good and Bad Horses) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of horses. What three? The horse that, when struck by a whip, runs backward; the horse that, when struck by a whip, stands its ground; and the horse that, when struck by a whip, runs forward. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of horses. So too, bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons who resemble horses. What three? The person who, when struck by a goad, runs backward; the person who, when struck by a goad, stands his ground; and the person who, when struck by a goad, runs forward. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who, when struck by a goad, runs backward? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is reproved by his fellow monks for some fault, he becomes angry and resentful, and he speaks in retaliation. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who, when struck by a goad, runs backward. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who, when struck by a goad, stands his ground? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is reproved by his fellow monks for some fault, he does not become angry or resentful, nor does he speak in retaliation; rather, he reflects: ‘This is indeed a loss for me, that my fellow monks reprove me for a fault. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who, when struck by a goad, stands his ground. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who, when struck by a goad, runs forward? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is reproved by his fellow monks for some fault, he reflects: ‘It is truly well for me that my fellow monks reprove me for a fault. This will lead to my restraint in the future. He trains himself accordingly. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who, when struck by a goad, runs forward. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of persons who resemble horses.”
“Monks, I will teach you about three kinds of thoroughbred horses and three kinds of thoroughbred persons.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of excellent horses?
In this case, monks, a certain noble steed possesses speed, but is not endowed with beauty nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
In this case, monks, another noble steed possesses speed and is endowed with beauty, but is not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
In this case, monks, yet another noble steed possesses speed, is endowed with beauty, and is also endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
“Monks, these are the three excellent horses.
And what, monks, are the three excellent persons?
Here, monks, a certain excellent person possesses speed, but is not possessed of beauty, nor possessed of the right proportions of height and girth.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain noble steed of a man is endowed with speed and endowed with beauty, but not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain noble steed of a man is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
And how, monks, is a noble steed of a man endowed with speed, but not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?"
"Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This, I say, is his speed.
But when questioned on a matter of higher Dhamma or higher Discipline, he falters and does not answer."
This, I say, is not his excellence in appearance.
Furthermore, he does not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is not his excellence in stature and girth. In this way, monks, a person who is like a thoroughbred horse possesses speed.
He is neither endowed with beauty nor endowed with height and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a thoroughbred horse endowed with speed and endowed with beauty, but not endowed with height and girth?
Here, monks, a monk, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned on a matter concerning the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he provides an answer and does not falter.
This, I say, is his beauty.
Furthermore, he does not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his lack of excellence in stature and girth.
Thus, monks, a person who is like a fine steed possesses speed and beauty, but lacks excellence in stature and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a noble steed endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?
Here, monks, a monk, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned on the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he provides an answer and does not falter.
This, I say, is his excellence.
Moreover, he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his excellence of height and girth.
Thus, monks, a noble steed among men is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with excellence of height and girth.
These, monks, are the three types of noble steeds among men.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.143 14. Yodhājīva-vagga First Discourse on the Deer-Feeding Ground “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a deer-feeding ground near a village or town. It would be well-grazed, well-watered, and free from danger and predators. Then a deer, having wandered about for many days, might enter that deer-feeding ground.

Having entered it, he would eat the grass, drink the water, and find no danger or predators. He would emerge from the deer-feeding ground and return to the forest. Then, bhikkhus, a hunter would set out from the village or town toward that deer-feeding ground. On the way, he would see the tracks of the deer’s footprints. Seeing them, he would think: ‘The deer has surely entered this deer-feeding ground; having entered it, he will eat the grass, drink the water, and find no danger or predators. He will emerge from the deer-feeding ground and return to the forest. Having reached the deer-feeding ground, the hunter would see the grass eaten and the water disturbed. Seeing this, he would think: ‘The deer has surely entered this deer-feeding ground; having entered it, he will eat the grass, drink the water, and find no danger or predators. He will emerge from the deer-feeding ground and return to the forest. Then, bhikkhus, the hunter would set a snare at the entrance to the deer-feeding ground. After setting the snare, he would hide nearby. Then the deer, wandering about for many days, might enter that deer-feeding ground. Having entered it, he would eat the grass, drink the water, and find no danger or predators. He would emerge from the deer-feeding ground and, while emerging, he would be caught in the snare set by the hunter. Now, bhikkhus, what do you think? Would that deer, being wise, reflect thus: ‘It is better for me to remain right here in this deer-feeding ground, where I have eaten grass, drunk water, and found no danger or predators, rather than go back to the forest’? “No, venerable sir. “Would he reflect thus: ‘It is better for me to go back to the forest, even if I must die there, rather than remain here in this deer-feeding ground’? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is subject to death, liable to death, and has not transcended death, he should reflect thus: ‘It is better for me to live the holy life under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, even if I must die while doing so, rather than live the household life, which is full of suffering and filled with despair. Therefore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is subject to death, liable to death, and has not transcended death, he should train himself thus: ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, even if I must die while doing so, rather than live the household life, which is full of suffering and filled with despair.’”

There, a peacock would eat the grain and drink the water. Then, as it was time for that peacock to go to its feeding ground, a hunter would set a snare at the place where the peacock usually goes.
