Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.155 15. Maṅgalavagga Pubbaṇhasutta (The Forenoon Discourse) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a forenoon lotus, the person who is like a midday lotus, and the person who is like an evening lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a forenoon lotus? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. Just as a forenoon lotus is blooming, open, and radiant, so too is this noble disciple called a person like a forenoon lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a midday lotus? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha… in the Dhamma… in the Saṅgha… and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones… leading to concentration. Just as a midday lotus is fully blossomed, open, and radiant, so too is this noble disciple called a person like a midday lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like an evening lotus? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha… in the Dhamma… in the Saṅgha… and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones… leading to concentration. Just as an evening lotus is blooming, open, and radiant, so too is this noble disciple called a person like an evening lotus. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, those beings who, in the morning,

“Bhikkhus, those beings who in the evening time engage in good conduct by body, engage in good conduct by speech, and engage in good conduct by mind—for those beings, bhikkhus, the evening is auspicious.
It is a lucky star, a lucky omen; it is a fortunate dawn and a fortunate rising.”

well-offered [gifts] to those who lead the holy life;

16. The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga).
“Bhikkhus, there are these three ways of practice.”
Which three?
The extreme practice, the scorching practice, and the middle practice.
And what, monks, is the extreme practice?
In this case, monks, a certain person holds such a doctrine and such a view:
"There is no fault in sensual pleasures.
He thus falls into the habit of indulging in sensual pleasures.
This, monks, is called the way that is sunken.
And what, monks, is the way that is parched?

Here, monks, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands; he does not come when asked, nor stay when asked; he accepts nothing brought to him, nothing specially prepared for him, nor an invitation.
Thus, he does not accept [food] from the mouth of a jar, nor from the mouth of a basket;

not when there is a sheep between, nor a staff between, nor a pestle between; not from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman who has gone into a man’s presence, nor from groups, nor where a dog is waiting, nor where flies are swarming.
He eats no fish, no meat, no wine, no liquor, and he drinks no grain-beverage.
He is a one-house seeker or a one-meal eater; or he is a two-house seeker or a two-meal eater... or he is a seven-house seeker or a seven-meal eater;
he subsists on a single gift, or he subsists on two gifts... or he subsists on as many as seven gifts.

He takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days... or he takes food once every seven days; thus, in such a manner, he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even for as long as half a month.

He becomes one who eats only greens, or one who eats millet, or one who eats wild rice, or one who eats the *daddula* grain, or one who eats horse-gram, or one who eats the husks of grain, or one who eats the scum of boiled rice, or one who eats oil-cake.
He becomes one who eats grass, he becomes one who eats cow dung; he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of its own accord.

He wears hemp garments, he wears flaxen garments, he wears shrouds from a cemetery, he wears rag-robes, he wears bark garments, he wears antelope skins, he wears strips of antelope skin, and he wears garments made of kusa grass.
He wears garments of bark, he wears garments of wood-shavings, he wears a blanket of human hair, he wears a blanket of animal hair,
he wears a cloak of owl feathers;
he is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard.
He is one who stands continuously, refusing seats;
he is one who squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting;
he is one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading his sleep upon a bed of thorns.
He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time at evening;
thus, he dwells devoted to such various forms of the practice of mortifying and tormenting the body.
This, monks, is called the parched way of practice.
And what, monks, is the middle way of practice?

Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; [he dwells] contemplating feelings as feelings... [and so on].
He dwells contemplating mind in the mind … and phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This, monks, is called the middle way of practice.
"These, monks, are the three ways of practice.
there are these three ways of practice."
What are the three?
The extreme practice, the scorching practice, and the middle practice.
And what, bhikkhus, is the extreme practice? …pe…
This, monks, is called the intense practice.
And what, monks, is the emaciated practice? ... [as before] ...
This, monks, is called the emaciated practice.
And what, monks, is the middle way of practice?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development,
and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen… He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving.

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the volitional formations of striving …pe… he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of mind and the volitional formations of striving …pe… he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of striving …pe….
He develops the faculty of faith … he develops the faculty of energy … he develops the faculty of mindfulness …
He develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom … [and so on] … He develops the power of faith …
He develops the power of energy … he develops the power of mindfulness … he develops the power of concentration …
He develops the power of wisdom … [as before] … He develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor … he develops the investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor …
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …
He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity … [and so on] … He develops right view …
He develops right intention … he develops right speech … he develops right action …
He develops right livelihood … he develops right effort … he develops right mindfulness …
“He develops right concentration….
This, monks, is called the middle way.
These, monks, are the three ways.”
The Sixth Chapter: On the Naked Ascetics.
Its summary verse:
Mindfulness-establishment and right exertion,
And by means of the bases of psychic power and the faculties;
one should apply the powers, the factors of enlightenment,
and the path to the practice.

“Bhikkhus, one who possesses three qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
What are the three?
One is a destroyer of life oneself, one incites others to destroy life, and one approves of the destruction of life. Possessing these three qualities, one is deposited in hell as if carried there.”
“Monks, one who possesses these three qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.

Which three?”
He himself abstains from taking life, he encourages others to abstain from taking life, and he approves of abstaining from taking life...
He himself takes what is not given, he encourages others to take what is not given, and he approves of taking what is not given...
He himself abstains from taking what is not given, he encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given, and he approves of abstaining from taking what is not given... [and so forth].

“Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge of lust, three things are to be developed.

“Bhikkhus, for direct knowledge of lust, these three things are to be developed: emptiness concentration, signless concentration, and desireless concentration.
(…) For full understanding of lust, bhikkhus, (…)”
for the complete destruction … for the abandoning … for the exhaustion …
for the fading away of desire … for dispassion … for cessation …
For the sake of relinquishment … for the sake of renunciation, these three things are to be developed. For the sake of hatred … [the same applies].
of delusion … of anger … of resentment …
Of hypocrisy … of spite … of envy …
of stinginess … of deceit … of guile …
of arrogance … of contentiousness … of conceit …
of overweening pride … of intoxication … of negligence …
for direct knowledge ...
for full understanding ...
for the total destruction ...

for the destruction...
for the passing away...
for the sake of dispassion … for the sake of cessation … for the sake of relinquishment …
“For the sake of relinquishment, these three things are to be developed.

Its summary verse is:
Passion, hatred, and delusion—
Anger and enmity as the fifth;
then hypocrisy, spite, envy,
stinginess, deceit, and fraud.
Arrogance, conceit, and pride,
as well as intoxication and negligence— these seventeen are thus described.
These [verses] are based on the drinking of passion;
they are [taught] by means of a simile,
through a footprint, and through direct knowledge.
Through full understanding, through complete destruction,
through abandoning, through wasting away, and through passing away; [there comes] dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment.
These ten [factors] pertain to relinquishment:
the void, the signless,
and the desireless— these three;
The series beginning with "rooted in concentration" is established even in these [terms].
The third fifty-section concludes.
The Pāḷi of the Tika-nipāta is concluded.
